dose.standard: Outpatient diabetes/HF/CKD dosing is indication-specific; inpatient continuation requires acute illness review.

renalAdj.regimen: Review eligibility and temporary hold during AKI, dehydration, sepsis, surgery, or poor intake
Hold during ketoacidosis or high-risk fasting states

sideEffects: Dose- or exposure-related toxicity in vulnerable patients
publicNotes: SGLT2 inhibitors are high-yield sick-day medicines: pause during acute illness, dehydration, surgery, or ketoacidosis concern.

drugs.name: Daptomycin
drugs.pkpd: Concentration-dependent (Cmax/MIC). Once-daily dosing essential. NOT for pneumonia — inactivated by pulmonary surfactant (critical failure mode).
drugs.mechanism: Inserts Ca²⁺-dependent into bacterial membrane → channel formation → rapid membrane depolarisation → bactericidal.
drugs.spectrum: MRSA, VRE, Enterococcus, S. pneumoniae. Excellent bactericidal activity vs. Gram+. NOT Gram-negative organisms. NOT for lung infections.

dose.standard: BSI/Endocarditis: 6–10 mg/kg IV q24h; Skin/SSTI: 4–6 mg/kg q24h

renalAdj.regimen: Standard dose q24h
6 mg/kg q48h
6 mg/kg q48h; when possible administer after completion of HD on dialysis days

sideEffects: Myopathy / rhabdomyolysis (CK elevation — dose-dependent; most important ADR)
Eosinophilic pneumonitis (rare — fever + new pulmonary infiltrates on daptomycin)
monitoring: CK weekly — stop if >5× ULN with symptoms or >10× ULN regardless
Review statins: consider temporary suspension or use enhanced CK/symptom monitoring when continuation is clinically important
publicNotes: Daptomycin should not be used for pneumonia because surfactant inactivates it
Weekly CK monitoring and statin review are important because myotoxicity is a major toxicity

references.text: IDSA Infective Endocarditis Guidelines — Baddour et al., Circulation 2015

drugs.name: Dexamethasone
drugs.pkpd: Potent, long-acting glucocorticoid with minimal mineralocorticoid activity. Biologic effects outlast plasma exposure, so cumulative dose and taper planning matter.
drugs.mechanism: Activates glucocorticoid receptors to suppress inflammatory gene transcription, capillary permeability, and immune activation.
drugs.spectrum: Cerebral edema, selected severe inflammatory or allergic disorders, antiemetic protocols, and other indication-specific corticosteroid regimens.

dose.standard: Indication-specific. Cerebral edema label regimen: 10 mg IV initially, then 4 mg q6h with reduction after response. Many acute inflammatory indications use 4–8 mg IV/IM initially.
dose.loading: Confirm indication, equivalent glucocorticoid exposure, intended duration, and taper before repeated dosing.

renalAdj.regimen: No routine renal dose adjustment
Dose is response-based; monitor cumulative toxicity rather than applying a CrCl formula

sideEffects: Insomnia, agitation, mood change, or psychosis
Infection risk and masking of infection
publicNotes: Dexamethasone has minimal mineralocorticoid effect and is not interchangeable milligram-for-milligram with hydrocortisone or methylprednisolone
Repeated or prolonged therapy needs an explicit stop or taper plan
Use narrative pregnancy and lactation risk information rather than historical letter categories

drugs.name: Dexmedetomidine
drugs.pkpd: Ward-reference summary focused on safety review, renal handling, and monitoring rather than exhaustive prescribing.
drugs.mechanism: See class-specific pharmacology; use this entry as a deterministic bedside safety reminder.
drugs.spectrum: General internal medicine ward reference and medication-lab safety rule support.

dose.standard: ICU sedation dosing is titrated to sedation target and hemodynamic tolerance.

renalAdj.regimen: No renal adjustment; hepatic impairment and frailty may require lower dosing
Reduce or stop when clinically significant

sideEffects: Dose- or exposure-related toxicity in vulnerable patients
publicNotes: Dexmedetomidine can preserve respiratory drive but bradycardia and hypotension often decide whether it is tolerated.

drugs.name: Dextrose 10% in Water (D10W)
drugs.pkpd: Hypertonic in the bag; glucose uptake and metabolism leave electrolyte-free water. Each 500 mL bag supplies 50 g of labelled dextrose. This is not a balanced maintenance fluid.
drugs.mechanism: Supplies glucose and water without added sodium or potassium. Infusion volume and glucose delivery must be considered together.
drugs.spectrum: Water and calorie supply; hypoglycemia when intravenous glucose is indicated.

dose.standard: Adult hypoglycemia requiring IV treatment — JBDS 2023: 200 mL of D10W (20 g glucose) IV over 15 minutes. Recheck glucose after 10 minutes; repeat treatment if still below 4.0 mmol/L (72 mg/dL). Once recovered and safe to swallow, give longer-acting carbohydrate; reassess the cause and recurrence risk.
dose.Other IV uses: Individualize the rate and volume to glucose response, fluid allowance and the indication-specific protocol. The 500 mL bag is a presentation, not a default dose.

renalAdj.regimen: No fixed CrCl-based dose. In renal or cardiac failure, minimize the required fluid volume and reassess glucose, electrolytes and fluid balance.

sideEffects: Potassium and phosphate depletion with prolonged glucose administration
monitoring: Serum sodium, potassium and phosphate as clinically indicated
publicNotes: D10W contains glucose in water, not saline. Set the prescribed volume so the whole 500 mL bag is not inadvertently given as a rescue dose.

500 mL products: Otsuka 滴舒樂 and Nang Kuang Gitose 吉多士. Gitose specifies dextrose monohydrate; the Otsuka insert does not specify hydration. Amounts shown follow each label, not an anhydrous conversion.

references.text: Taiwan Otsuka — Dextrose Injection 10%, product information
Otsuka Dextrose 10% — Taiwan manufacturer insert (100 mg/mL)
Nang Kuang Gitose 5% / 10% — Taiwan manufacturer insert (10%: 100 mg/mL dextrose monohydrate)
JBDS 01, January 2023 — adult inpatient hypoglycemia, IV treatment (pp. 15–17)
DailyMed — dextrose injection, US label (general IV precautions; not Taiwan product specifications)

drugs.name: Dextrose 5% + 0.9% NaCl (D5NS)
drugs.pkpd: Hypertonic in the bag (560 mOsm/L). Supplies isotonic saline plus dextrose calories; after glucose metabolism, the remaining effective tonicity is that of normal saline.
drugs.mechanism: Provides sodium/chloride replacement together with dextrose calories. Unlike Taita No. 5, this generic bag does not contain potassium, magnesium, phosphate, or acetate.
drugs.spectrum: Maintenance or replacement fluid when both saline and dextrose are desired, peri-procedural background fluids, and selected inpatient maintenance plans where a plain saline-dextrose bag is preferred.

dose.standard: Maintenance: individualize to sodium and glucose goals; common adult background rates are 75–125 mL/h, but it is not a preferred rapid resuscitation bolus fluid

renalAdj.regimen: Monitor glucose and sodium/chloride daily
Reduce rate if fluid-sensitive; monitor Na⁺ and glucose closely
Use cautiously because sodium/water overload can occur; reassess need frequently

sideEffects: Hypernatremia or hyperchloremia if sodium delivery exceeds needs
Less suitable for large resuscitation volumes because of glucose load and hypertonicity in the bag
monitoring: Whether a balanced crystalloid or a non-dextrose fluid would better fit the current goal
publicNotes: Generic D5NS is distinct from Taita No. 5
Use it when you want plain saline plus dextrose, without extra potassium, magnesium, phosphate, or acetate

drugs.name: Dextrose 5% in Water (D5W)
drugs.pkpd: Hypotonic (isotonic in bag, but after glucose metabolism → effective free water). Distributes throughout TBW (2/3 ICF, 1/3 ECF). NOT a volume expander. Provides 170 kcal/L (glucose 50g/L).
drugs.mechanism: After glucose metabolism provides free water + calories. No lasting intravascular volume expansion. Useful to prevent hypoglycaemia during insulin infusion or supply free water in hypernatraemia.
drugs.spectrum: Hypernatraemia treatment (free water replacement), prevent hypoglycaemia in DKA when glucose <250 mg/dL (co-infuse with NS or as D5-0.45% NS), drug diluent (amiodarone, potassium infusions, vasopressors), parenteral caloric support (hypoglycaemic states).

dose.standard: Hypernatraemia: free water deficit = 0.6 × weight × (Na/140 – 1); correct at ≤0.5–1 mEq/L/h Na (max 10–12 mEq/L per 24h); DKA transition: start when glucose <250 mg/dL — infuse D5-0.45% NS alongside insulin drip

renalAdj.regimen: Monitor glucose Q4–6h; fluid balance; Na⁺

sideEffects: Hyperglycaemia (especially DM, sepsis, critical illness — Q4–6h glucose monitoring)
Hyponatraemia (dilutional — avoid as standard maintenance; risk ↑ in SIADH, post-operative, paediatrics)
Volume overload (less than isotonic fluids but possible with large volumes)
monitoring: Serum Na⁺ (rate and direction of correction in hypernatraemia)
publicNotes: D5W is not a resuscitation fluid because it provides no sustained intravascular expansion
Add dextrose during DKA management once glucose falls to avoid hypoglycemia while insulin continues
Use D5W for free-water replacement and for drugs that are specifically incompatible with saline

drugs.name: Dextrose 50%
drugs.pkpd: Ward-reference summary focused on safety review, renal handling, and monitoring rather than exhaustive prescribing.
drugs.mechanism: See class-specific pharmacology; use this entry as a deterministic bedside safety reminder.
drugs.spectrum: General internal medicine ward reference and medication-lab safety rule support.

dose.standard: Rescue dosing is protocol-based.

renalAdj.regimen: No renal adjustment; reassess cause and recurrence risk

sideEffects: Dose- or exposure-related toxicity in vulnerable patients
publicNotes: Treats the number quickly; the cognitive task is preventing recurrence.

drugs.name: Diazepam
drugs.pkpd: Rapid onset with high lipid solubility gives fast CNS penetration and anticonvulsant effect, but its long elimination half-life (and active metabolites) means sedation can outlast the anticonvulsant effect — do not mistake ongoing sedation for ongoing seizure control, or the reverse.
drugs.mechanism: Potentiates GABA-A receptor activity, increasing chloride conductance and raising the seizure threshold; also produces sedation, anxiolysis, and muscle relaxation.
drugs.spectrum: First-line benzodiazepine for convulsive status epilepticus when lorazepam is unavailable, and for anxiolysis, muscle spasm, and alcohol-withdrawal protocols.

dose.standard: Status epilepticus: 0.15–0.2 mg/kg IV, maximum 10 mg per dose; may repeat once after 5 minutes if the seizure continues

renalAdj.regimen: No renal dose adjustment needed for acute seizure dosing
Active metabolites accumulate in hepatic impairment; expect prolonged sedation and use with caution

sideEffects: Respiratory depression, especially with repeat dosing or in combination with another sedating drug
Sedation that can outlast the anticonvulsant effect
monitoring: Airway, respiratory rate, and oxygenation after every dose
Seizure activity and level of consciousness
Cumulative benzodiazepine exposure if additional sedating agents are given
publicNotes: Shorter anticonvulsant duration than lorazepam despite a longer sedative half-life — a patient can still be at seizure risk after the sedation seems to be wearing off, or still deeply sedated after the anticonvulsant effect has ended
Have airway equipment and reversal readiness available whenever treating active seizures with a benzodiazepine

references.text: American Epilepsy Society — Guideline for Treatment of Prolonged Seizures

drugs.name: Diclofenac (Voltaren)
drugs.pkpd: PO standard-release: onset 30–60 min, peak 2h, duration 6–8h. Slow-release (SR/XR): 75–100 mg, duration 12–24h. IM: onset 20–30 min. Topical gel: minimal systemic absorption (<10%).
drugs.mechanism: Non-selective COX inhibitor with preferential COX-2 selectivity (among highest selectivity of tNSAIDs) → highest CV thrombotic risk. Inhibits phospholipase A₂ additionally. Highest hepatotoxicity risk of common NSAIDs.
drugs.spectrum: OA, RA, acute musculoskeletal pain (IM for rapid effect), renal/biliary colic (IM), dysmenorrhoea, postoperative pain. Topical gel: OA of hands and knees (minimises systemic exposure in elderly).

dose.standard: PO: 50 mg TID or 75 mg SR BID (with food); IM: 75 mg once (max 2 days IM); Topical 1% gel: 2–4 g QID to affected joint (hands/knees — use dosing card)

renalAdj.regimen: Standard; shortest effective course
Lowest effective dose; monitor closely; prefer topical route
AVOID systemic; topical has minimal renal risk (acceptable with monitoring)

sideEffects: Hepatotoxicity: highest among common NSAIDs — LFT elevation in ~15% (usually transient); rare fulminant hepatic failure; monitor LFTs with prolonged use
CV risk: highest CV thrombotic risk among common NSAIDs (COX-2 preferential — similar to celecoxib); avoid in established CV disease
GI: moderate risk (better than indomethacin, similar to ibuprofen)
monitoring: LFTs (baseline; recheck if symptomatic or >4 weeks use)
publicNotes: Topical diclofenac is useful when you want local NSAID effect with less systemic exposure
Oral and IM diclofenac carry comparatively higher cardiovascular and hepatic risk than many alternatives

references.text: FDA Safety Communication — NSAID Cardiovascular and GI Risks (2015)

drugs.name: Digoxin
drugs.pkpd: Narrow therapeutic index with major renal dependence and clinically important electrolyte sensitivity. Toxicity is often a combined problem of kidney function, potassium status, interacting drugs, and tissue vulnerability rather than a single number alone.
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits Na+/K+-ATPase, indirectly increasing intracellular calcium and vagal tone; this can improve symptoms in selected HF patients and slow AV nodal conduction in atrial arrhythmias.
drugs.spectrum: Selected HFrEF symptom support and atrial fibrillation rate control when other agents are not enough or are poorly tolerated.

dose.standard: Indication-specific and conservative. Chronic maintenance often uses 0.125 mg daily or less; loading, if used, is specialized and should account for age, renal function, and interacting drugs

renalAdj.regimen: Low-dose maintenance may be acceptable, but start conservatively and avoid assuming standard daily dosing is harmless
Lower maintenance dosing or alternate-day dosing is often needed
Use very cautious individualized dosing with level-guided follow-up because accumulation risk is high

sideEffects: Visual disturbance such as yellow vision or halos
monitoring: Serum digoxin level when clinically indicated or toxicity is suspected
Interaction review, especially amiodarone and verapamil
publicNotes: A “normal” digoxin level does not overrule clear toxicity if the patient is bradycardic, symptomatic, and clinically exposed to accumulation risks
Whenever digoxin seems suddenly problematic, check kidney function, potassium, and whether amiodarone or another interaction changed recently

drugs.name: Diltiazem
drugs.pkpd: AV-nodal slowing and vasodilation. IV onset is rapid; continuous ECG and blood-pressure monitoring are required because bradycardia and hypotension can evolve quickly.
drugs.mechanism: Blocks L-type calcium channels in myocardium, AV nodal tissue, and vascular smooth muscle, slowing conduction and reducing contractility and vascular tone.
drugs.spectrum: Temporary ventricular-rate control in atrial fibrillation/flutter, conversion of selected PSVT, chronic rate control, and selected angina/hypertension indications.

dose.standard: IV rate control: 0.25 mg/kg actual body weight over 2 min; if inadequate after 15 min, 0.35 mg/kg over 2 min. Begin infusion 5 mg/h and titrate by 5 mg/h to maximum 15 mg/h as needed and tolerated.
dose.loading: Do not use IV diltiazem for AF/flutter with an accessory pathway such as WPW; verify rhythm, BP, ventricular function, and other AV-nodal blockers.

renalAdj.regimen: No routine renal dose adjustment
Use cautious titration because hepatic metabolism and hemodynamic sensitivity may increase toxicity

sideEffects: Worsening heart failure or negative inotropy
monitoring: Continuous ECG and frequent BP with IV use
Concurrent beta-blocker, digoxin, or other AV-nodal blocker use
publicNotes: Avoid IV diltiazem in pre-excited AF/flutter and use caution in hemodynamic compromise or significant systolic dysfunction
Immediate-release and extended-release oral products are not automatically interchangeable
Use narrative pregnancy/lactation information rather than historical letter categories

drugs.name: Diosmectite (Smecta)
drugs.pkpd: Remains in the intestinal lumen, is not absorbed or metabolized, and is eliminated in stool. Its adsorbent action can also delay or reduce absorption of other oral medicines.
drugs.mechanism: A layered natural clay with adsorbent and mucosal-coating properties that can reduce stool output as an adjunct to rehydration; it does not correct the cause of dehydration or invasive diarrhoea.
drugs.spectrum: Regional symptomatic adjunct for acute diarrhoea and selected functional intestinal symptoms. This entry follows the cited French Smecta 3 g powder label; indications, age limits, excipients, and availability differ by country and product.

dose.standard: Cited Smecta 3 g label: adults with acute diarrhoea average 1 sachet (3 g) PO three times daily for 7 days; the daily dose may be doubled at treatment initiation. Suspend each sachet just before use. Rehydration remains primary therapy. Verify the local product label before use.
dose.loading: No resuscitation role. Oral or IV rehydration and evaluation of red flags must not be delayed by adsorbent therapy.

renalAdj.regimen: The cited label gives no kidney-function dosing table; diosmectite remains luminal and is not absorbed.
Do not let the absence of systemic dosing obscure the clinical priority: assess dehydration, electrolytes, renal perfusion, and need for oral or IV rehydration.

sideEffects: Severe constipation or bezoar with overdose
monitoring: Hydration status and ability to take oral rehydration
Diarrhoea red flags and underlying cause
Constipation, especially with prior severe chronic constipation
Timing of every other oral medicine
publicNotes: Diosmectite is adjunctive: oral rehydration is the core treatment for acute diarrhoea
Give other oral medicines separately—more than 2 hours apart if possible—because adsorption may reduce or delay absorption
The cited product should be avoided in children under 2 years; pediatric use over age 2 is short-course and must accompany early oral rehydration
Country and product labels differ, including pediatric cutoffs and pregnancy/lactation advice; verify the locally stocked formulation rather than extrapolating this French label

references.text: French Public Medicines Database (ANSM) — Smecta 3 g Product Characteristics

drugs.name: Diphenhydramine
drugs.pkpd: Rapid first-generation H1 blockade with substantial CNS penetration and antimuscarinic activity; sedation and anticholinergic toxicity are clinically important.
drugs.mechanism: Competitively blocks histamine H1 receptors and also has clinically meaningful antimuscarinic activity.
drugs.spectrum: Short-term relief of histamine-mediated allergic symptoms and selected acute reactions. It is adjunctive—not a substitute for intramuscular epinephrine—in anaphylaxis.

dose.standard: Adults: 25–50 mg PO q4–6h when appropriate (do not exceed labeled product limits). When oral therapy is impractical, label injection dosing is 10–50 mg IV or deep IM; IV rate generally must not exceed 25 mg/min. Use the lowest effective dose.

renalAdj.regimen: No established label-based renal dose adjustment.
Prefer avoidance or the lowest effective dose when possible; monitor closely for sedation, delirium, urinary retention, and falls.

sideEffects: Dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and urinary retention
monitoring: Respiratory status when combined with other CNS depressants
IV administration rate and blood pressure when parenteral therapy is used
publicNotes: Do not use diphenhydramine as the primary treatment for anaphylaxis; intramuscular epinephrine is first-line and should not be delayed.
Avoid using it simply as a hypnotic, particularly in older adults or patients with delirium, falls, glaucoma, urinary retention, or high anticholinergic burden.
Check all oral, topical, and combination products to avoid duplicate diphenhydramine exposure.

references.text: DailyMed — Diphenhydramine 25 mg Oral Capsule Drug Facts

drugs.name: Dobutamine
drugs.pkpd: Rapid-onset, short-acting inotrope administered by continuous IV infusion. Titrate to perfusion and hemodynamics rather than a fixed maintenance dose.
drugs.mechanism: Predominantly beta-1 agonism increases myocardial contractility and stroke volume, with variable beta-2 and alpha-1 vascular effects.
drugs.spectrum: Short-term inotropic support for low-output states with cardiac dysfunction when improved contractility is appropriate.

dose.standard: Start 0.5–1 mcg/kg/min IV and titrate every few minutes; usual effective range 2–20 mcg/kg/min. Higher rates are exceptional and require intensive monitoring.
dose.loading: Correct hypovolemia, hypoxia, and major acid-base abnormalities before escalating dose.

renalAdj.regimen: No fixed renal dose adjustment; titrate to perfusion and adverse effects
Use urine output, perfusion, hemodynamics, and arrhythmia burden rather than a CrCl table

sideEffects: Myocardial ischemia from increased oxygen demand
Phlebitis or tissue injury with extravasation
publicNotes: Dobutamine is not a substitute for adequate preload or correction of reversible shock physiology
Escalating dose despite worsening tachyarrhythmia can reduce effective cardiac output
Use narrative pregnancy/lactation risk information and the urgency of maternal hemodynamic support

drugs.name: Dopamine
drugs.pkpd: Dose-dependent receptor effects — lower infusion rates favor beta-1/dopaminergic activity, higher rates favor alpha-1 vasoconstriction — so the clinical effect can shift as the rate is titrated, not just its intensity.
drugs.mechanism: Endogenous catecholamine precursor acting on dopaminergic, beta-1, and (at higher doses) alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, increasing heart rate, contractility, and vascular tone.
drugs.spectrum: Alternative to transcutaneous pacing for atropine-refractory symptomatic bradycardia, and second-line vasopressor/inotrope support in selected shock states.

dose.standard: 5–20 micrograms/kg/minute IV infusion, titrated to heart rate, blood pressure, and perfusion response

renalAdj.regimen: Dose is titrated to hemodynamic response, not renal function

sideEffects: Tachyarrhythmia and increased myocardial oxygen demand
Extravasation injury/tissue necrosis with peripheral infiltration
Excessive vasoconstriction at higher doses can reduce peripheral/splanchnic perfusion
monitoring: Continuous ECG, BP, and perfusion during the infusion
IV site for extravasation, especially with peripheral administration
Taper rather than stop abruptly once hemodynamics stabilize
publicNotes: Central access is preferred for a sustained infusion; a reliable large-bore peripheral line can be used short-term while central access is obtained
Correct hypovolemia before or alongside starting an infusion rather than using dopamine to compensate for unaddressed volume depletion

drugs.name: Doxycycline
drugs.pkpd: AUC/MIC-dependent. PO bioavailability ~93% — excellent oral option. Penetrates intracellularly and into most tissue compartments.
drugs.mechanism: Binds 30S ribosomal subunit → inhibits aminoacyl-tRNA binding → bacteriostatic.
drugs.spectrum: Atypicals: Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Rickettsia, Leptospira, Borrelia. CA-MRSA SSTI (alternative). Some Acinetobacter (combination). NOT reliable GNRs, Streptococcus (in Taiwan — resistance).

dose.standard: 100 mg PO/IV BID (loading: 200 mg PO day 1)

renalAdj.regimen: No adjustment needed (fecal/biliary elimination)

sideEffects: Oesophageal ulceration (take with full glass of water; remain upright 30 min — counselling essential)
Pregnancy/young-child use is indication- and duration-specific; do not withhold doxycycline for suspected life-threatening rickettsial disease solely because of age or pregnancy
monitoring: Ensure patient remains upright 30 min after taking (prevent oesophageal damage)
publicNotes: Doxycycline is a strong oral option for atypical pathogens and several tick-borne or zoonotic infections
Take with water and stay upright afterward to reduce esophageal injury risk

references.text: IDSA SSTI Guidelines — Stevens et al., CID 2014

drugs.name: Edoxaban
drugs.pkpd: Ward-reference summary focused on safety review, renal handling, and monitoring rather than exhaustive prescribing.
drugs.mechanism: See class-specific pharmacology; use this entry as a deterministic bedside safety reminder.
drugs.spectrum: General internal medicine ward reference and medication-lab safety rule support.

dose.standard: Indication- and renal-function-specific oral dosing.

renalAdj.regimen: Dose review required
Generally avoid/review alternatives

sideEffects: Dose- or exposure-related toxicity in vulnerable patients
publicNotes: Review renal function and antiplatelet/NSAID combinations on admission and discharge.

drugs.name: Empagliflozin (Jardiance)
drugs.pkpd: Promotes glucosuria and natriuresis by blocking proximal tubular glucose-sodium reabsorption. Cardiorenal benefit often persists even when glucose-lowering effect fades at lower eGFR.
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 in the proximal tubule, reducing glucose and sodium reabsorption.
drugs.spectrum: Type 2 diabetes, heart failure, and CKD regimens where SGLT2 therapy is indicated for cardiorenal benefit as well as or instead of glycemic control.

dose.standard: 10 mg PO daily; may increase to 25 mg daily when additional glycemic lowering is desired and tolerated

renalAdj.regimen: 10 mg daily; may increase to 25 mg daily for glycemic control if tolerated and indicated
10 mg daily may still be reasonable for cardiorenal indications, but glucose-lowering effect is reduced

Avoid using it primarily for glycemic control; if the indication is heart failure or CKD, follow current labeling or specialist/institutional guidance rather than assuming routine outpatient diabetes dosing

publicNotes: The key operational safety issue is knowing when to hold it: acute illness, poor oral intake, dehydration, or upcoming surgery all raise ketoacidosis risk
Do not be reassured by a normal or only mildly elevated glucose if ketoacidosis is clinically suspected

drugs.name: Enoxaparin (Lovenox)
drugs.pkpd: Anti-factor Xa predominant activity with more predictable SC absorption than unfractionated heparin. Renally cleared, so accumulation occurs in advanced CKD.
drugs.mechanism: Low-molecular-weight heparin potentiates antithrombin, predominantly inhibiting factor Xa with less thrombin inhibition than unfractionated heparin.
drugs.spectrum: Treatment and prophylaxis of venous thromboembolism, ACS adjunct anticoagulation, bridging anticoagulation in selected patients.

dose.standard: Treatment: 1 mg/kg SC q12h or 1.5 mg/kg SC q24h; prophylaxis: 40 mg SC q24h

renalAdj.regimen: Treatment: 1 mg/kg q12h; prophylaxis: 40 mg q24h
Treatment: 1 mg/kg q24h; prophylaxis: 20–30 mg q24h per local protocol
Generally avoid routine therapeutic use without specialist guidance; consider UFH instead

sideEffects: HIT (less common than UFH but still possible)
Drug accumulation in renal impairment with supratherapeutic anti-Xa levels
monitoring: Anti-Xa level in severe renal impairment, obesity, pregnancy, or prolonged therapy when clinically needed
publicNotes: Renal impairment and thrombocytopenia are the two highest-yield safety checks before continuing enoxaparin
If HIT is a concern, do not rely on platelet count alone; review timing and thrombosis pattern

drugs.name: Epinephrine (Adrenaline)
drugs.pkpd: Very rapid onset and short duration. Alpha-1 vasoconstriction, beta-1 cardiac stimulation, and beta-2 bronchodilation make concentration, route, and titration errors especially dangerous.
drugs.mechanism: Agonist at alpha-1, alpha-2, beta-1, and beta-2 receptors, producing vasoconstriction, increased cardiac output, and bronchodilation.
drugs.spectrum: First-line emergency treatment of anaphylaxis and titratable vasopressor support for selected shock states.

dose.standard: Anaphylaxis: 0.3–0.5 mg of 1 mg/mL solution IM into the anterolateral thigh; repeat q5–10 min as needed. Septic-shock hypotension: IV infusion 0.05–2 mcg/kg/min titrated to MAP after protocol dilution.
dose.loading: Verify concentration and route aloud: 1 mg/mL IM anaphylaxis dosing is not interchangeable with diluted IV infusion preparations.

renalAdj.regimen: No renal dose adjustment; titrate to clinical response
Monitor perfusion, lactate, urine output, and ischemic complications

sideEffects: Extravasation-related tissue necrosis with IV infusion
monitoring: Continuous ECG and frequent blood pressure during IV use
Lactate interpreted with beta-adrenergic effect in mind
Response after each IM anaphylaxis dose
publicNotes: Epinephrine is first-line for anaphylaxis and should not be delayed for antihistamines or corticosteroids
Emergency epinephrine should not be withheld for anaphylaxis in pregnancy
Concentration and route confusion is a critical medication-error risk

drugs.name: Ertapenem
drugs.pkpd: Time-dependent killing. Once-daily dosing (long half-life ~4h). 95% protein-bound. NOT active vs. Pseudomonas or Acinetobacter — stewardship advantage.
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits PBPs → bactericidal. Similar to meropenem but narrower Gram-negative spectrum — lacks antipseudomonal activity.
drugs.spectrum: ESBL Enterobacteriaceae, MSSA, streptococci, anaerobes. NOT Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, Enterococcus, MRSA, Stenotrophomonas.

dose.standard: 1 g IV/IM q24h

renalAdj.regimen: 1 g q24h (standard)
500 mg q24h
500 mg q24h; supplement 150 mg after HD on dialysis days

publicNotes: Ertapenem is useful when ESBL coverage is needed but Pseudomonas coverage is not
Its once-daily dosing makes it a practical outpatient parenteral option

references.text: IDSA Intra-Abdominal Infection Guidelines — Solomkin et al., CID 2010

drugs.name: Famotidine
drugs.pkpd: Competitive histamine H2 blockade lowers acid secretion with quicker onset but less profound suppression than PPIs. A meaningful fraction is renally cleared, so accumulation matters in CKD.
drugs.mechanism: Blocks parietal-cell histamine H2 receptors, reducing basal and stimulated gastric acid secretion.
drugs.spectrum: GERD, dyspepsia, selected ulcer regimens, and lower-intensity acid suppression when a full PPI is not necessary.

dose.standard: 20 mg PO/IV BID or 40 mg PO nightly depending on indication and severity

renalAdj.regimen: Standard dose
Usual dose often acceptable, but consider lower total daily dose if prolonged therapy or CNS toxicity risk is high
Reduce dose or extend interval because accumulation can increase confusion and other adverse effects; give after dialysis if applicable

sideEffects: Confusion or delirium in elderly or advanced CKD
monitoring: Mental status in older adults or CKD
publicNotes: Famotidine is often a cleaner option than a PPI when only modest acid suppression is needed
In advanced CKD, neurocognitive adverse effects are a bigger practical issue than many people expect

drugs.name: Fentanyl
drugs.pkpd: Ward-reference summary focused on safety review, renal handling, and monitoring rather than exhaustive prescribing.
drugs.mechanism: See class-specific pharmacology; use this entry as a deterministic bedside safety reminder.
drugs.spectrum: General internal medicine ward reference and medication-lab safety rule support.

dose.standard: Dose depends heavily on route and opioid tolerance; patch is only for opioid-tolerant chronic pain.

renalAdj.regimen: No active renal metabolite, but sedation/respiratory monitoring still required

sideEffects: Dose- or exposure-related toxicity in vulnerable patients
publicNotes: Patch misuse in opioid-naive patients is dangerous; distinguish IV rescue from transdermal chronic therapy.

drugs.name: Fexofenadine (Allegra)
drugs.pkpd: Peripherally selective H1 antagonist with relatively little CNS penetration. Renal impairment increases exposure and prolongs elimination.
drugs.mechanism: Selectively blocks peripheral histamine H1 receptors, reducing histamine-mediated nasal, ocular, and cutaneous symptoms.
drugs.spectrum: Seasonal allergic rhinitis and uncomplicated skin manifestations of chronic idiopathic urticaria; it is not a treatment for anaphylaxis or bronchospasm.

dose.standard: Adults and adolescents ≥12 years: 60 mg PO BID or 180 mg PO once daily, taken with water. Use 60 mg once daily as the starting dose when renal function is decreased.

renalAdj.regimen: 60 mg BID or 180 mg once daily.

renalAdj.crcl: Decreased renal function (mild, moderate, or severe)
renalAdj.regimen: Start 60 mg once daily; reassess response and tolerability rather than using the 180 mg product.

monitoring: Administration with water and separation from aluminum- or magnesium-containing antacids
publicNotes: Take with water. Grapefruit, orange, and apple juice can reduce absorption; aluminum- or magnesium-containing antacids also reduce bioavailability.
Renal impairment requires a lower starting regimen even though fexofenadine is generally less sedating than first-generation antihistamines.
Do not use fexofenadine as a substitute for epinephrine in anaphylaxis.

references.text: DailyMed — Fexofenadine Hydrochloride Tablets Prescribing Information
FDA — Allegra Oral Suspension Prescribing Information

drugs.name: Fluconazole
drugs.pkpd: AUC/MIC-dependent. Oral bioavailability >90% (bioequivalent IV/PO). Long half-life ~30h → once-daily dosing. Good CNS, urine, peritoneal penetration.
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits CYP51 (lanosterol 14α-demethylase) → blocks ergosterol synthesis → cell membrane disruption → fungistatic.
drugs.spectrum: Candida albicans, C. tropicalis, C. parapsilosis. NOT C. krusei (intrinsic resistance), C. glabrata (variable/resistant), Aspergillus, Mucorales.

dose.standard: Candidemia: 800 mg IV/PO loading, then 400 mg q24h; Mucosal: 100–200 mg q24h × 7–14d
dose.loading: 800 mg loading dose for invasive candidiasis

renalAdj.regimen: Standard dose
50% of standard dose (single dose for vaginal candidiasis: no adjustment)
Standard dose after each dialysis session (dialysable)

sideEffects: QT prolongation (avoid with other QT-prolonging drugs)
Drug interactions: major CYP2C9/CYP3A4 inhibitor — warfarin (INR ↑↑), calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus ×2–3, cyclosporin), statins, many others
monitoring: Drug interactions — CRITICAL in transplant patients (tacrolimus levels)
Confirm species ID and susceptibility before initiating (C. glabrata/krusei → use echinocandin)
publicNotes: Fluconazole is a good IV-to-PO step-down agent when the Candida species is confirmed susceptible
Renal dose adjustment and interaction review are both essential for longer courses

references.text: IDSA Candida Guidelines — Pappas et al., CID 2016

drugs.name: Fondaparinux
drugs.pkpd: Ward-reference summary focused on safety review, renal handling, and monitoring rather than exhaustive prescribing.
drugs.mechanism: See class-specific pharmacology; use this entry as a deterministic bedside safety reminder.
drugs.spectrum: General internal medicine ward reference and medication-lab safety rule support.

dose.standard: Dose depends on prophylaxis vs treatment indication.

renalAdj.regimen: Contraindicated or avoid in many workflows due to accumulation
Use caution and monitor bleeding

sideEffects: Dose- or exposure-related toxicity in vulnerable patients
publicNotes: Fondaparinux is strongly renal-cleared; AKI should trigger medication review.

drugs.name: Fosfomycin
drugs.pkpd: Concentration-dependent (Cmax/MIC). Oral sachet: single-dose 3g achieves very high urinary concentrations (persistent >24–48h). IV form available for systemic infections (less commonly used in Taiwan).
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits MurA enzyme → blocks UDP-N-acetylmuramic acid synthesis → disrupts early peptidoglycan synthesis. Unique mechanism → no cross-resistance with other antibiotic classes.
drugs.spectrum: Uncomplicated UTI pathogens: E. coli (incl. ESBL), Enterococcus faecalis. Activity vs. MRSA (IV form, in combination). NOT Pseudomonas (variable), Klebsiella (often resistant), Proteus.

dose.standard: Uncomplicated UTI (female): 3 g PO sachet × 1 dose; Complicated UTI/systemic (IV): 8–24 g/day in divided doses (q6–8h)

renalAdj.regimen: 3g PO × 1 (standard)
Oral: consider longer course (single dose may be insufficient); IV: reduce dose
Avoid oral form for systemic coverage; HD removes fosfomycin — supplement post-dialysis if IV used

sideEffects: GI: diarrhoea, nausea, headache (oral single dose — usually mild)
Hypernatraemia (IV form — high sodium load, 1g IV = ~14 mEq Na⁺; caution in CHF/CKD)
monitoring: Urine culture susceptibility (ESBL E. coli: oral fosfomycin active for lower UTI — NOT for systemic ESBL infections)
publicNotes: Single-dose oral fosfomycin is mainly for uncomplicated lower UTI, not systemic infection
The IV formulation has a sodium load worth watching in fluid-sensitive patients

references.text: IDSA UTI Guidelines — Gupta et al., CID 2011

drugs.name: Fosphenytoin
drugs.pkpd: A water-soluble prodrug of phenytoin, dosed in phenytoin-equivalents (PE) and converted in the body over roughly 8–15 minutes; this avoids the propylene-glycol vehicle and injection-site toxicity ("purple glove syndrome") associated with IV phenytoin.
drugs.mechanism: Blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, stabilizing neuronal membranes and reducing repetitive firing, which raises the seizure threshold.
drugs.spectrum: Second-line agent for benzodiazepine-refractory convulsive status epilepticus, alongside levetiracetam and valproate.

dose.standard: 20 mg PE/kg IV, maximum 1500 mg, infused over about 10 minutes

renalAdj.regimen: No routine renal dose adjustment for the acute loading dose; hypoalbuminemia and renal/hepatic impairment affect free-phenytoin levels with ongoing use

sideEffects: Hypotension and cardiac arrhythmia with rapid infusion
Purple glove syndrome is rare with fosphenytoin compared with IV phenytoin, but injection-site reactions can still occur
Long-term use: gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, osteopenia
monitoring: Continuous cardiac and BP monitoring during infusion
Seizure activity and level of consciousness after the infusion completes
Phenytoin level and albumin if continuing therapy beyond the acute load
publicNotes: The fixed 1500 mg maximum may be relatively low (under-dosed on a per-kg basis) for patients over about 75 kg — this is a known limitation of the standard dosing cap, not a reason to exceed it without expert input
Convert to an equivalent oral phenytoin regimen — or a different agent — once the acute status-epilepticus episode is controlled

references.text: ESETT trial — Randomized Trial of Three Anticonvulsant Medications for Status Epilepticus (NEJM 2019)

drugs.name: Furosemide (Lasix)
drugs.pkpd: Rapid natriuresis with variable oral bioavailability and a brisker IV effect. Diuretic response falls when renal perfusion is poor or nephron sodium avidity is high, so escalating dose or IV strategy is often more important than sticking to one nominal dose.
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb, causing potent natriuresis, kaliuresis, and venodilation.
drugs.spectrum: Volume overload from heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, or CKD; adjunct BP control when edema is present; pulmonary edema and hyperkalemia support in selected settings.

dose.standard: PO: 20–80 mg once or twice daily, titrated to response. IV: 20–40 mg, then titrate based on prior diuretic exposure and response; higher doses are often needed in CKD or chronic loop use

renalAdj.regimen: Standard starting doses usually work, but titrate to urine output, weight, edema, and creatinine response
Higher doses are commonly required because diuretic delivery to the tubule is reduced; monitor renal function and electrolytes closely
Only useful if meaningful residual urine output remains; otherwise routine loop escalation adds little benefit

sideEffects: AKI or prerenal azotemia from overdiuresis
Ototoxicity with high-dose rapid IV use or concurrent ototoxins
publicNotes: The right furosemide dose is the dose that actually produces decongestion, not the dose that looks conservative on paper
If urine output is poor, check adherence, gut edema, renal perfusion, NSAID exposure, and whether a higher or IV dose is needed before declaring failure

drugs.name: Ganciclovir
drugs.pkpd: Time-dependent intracellular antiviral effect after phosphorylation. Predominantly renal clearance. Exposure rises quickly as renal function worsens, so dose adjustment matters early.
drugs.mechanism: Guanylate analogue phosphorylated by CMV UL97 kinase, then inhibits viral DNA polymerase UL54 and terminates viral DNA elongation.
drugs.spectrum: CMV treatment and prophylaxis. Active against HSV and VZV with less routine use than acyclovir-family agents. No bacterial coverage.

dose.standard: Induction: 5 mg/kg IV q12h; maintenance: 5 mg/kg IV q24h

renalAdj.regimen: 5 mg/kg q12h induction; 5 mg/kg q24h maintenance
2.5 mg/kg q12h induction; 2.5 mg/kg q24h maintenance
2.5 mg/kg q24h induction; 1.25 mg/kg q24h maintenance
1.25 mg/kg q24h induction; 0.625 mg/kg q24h maintenance
Specialist/pharmacy-guided post-HD dosing only

sideEffects: AKI if overdosed in renal impairment
monitoring: CBC with differential at least twice weekly during induction
Review concurrent marrow-suppressive drugs (mycophenolate, TMP-SMX, valganciclovir, chemotherapy)
publicNotes: Renal adjustment is essential because toxicity increases rapidly when kidney function declines
ANC and platelet trends are often the deciding factor in whether therapy can continue

drugs.name: Gentamicin
drugs.pkpd: Concentration-dependent (Cmax/MIC target ≥8–10×MIC) + prolonged post-antibiotic effect. Once-daily extended-interval dosing preferred (maximizes Cmax, exploits PAE, reduces nephrotoxicity).
drugs.mechanism: Binds 30S ribosomal subunit → mistranslation + bactericidal (irreversible membrane damage). Requires aerobic conditions — NOT active vs. anaerobes or in acidic/anaerobic abscesses.
drugs.spectrum: Most Gram-negative rods (Enterobacteriaceae, Pseudomonas). Synergy with cell-wall-active agents (ampicillin + gentamicin for enterococcal endocarditis). NOT reliable alone for Streptococcus or Staphylococcus.

dose.standard: Extended-interval: 5–7 mg/kg IV q24h (Hartford nomogram); Synergy: 1 mg/kg IV q8h
dose.loading: 5–7 mg/kg IV (single loading dose for extended-interval)

renalAdj.crcl: Normal or mildly reduced renal function
renalAdj.regimen: Use institutional extended-interval or traditional dosing protocol with serum-level monitoring rather than a fixed one-line schedule
Individualize dose and interval with pharmacy/TDM guidance; official labeling uses reduced-dose or prolonged-interval approaches based on renal function
Modality-specific, post-dialysis or level-guided dosing only; do not rely on a single empiric regimen across dialysis strategies

sideEffects: Nephrotoxicity (dose- and duration-dependent; potentiated by vancomycin, NSAIDs, contrast — avoid combinations)
Ototoxicity: cochlear (irreversible high-frequency hearing loss) + vestibular (ataxia, oscillopsia)
Neuromuscular blockade (rare — myasthenia gravis patients: use with caution)
monitoring: Extended-interval: 6–14h post-dose random level (Hartford nomogram) or peak/trough per protocol
publicNotes: Extended-interval dosing is usually preferred for gentamicin when clinically appropriate
Use level-guided dosing and watch renal and vestibular toxicity closely

references.text: Aminoglycoside TDM — Nicolau et al., Antimicrob Agents Chemother 1995

drugs.name: Gliclazide
drugs.pkpd: Ward-reference summary focused on safety review, renal handling, and monitoring rather than exhaustive prescribing.
drugs.mechanism: See class-specific pharmacology; use this entry as a deterministic bedside safety reminder.
drugs.spectrum: General internal medicine ward reference and medication-lab safety rule support.

dose.standard: Oral dosing should be conservative and reconciled against meals and hypoglycemia history.

renalAdj.regimen: Hypoglycemia risk rises with reduced clearance or poor intake; hold or reduce during acute illness
Hold while intake is unreliable

sideEffects: Dose- or exposure-related toxicity in vulnerable patients
publicNotes: Sulfonylureas are common hidden causes of inpatient hypoglycemia when appetite changes.

renalAdj.regimen: Start low or avoid during acute illness; hypoglycemia risk increases

sideEffects: Dose- or exposure-related toxicity in vulnerable patients

drugs.name: Glucagon
drugs.pkpd: Ward-reference summary focused on safety review, renal handling, and monitoring rather than exhaustive prescribing.
drugs.mechanism: See class-specific pharmacology; use this entry as a deterministic bedside safety reminder.

renalAdj.regimen: No renal adjustment

sideEffects: Dose- or exposure-related toxicity in vulnerable patients
publicNotes: Effect may be limited when glycogen stores are depleted.

drugs.name: Glycerin Suppository
drugs.pkpd: Onset: 15–30 min after rectal insertion. Acts locally — minimal systemic absorption. Softens hardened stool and lubricates rectal vault.
drugs.mechanism: Hyperosmotic agent → draws water into rectal lumen → softens stool. Direct lubricant action. Mild rectal mucosal irritation → reflex peristalsis.
drugs.spectrum: Acute constipation (especially hard, impacted stool in distal rectum), post-operative constipation, constipation in elderly or post-partum patients, faecal impaction as initial adjunct.

dose.standard: Adult: 1 suppository (2–3 g) PR; insert pointed end first; retain as long as possible; onset 15–30 min; may repeat once after 30 min if no effect

renalAdj.regimen: No adjustment needed (local rectal action only)

publicNotes: Glycerin suppositories have minimal systemic absorption and are often a low-risk option for rapid rectal relief of constipation
Pregnant patients should still follow product labeling and clinician advice rather than assuming unrestricted use
Ideal for acute symptomatic relief when oral laxatives would take too long (need effect within 15–60 min)

drugs.name: Haloperidol
drugs.pkpd: Ward-reference summary focused on safety review, renal handling, and monitoring rather than exhaustive prescribing.
drugs.mechanism: See class-specific pharmacology; use this entry as a deterministic bedside safety reminder.
drugs.spectrum: General internal medicine ward reference and medication-lab safety rule support.

dose.standard: Use the lowest effective dose; route and monitoring depend on agitation/delirium context.

renalAdj.regimen: No renal dose formula, but frailty and QT/electrolytes drive safety

sideEffects: Dose- or exposure-related toxicity in vulnerable patients
publicNotes: QT and electrolyte review matters before repeated dosing.

drugs.name: Hartmann's / Lactated Ringer's
drugs.pkpd: Near-isotonic (273 mOsm/L). Composition: Na⁺ 130, K⁺ 4, Ca²⁺ 3, Cl⁻ 109, lactate 28 mEq/L. Lactate metabolised → bicarbonate in liver (mild buffering). Closer to plasma composition than NS.
drugs.mechanism: Balanced crystalloid expands ECF with less hyperchloraemic acidosis than NS. Ca²⁺ content → incompatible with blood products and certain IV medications (check before co-infusion).
drugs.spectrum: First-line resuscitation fluid (sepsis, trauma, surgical), perioperative fluid replacement, burns (Parkland formula — 4 mL/kg/% TBSA in 24h), DKA (after initial NS phase, once glucose <250 mg/dL), general maintenance.

dose.standard: Resuscitation bolus: 500 mL–1 L IV over 15–30 min; Maintenance: 1–2 mL/kg/h; Burns (Parkland): 4 mL/kg × %TBSA burned in 24h (half in first 8h, half in next 16h)

renalAdj.regimen: Standard; monitor fluid balance
Monitor K⁺ (LR contains 4 mEq/L K⁺); withhold if hyperkalaemic
CAUTION with K⁺ — 4 mEq/L can worsen hyperkalaemia in ESRD; switch to NS if K⁺ elevated

sideEffects: Hyperkalaemia (4 mEq/L K⁺ per litre — clinically relevant in ESRD/AKI; minimal risk in normal renal function)
Volume overload (same risks as NS in CHF, cirrhosis, ESRD)
Mild lactate elevation (LR infusion mildly elevates serum lactate — interpret lactate cautiously in first few hours of resuscitation)
monitoring: Lactate (note that LR may transiently ↑ serum lactate 0.5–1 mmol/L)
publicNotes: Often preferred over normal saline for large-volume resuscitation because it causes less hyperchloremic acidosis
Do not run LR through the same line as blood products without confirming compatibility
Check medication compatibility before co-infusing because calcium content matters

references.text: SMART Trial — Semler et al., NEJM 2018

drugs.name: Heparin (Unfractionated Heparin, UFH)
drugs.pkpd: Immediate effect with IV dosing and short functional half-life, but interpatient response is variable because of protein binding and acute-phase effects. Therapeutic use needs aPTT or anti-Xa titration.
drugs.mechanism: Potentiates antithrombin and accelerates inhibition of thrombin (IIa) and factor Xa, preventing further clot propagation.
drugs.spectrum: Inpatient VTE treatment or prophylaxis, ACS regimens, bridging, and situations where rapid on/off anticoagulation is needed or kidney function is changing quickly.

dose.standard: Prophylaxis: 5000 units SC q8–12h. Therapeutic IV regimens are protocol-based; label and institutional nomograms commonly use an IV bolus followed by continuous infusion titrated to aPTT or anti-Xa

renalAdj.regimen: No formal renal dose adjustment; therapeutic infusions are titrated to aPTT or anti-Xa rather than CrCl alone
Often preferred over LMWH when rapid reversal or close titration is important

monitoring: aPTT or anti-Xa for therapeutic dosing
K⁺ if prolonged therapy or other hyperkalemia risks are present
publicNotes: Do not confuse therapeutic heparin with heparin flush products because concentrations and intent are very different
UFH is often a safer anticoagulant starting point than LMWH when kidney function is unstable or urgent procedures are likely

drugs.spectrum: General internal medicine ward reference and medication-lab safety rule support.

dose.standard: Oral or IV dosing is indication-specific; avoid using as a reflex number-only BP treatment without context.

renalAdj.regimen: No simple renal dose formula; monitor BP response and tachycardia
Risk rises with prolonged higher-dose exposure

sideEffects: Dose- or exposure-related toxicity in vulnerable patients
publicNotes: Hydralazine can cause reflex tachycardia and variable BP swings; pair the dose with a clear indication and monitoring plan.

drugs.name: Hydrochlorothiazide
drugs.pkpd: Ward-reference summary focused on safety review, renal handling, and monitoring rather than exhaustive prescribing.
drugs.mechanism: See class-specific pharmacology; use this entry as a deterministic bedside safety reminder.
drugs.spectrum: General internal medicine ward reference and medication-lab safety rule support.

dose.standard: Oral dosing varies by indication; effect is weaker at low GFR.

renalAdj.regimen: Often less effective; monitor electrolytes closely if continued

sideEffects: Dose- or exposure-related toxicity in vulnerable patients
publicNotes: Common cause of hyponatremia/hypokalemia; reassess during AKI or poor intake.

drugs.name: Hydrocortisone (Sodium Succinate)
drugs.pkpd: Short-acting systemic glucocorticoid with clinically meaningful mineralocorticoid activity. Rapid parenteral delivery is used when oral therapy is not feasible or adrenal crisis is suspected.
drugs.mechanism: Binds cytosolic glucocorticoid receptors and changes gene transcription, reducing inflammatory signaling while replacing cortisol activity in adrenal insufficiency.
drugs.spectrum: Adrenal crisis, stress-dose steroid replacement, selected steroid-responsive inflammatory disorders, and corticosteroid support in vasopressor-dependent septic shock when indicated.

dose.standard: Adrenal crisis: 100 mg IV/IM immediately, then 200 mg over 24 h by continuous infusion or 50 mg IV/IM q6h. Other indications require an individualized regimen.
dose.loading: Do not delay the initial 100 mg dose when adrenal crisis is suspected.

renalAdj.regimen: No renal dose adjustment; monitor sodium, potassium, glucose, blood pressure, and volume status
Dose is not CrCl-based, but sodium/fluid retention and glycemic effects require closer monitoring

sideEffects: Infection risk and masking of infection
GI irritation or bleeding risk, especially with NSAIDs
publicNotes: Adrenal-crisis treatment should not wait for confirmatory testing when clinical suspicion is high
For septic shock, avoid reflex high-dose short-course corticosteroid regimens; use a guideline-supported low-dose strategy when indicated
Use narrative pregnancy/lactation risk information; emergency adrenal replacement should not be withheld because untreated crisis threatens mother and fetus

drugs.name: Hydroxyzine (Atarax)
drugs.pkpd: Onset PO: 15–30 min. Peak: 2h. Duration: 4–6h. T½: 20–25h (longer in elderly). Hepatic metabolism → active metabolite cetirizine (non-sedating antihistamine). CYP3A4/2D6 substrate.
drugs.mechanism: H1 receptor antagonist with significant CNS penetration → sedation. Also anticholinergic and mild anxiolytic (serotonin antagonism, GABA potentiation). Active metabolite cetirizine provides antihistamine effects without sedation.
drugs.spectrum: Pruritus (first-line antihistamine for itching), anxiety/tension (adjunct, short-term), sleep induction (short-term), nausea/vomiting, procedural anxiolysis.

dose.standard: Pruritus/anxiety: 25–50 mg PO QID PRN; Sleep: 50–100 mg PO at bedtime; IM: 25–100 mg IM q4–6h PRN (IM only — NEVER IV: causes thrombosis and tissue necrosis)

renalAdj.regimen: Official labeling does not provide a renal-dose table; start at the low end of the dosing range and monitor closely for oversedation and anticholinergic adverse effects
No standard post-dialysis supplemental dosing is established; if sedation risk is high, consider an alternative agent

sideEffects: Drowsiness (therapeutic at sleep doses; can be excessive in elderly)
QTc prolongation (higher doses — avoid with other QTc-prolonging drugs)
Severe tissue necrosis if given IV (NEVER give IV — IM only for injectable)
Falls and cognitive impairment in elderly (Beers Criteria)
monitoring: QTc (ECG) at higher doses or with baseline QTc prolongation
Anticholinergic effects (urinary retention, confusion in elderly)
publicNotes: Never administer hydroxyzine IV — IM only for injectable form; IV causes severe thrombosis and tissue necrosis
QT risk is most relevant in patients with prolonged QT, structural heart disease, electrolyte abnormalities, bradyarrhythmia, or concomitant QT-prolonging drugs
Avoid routine use for insomnia in older adults because its strong anticholinergic, cognitive, fall, and QT risks can outweigh benefit

drugs.name: Ibuprofen (Advil / Brufen)
drugs.pkpd: Onset: PO 30–60 min. Peak: 1–2h. Duration: 4–6h (standard-release), 8–12h (extended-release). Highly protein-bound (~99%). Hepatic metabolism via CYP2C9. Half-life ~2h.
drugs.mechanism: Non-selective COX-1/COX-2 inhibitor → reduced prostaglandins → analgesic, anti-inflammatory, antipyretic. Reversible platelet inhibition (unlike aspirin — recovers within 24h of last dose).
drugs.spectrum: Mild-to-moderate pain (musculoskeletal, dental, headache, post-operative), fever, dysmenorrhoea, inflammatory conditions (OA, RA, gout flare), patent ductus arteriosus closure (IV neonatal formulation).

dose.standard: Analgesia/antipyresis: 400 mg PO q4–6h (max 1200 mg/day OTC); Anti-inflammatory: 400–600 mg PO TID–QID with food (max 2400 mg/day); take with food or milk

renalAdj.regimen: Standard; limit to shortest effective duration

drugs.name: Imipenem-Cilastatin-Relebactam
drugs.pkpd: Time-dependent carbapenem killing. Relebactam restores activity against selected serine β-lactamase-producing Gram-negative organisms.
drugs.mechanism: Imipenem inhibits PBPs; cilastatin reduces renal metabolism of imipenem; relebactam inhibits class A and C β-lactamases including KPC and AmpC.
drugs.spectrum: Susceptible Gram-negative organisms including some KPC-producing Enterobacterales and difficult Pseudomonas isolates. NOT metallo-β-lactamase producers, MRSA, VRE, or atypicals.

drugs.name: Indomethacin (Indocid)
drugs.pkpd: PO: onset 30 min–2h, peak 2h, duration 4–6h. PR (rectal suppository): onset 30–60 min. Most potent anti-inflammatory NSAID. Good CNS penetration. Strong uricosuric effect.
drugs.mechanism: Most potent non-selective COX-1/COX-2 inhibitor. Also inhibits phospholipase A₂ and leukocyte migration. Closes patent ductus arteriosus by reducing prostaglandin E₂ → ductal smooth muscle constriction.
drugs.spectrum: Acute gout (highly effective first-line), pericarditis (+ colchicine standard combination), ankylosing spondylitis, pleuritis, patent ductus arteriosus closure (IV neonatal), heterotopic ossification prophylaxis post-THA.

dose.standard: Acute gout: 50 mg PO/PR TID until pain is tolerable, then taper rapidly to discontinuation; Pericarditis: 25–50 mg PO TID × 2 weeks then taper; AS: 25–75 mg PO BID–TID; PDA (IV neonatal): 0.2 mg/kg per protocol
dose.loading: Gout: 50 mg initial dose with rapid titration only if clinically needed

renalAdj.regimen: No label-based reduced-dose table is provided; use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration and monitor renal function closely
Avoid unless benefits are expected to outweigh the risk of worsening renal function; if used, monitor closely

sideEffects: GI: among the highest ulceration/bleeding risks of the traditional NSAIDs (very potent COX-1 inhibition) — consider gastroprotection in patients with meaningful GI risk factors
CNS: headache, dizziness, confusion, delirium (significant especially in elderly — most common reason for discontinuation)
monitoring: GI symptoms (use gastroprotection when GI risk is elevated)
CNS symptoms (confusion/dizziness — reduce dose or switch if significant; avoid in elderly >65)
publicNotes: Indomethacin is potent for acute gout and pericarditis but has enough GI and CNS toxicity that it deserves selective use
Older adults often tolerate it poorly compared with other options

drugs.name: Ipratropium Bromide
drugs.pkpd: Locally acting inhaled antimuscarinic with limited systemic absorption. Onset is slower than a short-acting beta-2 agonist, so it should not displace faster rescue therapy in acute distress.
drugs.mechanism: Blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in bronchial smooth muscle, reducing vagally mediated bronchoconstriction.
drugs.spectrum: Maintenance bronchodilation in COPD and adjunctive bronchodilation in acute obstructive-airway exacerbations with an appropriate rescue strategy.

dose.standard: Nebulized solution: 500 mcg by oral nebulization three to four times daily, with doses 6–8 h apart. Follow the acute-exacerbation protocol when more frequent combination treatment is intended.

renalAdj.regimen: No renal dose adjustment for inhaled therapy
Minimize ocular exposure and monitor anticholinergic complications

monitoring: Urinary retention, especially with other anticholinergic drugs
publicNotes: Avoid spraying or nebulizing the medication into the eyes

drugs.name: Ketorolac (Toradol)
drugs.pkpd: Analgesic onset: IV ~10 min, IM 30 min, PO 30–60 min. Peak effect: 1–2h. Duration: 4–6h. Potent parenteral NSAID — analgesia equivalent to ~12 mg morphine IV. Non-selective COX-1/COX-2 inhibitor.
drugs.mechanism: Non-selective COX-1/COX-2 inhibition → reduced prostaglandin synthesis → anti-inflammatory, analgesic, antipyretic. Reversible platelet inhibition (antiplatelet effect lasts ~2 days).
drugs.spectrum: Post-operative pain (opioid-sparing analgesia), renal colic (highly effective — prostaglandin-dependent ureteral contraction), musculoskeletal pain (IV/IM when PO unavailable), moderate-to-severe acute pain, gout flare adjunct.

dose.standard: Single dose: 30 mg IV once or 60 mg IM once; Multiple-dose IV/IM: 30 mg q6h (max 120 mg/day); PO continuation only after IV/IM lead-in: 20 mg once, then 10 mg q4–6h PRN (max 40 mg/day); MAXIMUM DURATION: 5 days total across all routes
dose.loading: Special populations (age ≥65, renally impaired, or weight <50 kg) require lower single and repeated doses

renalAdj.crcl: Renally impaired but not advanced renal failure
renalAdj.regimen: Use the reduced special-population regimen: 15 mg IV/IM q6h (max 60 mg/day); if transitioning to PO, 10 mg once then 10 mg q4–6h PRN after parenteral dosing

renalAdj.crcl: Advanced renal impairment or volume-depleted patients at risk for renal failure
renalAdj.regimen: Contraindicated; correct hypovolemia and choose an alternative analgesic

sideEffects: AKI (prostaglandin-dependent renal perfusion — especially in hypovolaemia, CKD, CHF, NSAID-naïve elderly, concurrent nephrotoxins; holds renal function in afferent arteriole dilation)
GI ulceration/bleeding (COX-1 gastric mucosal depletion — highest risk with prolonged use; add PPI for courses >3 days or high-risk patients)
Platelet dysfunction (antiplatelet effect — avoid pre-op and in active bleeding/coagulopathy)
monitoring: Renal function (SCr, urine output — baseline CrCl before use)
Strict ≤5 day duration limit — document start date, verify daily
publicNotes: Ketorolac has a strict short-course role; do not let it drift into prolonged NSAID use
Its renal and bleeding risks make patient selection important from the start

drugs.name: Labetalol
drugs.pkpd: Combined alpha-1 and non-selective beta blockade lowers BP without the reflex tachycardia typical of a pure vasodilator; usable as an IV bolus, IV infusion, or oral tablet.
drugs.mechanism: Blocks alpha-1 adrenergic receptors (vasodilation) together with beta-1/beta-2 receptors (reduced heart rate and contractility), lowering BP with relatively preserved cardiac output.
drugs.spectrum: Hypertensive emergency — including the aortic-dissection rate-then-pressure sequence and pregnancy-associated severe hypertension/eclampsia — and post-thrombolysis/thrombectomy stroke BP control.

dose.standard: Bolus: 20 mg IV over 2 minutes, then repeat/double every 10 minutes to a maximum cumulative 300 mg; or infusion starting at 0.5–2 mg/minute titrated to a maximum of about 3 mg/kg/hour

renalAdj.regimen: No routine renal dose adjustment; titrate to hemodynamic response

sideEffects: Bronchospasm in susceptible patients (nonselective beta blockade)
Transient scalp tingling with rapid IV administration
monitoring: Continuous or very frequent BP and heart-rate monitoring during titration
Avoid as first-line in decompensated heart failure with poor forward flow
publicNotes: Preferred first-line agent for pregnancy-associated severe hypertension/eclampsia alongside magnesium sulfate and obstetric involvement
In aortic dissection, labetalol's combined alpha/beta blockade can be used alone for the rate-then-pressure sequence, or paired with a separate vasodilator per local protocol

drugs.name: Lactulose (Duphalac)
drugs.pkpd: Onset: 24–48h for laxative effect; 1–3 days for full effect. Not systemically absorbed. Acts locally in colon. For hepatic encephalopathy: ammonia reduction begins within hours. Dose-dependent laxative effect.
drugs.mechanism: Non-absorbable disaccharide → colonic bacteria metabolize to organic acids (lactic, acetic) → acidification → osmotic water retention → stool softening and increased bulk. For HE: acidification traps NH₃ as NH₄⁺ (non-absorbable) → reduces ammonia absorption.
drugs.spectrum: Constipation (1st-line in many guidelines), Hepatic encephalopathy (primary treatment), portal-systemic encephalopathy prevention.

dose.standard: Constipation: 15–30 mL (10–20 g) PO BID–TID, titrate to 2–3 soft stools/day; Hepatic encephalopathy: 30–45 mL PO q1–2h until bowel movement, then TID–QID; Retention enema: 300 mL in 700 mL water q4–6h

renalAdj.regimen: No renal adjustment needed (not systemically absorbed)

sideEffects: Diarrhoea (dose-dependent — most common reason to reduce dose)
Electrolyte imbalance with prolonged use or diarrhoea (hypokalaemia)
Hypernatraemia (rare, with diarrhoeal fluid losses in elderly)
monitoring: Stool frequency and consistency (aim: 2–3 soft stools/day)
Electrolytes (K⁺, Na⁺) with prolonged use or diarrhoea
Mental status in HE patients (clinical assessment preferred over serum ammonia alone)
Blood glucose (lactulose contains galactose + fructose — monitor in diabetes)
publicNotes: Lactulose remains a standard treatment for hepatic encephalopathy alongside rifaximin
Titrate dose to achieve soft regular stools, not frank diarrhoea
Expected onset 24–48h — counsel patients to start at a lower dose and titrate up

drugs.name: Levetiracetam (Keppra)
drugs.pkpd: Rapid, near-complete oral absorption with equivalent total daily IV and PO dosing. Primarily renally eliminated with few CYP-mediated interactions.
drugs.mechanism: Binds synaptic vesicle protein SV2A and modulates neurotransmitter release, reducing neuronal hypersynchronization.
drugs.spectrum: Focal-onset, myoclonic, and primary generalized tonic-clonic seizure treatment; IV formulation when oral administration is temporarily not feasible.

dose.standard: Start 500 mg PO/IV q12h for labeled adult seizure indications; titrate by indication and response up to 1,500 mg q12h. IV and PO total daily dose/frequency are equivalent.
dose.loading: Status-epilepticus loading regimens are protocol-based and are not the same as labeled chronic initiation.

renalAdj.regimen: 500–1,000 mg q24h plus 250–500 mg after each dialysis session

sideEffects: Irritability, agitation, depression, aggression, or other behavioral change
Suicidal ideation warning applicable to antiseizure medications
monitoring: Pregnancy-related seizure control and exposure when applicable
publicNotes: Do not stop levetiracetam abruptly because withdrawal can increase seizure frequency or precipitate status epilepticus
Behavioral adverse effects can be important even when pharmacokinetic interactions are minimal
Use current narrative pregnancy information and monitor seizure control; pregnancy can lower exposure

drugs.name: Levofloxacin
drugs.pkpd: Concentration-dependent (AUC/MIC + Cmax/MIC). PO bioavailability ~99% → IV/PO bioequivalent (switch early). AUC/MIC target ≥125 for S. pneumoniae.

drugs.spectrum: "Respiratory FQ": S. pneumoniae (resistant strains), H. influenzae, Legionella, Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, E. coli (susceptible). NOT reliable MRSA or Pseudomonas at standard doses.

dose.standard: 750 mg PO/IV q24h

750 mg q48h

Dysglycemia (hypo or hyperglycemia — especially in diabetics)

drugs.pkpd: AUC/MIC-dependent. 100% oral bioavailability — switch to PO at first opportunity. No renal dose adjustment (hepatic metabolism).

Review ALL serotonergic medications before prescribing (SSRIs very common!)
Visual acuity and colour vision monthly for courses >28 days

drugs.name: Long-Acting Insulin (Lantus / Tresiba)
drugs.pkpd: Glargine (Lantus): onset 2–4h, no peak, duration ~24h. Degludec (Tresiba): onset 1h, duration >42h (ultra-long, flexible timing). Detemir (Levemir): onset 1–2h, duration 12–24h (may need BID).
drugs.mechanism: Glargine: microprecipitates at neutral SC pH → slow dissolution depot. Degludec: forms multi-hexamer chains → ultra-prolonged absorption. Detemir: albumin binding → buffered release.
drugs.spectrum: Basal insulin: T1DM (mandatory) and T2DM (basal-only or basal-bolus). Controls fasting glucose. NOT for IV use (never). Targets overnight and interprandial glucose stability.

drugs.name: Lorazepam (Ativan)
drugs.pkpd: Onset PO: 15–30 min; IV: 2–5 min; IM: 15–30 min. Duration: 6–8h. T½: 10–20h. Direct glucuronidation (no hepatic CYP oxidation) → safer in hepatic impairment and elderly. No active metabolites.
drugs.mechanism: Positive allosteric modulator of GABA-A receptor → increased chloride channel opening frequency → neuronal hyperpolarisation → CNS depression (sedation, anxiolysis, anterograde amnesia, anticonvulsant, muscle relaxation).
drugs.spectrum: Acute anxiety, alcohol withdrawal (CIWA protocol), status epilepticus (first-line IV), procedural sedation, pre-operative anxiolysis, acute agitation, short-term insomnia.

dose.standard: Anxiety/sedation: 0.5–2 mg PO/IV/IM q4–8h PRN; Status epilepticus: 0.1 mg/kg IV (max 4 mg) q5–10 min × 2; Alcohol withdrawal (CIWA): 1–4 mg IV/PO q1–4h PRN by score; ICU infusion: 0.02–0.06 mg/kg/h IV
dose.loading: Status epilepticus: 4 mg IV push (may repeat × 1 in 5–10 min)

renalAdj.regimen: No specific dosage adjustment is recommended in the official label; monitor sedation and respiratory status
Use cautiously, especially repeated IV/IM dosing, because lorazepam glucuronide can accumulate and prolong CNS effects
No routine supplemental dose is established; individualize based on clinical response and monitoring

sideEffects: Respiratory depression (IV — have airway equipment available)
Tolerance and physical dependence with prolonged use
Rebound anxiety and withdrawal seizures on abrupt discontinuation
Paradoxical agitation (especially in children and elderly)
Propylene glycol toxicity with high-dose prolonged IV infusion (lactic acidosis, AKI)
monitoring: Respiratory rate and SpO₂ (IV use — continuous monitoring)
CIWA score (alcohol withdrawal — document before each PRN dose)
Osmol gap and lactate with prolonged high-dose IV infusion (PG toxicity)
Benzodiazepine withdrawal signs if stopping after prolonged use
publicNotes: Lorazepam is preferred over diazepam for alcohol withdrawal in hepatic impairment — direct glucuronidation, no CYP oxidation, no active metabolites
For status epilepticus, IV lorazepam is first-line benzodiazepine before levetiracetam or fosphenytoin
Respiratory monitoring is essential for IV administration — resuscitation equipment must be at bedside

drugs.name: Losartan
drugs.pkpd: Once-daily ARB with active metabolite contribution. BP effect accumulates over days to weeks rather than after one dose, while creatinine and potassium effects can appear quickly if renal perfusion is marginal.
drugs.mechanism: Blocks the angiotensin II AT1 receptor, reducing vasoconstriction, aldosterone signaling, and maladaptive glomerular efferent arteriolar tone.
drugs.spectrum: Hypertension, albuminuric diabetic kidney disease, CKD or HF regimens where RAAS blockade is indicated, and proteinuria reduction.

dose.standard: Usually 25–50 mg PO daily to start; common maintenance 50–100 mg/day in 1 or 2 doses depending on BP, kidney function, and tolerance

renalAdj.regimen: No formal renal dose adjustment, but start lower and monitor closely if volume-depleted, advanced CKD, or hemodynamically fragile
Reassess dose, volume status, NSAID exposure, and whether continued RAAS blockade still offers net benefit

monitoring: K⁺ and creatinine after start or dose change
Concurrent NSAID, potassium supplement, or duplicate RAAS exposure review
publicNotes: A small creatinine rise after starting an ARB can be expected, but a large jump should trigger a search for overdiuresis, renal artery disease, sepsis, or NSAID-related hemodynamic injury
ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy and should be stopped if pregnancy occurs

drugs.name: Magnesium Oxide (MgO)
drugs.pkpd: Onset: 30 min–6h. About 4–20% of Mg²⁺ is systemically absorbed — excreted renally (risk of hypermagnesaemia in renal impairment). Most retained in GI lumen → osmotic effect.
drugs.mechanism: Mg²⁺ ions → osmotically retain water in intestinal lumen → increased bowel water content → softened stool and increased peristalsis. Mg²⁺ also activates cholecystokinin → stimulates bowel motility.
drugs.spectrum: Chronic constipation (daily prevention), dyspepsia/antacid use, adjunct in hypomagnesaemia prevention (especially with long-term PPI use).

dose.standard: Constipation: 250–500 mg PO BID–TID (low preventive dose); 1–2 g PO at bedtime (higher dose for active constipation); take with water; Antacid: 400–800 mg PO QID PRN between meals

renalAdj.regimen: Standard
Reduce dose; monitor Mg²⁺; avoid prolonged high-dose use
AVOID or use with extreme caution — hypermagnesaemia risk (nausea, bradycardia, respiratory depression); monitor Mg²⁺ closely

sideEffects: Hypermagnesaemia in renal impairment (nausea → flushing → bradycardia → respiratory depression at severe levels)
monitoring: Serum magnesium (especially if CKD or daily dosing)
publicNotes: Magnesium oxide is widely used as a daily mild laxative in many Asian countries
Do not confuse magnesium oxide tablets with milk of magnesia, which is magnesium hydroxide
Avoid in significant renal impairment due to risk of magnesium accumulation
MgO has poor bioavailability — not reliable for correcting true hypomagnesaemia; higher-bioavailability forms preferred for supplementation

drugs.name: Melatonin
drugs.pkpd: Onset: 30–60 min. T½: 45–65 min (short). Hepatic CYP1A2 metabolism. Extensive first-pass effect → bioavailability ~15%. Peak levels delayed by food. Does not produce pharmacological CNS depression.
drugs.mechanism: Agonist at MT1 and MT2 receptors in suprachiasmatic nucleus → MT1: acute sleep onset promotion; MT2: circadian phase shifting. Reinforces the endogenous circadian signal for sleep without sedation, dependence, or respiratory depression.
drugs.spectrum: Jet lag, circadian rhythm disorders, insomnia adjunct (especially in elderly), ICU delirium prevention (adjunct), insomnia where sedative-hypnotics are contraindicated.

dose.standard: Insomnia: 0.5–5 mg PO 30–60 min before desired sleep time; Start 1–3 mg; titrate; Elderly: 0.5–2 mg; Jet lag: 3–5 mg at destination bedtime for 3–5 days; Take in dim light

renalAdj.regimen: No dose adjustment necessary; caution in severe renal impairment (clearance reduced — accumulation possible)

sideEffects: Daytime drowsiness if taken at wrong time or at high dose
publicNotes: Melatonin is not a sedative — it shifts and reinforces the circadian sleep signal rather than inducing pharmacological sedation
Timing matters more than dose — take 30–60 min before desired sleep time, in dim light conditions
Much safer than benzodiazepines or Z-drugs — no dependence risk, no rebound insomnia, minimal next-day impairment at standard doses

drugs.name: Meropenem
drugs.pkpd: Time-dependent killing. Extended infusion (2–3h) optimizes %T>MIC for elevated-MIC organisms. NOT inactivated by renal dehydropeptidase (unlike imipenem).
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits PBPs 1a, 1b, 2 — ultra-broad bactericidal activity. Stable to most β-lactamases (NOT carbapenemases: KPC, MBL, OXA-48).
drugs.spectrum: Broadest β-lactam spectrum: most GNRs (incl. ESBL, Pseudomonas, AmpC), most Gram+, anaerobes. NOT MRSA, VRE, CRE, Stenotrophomonas.

dose.standard: 1 g IV q8h (2h extended infusion)
dose.loading: Severe / Pseudomonas / high-MIC: 2 g IV q8h extended 3h infusion

renalAdj.regimen: 1–2 g q8h
1 g q12h
500 mg q12h
500 mg q24h
Not specified in the official label; use institution/pharmacy guidance for HD or peritoneal dialysis
Not covered by the official label; use institution/pharmacy guidance based on effluent flow and infusion strategy

monitoring: Neurological status (high doses in renal failure)
publicNotes: Use extended infusion for severe infection or elevated MICs when feasible
