drugs.name: Meropenem-Vaborbactam
drugs.pkpd: Time-dependent carbapenem killing. Vaborbactam restores meropenem activity against many KPC-producing Enterobacterales.
drugs.mechanism: Meropenem inhibits PBPs; vaborbactam inhibits serine β-lactamases, especially KPC. It does not inhibit metallo-β-lactamases.
drugs.spectrum: Susceptible Enterobacterales including many KPC-producing CRE. Limited role for OXA-48-like producers and no metallo-β-lactamase activity; not a MRSA/VRE/atypical agent.

dose.standard: 4 g IV q8h by 3h infusion when renal function is normal; adjust by renal function.

renalAdj.regimen: Use standard dosing
Dose reduction required
Further dose reduction required
Use labeled severe renal impairment or HD dosing
Use ID/pharmacy dosing based on clearance and severity

publicNotes: Most useful when KPC-producing Enterobacterales are suspected or confirmed and susceptibility supports use
Do not assume activity against metallo-β-lactamase producers without susceptibility and expert review

drugs.name: Metformin
drugs.pkpd: Primarily renal elimination unchanged. No hypoglycemia by itself, but exposure rises in CKD and acute illness. Tissue accumulation matters more than serum peak effect.
drugs.mechanism: Reduces hepatic gluconeogenesis, improves peripheral insulin sensitivity, and modestly reduces intestinal glucose absorption. Activates AMPK-related metabolic pathways.
drugs.spectrum: First-line glucose-lowering therapy for type 2 diabetes when kidney function and acute illness context permit.

dose.standard: 500–1000 mg PO BID with meals (typical max 2000 mg/day)

renalAdj.regimen: Standard dosing generally acceptable
Reduce total daily dose and reassess risk-benefit frequently; avoid new starts
Contraindicated
Temporarily hold regardless of chronic baseline eGFR until the acute trigger resolves
Hold for eGFR 30–60, liver disease, alcoholism, heart failure, or intra-arterial contrast; reassess renal function after 48 hours before restarting

sideEffects: Vitamin B12 deficiency with long-term use
Lactic acidosis risk in severe renal dysfunction or major acute illness (rare but high-stakes)
monitoring: Vitamin B12 periodically in long-term therapy
Review for sepsis, hypoxia, shock, liver failure, or contrast exposure before restarting
publicNotes: The important metformin question in the hospital is often not the chronic eGFR threshold but whether the patient is acutely septic, hypoxic, or acidotic
Contrast holds should follow label risk criteria rather than applying to every contrast exposure

drugs.name: Methylprednisolone (Sodium Succinate)
drugs.pkpd: Intermediate-acting glucocorticoid with less mineralocorticoid activity than hydrocortisone. Review dose equivalence and cumulative exposure when switching systemic steroids.
drugs.mechanism: Activates glucocorticoid receptors and alters inflammatory and immune gene transcription.
drugs.spectrum: Severe steroid-responsive inflammatory, allergic, pulmonary, neurologic, rheumatologic, and transplant-related conditions when parenteral therapy is appropriate.

dose.standard: Indication-specific. The label describes initial doses of 10–40 mg IV/IM for many systemic indications; pulse or weight-based high-dose therapy is reserved for selected protocols.
dose.loading: Do not use a high-dose pulse regimen as a generic default; verify indication, infusion time, and cumulative exposure.

renalAdj.regimen: No routine renal dose adjustment
Dose is not CrCl-based; intensify metabolic, volume, and infection monitoring

sideEffects: Infection risk and masking of infection
publicNotes: Systemic steroid equivalents are not milligram-for-milligram; document intended glucocorticoid-equivalent exposure when switching
High-dose pulse therapy should remain tied to a defined protocol or specialist indication
Use narrative pregnancy and lactation risk information rather than historical letter categories

drugs.name: Metoclopramide (Reglan)
drugs.pkpd: Combined antiemetic and upper-GI prokinetic effects via dopamine antagonism. Renal clearance is clinically important, so repeated dosing accumulates in CKD more than many teams expect.
drugs.mechanism: Blocks central dopamine D2 receptors for antiemetic effect and enhances upper-GI motility through dopamine antagonism and downstream cholinergic facilitation.
drugs.spectrum: Gastroparesis, nausea with delayed gastric emptying, selected refractory nausea contexts, and short-course adjunctive prokinetic use.

dose.standard: 5–10 mg PO/IV q6–8h PRN or scheduled depending on indication; use the lowest effective dose and shortest duration possible

renalAdj.regimen: Usual short-course dosing generally acceptable
Consider lower dose or longer interval if repeated dosing is planned
Reduce dose substantially or extend interval because CNS and extrapyramidal toxicity risk rises with accumulation

sideEffects: Tardive dyskinesia with longer exposure or high cumulative dose
monitoring: Restlessness, dystonia, parkinsonism, or other extrapyramidal symptoms
Renal function if scheduled therapy is used
Duration of therapy, because longer exposure increases tardive dyskinesia risk
publicNotes: Metoclopramide is most useful when nausea has a motility component, not simply because it is another antiemetic to stack automatically
If a patient becomes agitated or restless after a dose, think akathisia rather than worsening primary anxiety

drugs.name: Metoprolol
drugs.pkpd: Beta1-selective blockade with different practical formulations: tartrate is usually immediate-release and often BID, while succinate is extended-release and often daily. Acute heart-rate effects appear quickly, but chronic HF or BP benefit depends on sustained titration.
drugs.mechanism: Blocks cardiac beta1 receptors, lowering heart rate, AV nodal conduction, contractility, and myocardial oxygen demand.
drugs.spectrum: Rate control, hypertension, chronic coronary disease, HFrEF when the succinate formulation is intended, and selected inpatient tachyarrhythmia support.

dose.standard: Formulation-specific. Tartrate often starts at 12.5–25 mg PO BID or small IV doses for acute rate control; succinate commonly starts at 12.5–25 mg PO daily for chronic therapy and is titrated to indication and tolerance

renalAdj.regimen: No routine renal dose adjustment needed
Dose is not renal-based, but the clinical state may make continuation or escalation inappropriate

sideEffects: Worsening bronchospasm in susceptible patients despite beta1 selectivity
monitoring: Whether the formulation is tartrate or succinate
Signs of low-output state or decompensated HF
Bronchospasm history if airway disease is present
publicNotes: Metoprolol tartrate and succinate are not interchangeable in a casual way because the release profile and common indications differ
Do not reflexively stop every chronic beta-blocker on admission, but do not push it through shock or active low-output states either

drugs.name: Metronidazole
drugs.pkpd: Concentration-dependent (MBC/MIC). Excellent tissue penetration including CNS, abscesses, and intracellular. PO bioavailability ~100%.
drugs.mechanism: Reduced to toxic intermediates by anaerobic/microaerophilic organisms → DNA strand breakage. Active ONLY under anaerobic/microaerophilic conditions.
drugs.spectrum: Obligate anaerobes: B. fragilis, Peptostreptococcus, Fusobacterium, Prevotella, Clostridium (incl. C. difficile). Protozoa: Giardia, Trichomonas, E. histolytica.

dose.standard: 500 mg PO/IV TID or 1 g IV q12h; for initial nonsevere C. difficile, use only when fidaxomicin and oral vancomycin are unavailable

renalAdj.regimen: No adjustment needed (hepatic metabolism)
Standard dose; metabolites may accumulate — monitor for neurotoxicity in ESRD

sideEffects: Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol (avoid alcohol during + 48h after course)
CNS toxicity: encephalopathy, ataxia, cerebellar dysfunction (MRI: T2 signal in dentate nucleus — rare)
monitoring: Duration: avoid continuous courses >4 weeks (peripheral neuropathy)
Neurological symptoms in hepatic impairment (reduced clearance)
publicNotes: Switch from IV to PO promptly when the patient can take enteral medication because bioavailability is excellent
Avoid alcohol during therapy and for 48 hours afterward because of the disulfiram-like reaction risk

references.text: IDSA/SHEA C. difficile Guidelines — McDonald et al., CID 2018
IDSA Intra-Abdominal Infection Guidelines — Solomkin et al., CID 2010

drugs.name: Micafungin
drugs.pkpd: Concentration-dependent (AUC/MIC). Once-daily dosing. Highly protein-bound (>99%). Poor CNS, urinary tract, and eye penetration — similar to caspofungin.
drugs.mechanism: Non-competitive inhibitor of β-(1,3)-D-glucan synthase → disrupts fungal cell wall. Fungicidal vs. Candida; fungistatic vs. Aspergillus.
drugs.spectrum: All Candida species (incl. C. krusei, C. glabrata, fluconazole-resistant strains). Aspergillus (combination/salvage). NOT Cryptococcus, Mucorales, Fusarium.

dose.standard: Candidemia: 100 mg IV q24h; Oesophageal candidiasis: 150 mg IV q24h; Prophylaxis (HSCT): 50 mg IV q24h

renalAdj.regimen: No dose adjustment needed
Standard dose; not cleared by dialysis

monitoring: Drug interactions (fewer than azoles — major advantage)
publicNotes: Micafungin is another practical first-line echinocandin for invasive candidiasis
Its interaction burden is lower than that of azoles, which is often clinically useful

references.text: IDSA Candida Guidelines — Pappas et al., CID 2016

drugs.name: Midazolam (Dormicum)
drugs.pkpd: Onset IV: 1–5 min; IM: 5–15 min; IN: 5–10 min. Duration IV: 15–80 min (dose-dependent). T½: 1.5–2.5h (active metabolite α-hydroxymidazolam T½ ~1h). Hepatic CYP3A4 metabolism — significantly prolonged in hepatic impairment, elderly, and ICU (drug accumulation with prolonged infusions).
drugs.mechanism: Most potent GABA-A positive allosteric modulator among benzodiazepines. Water-soluble at pH <4 → lipophilic at physiologic pH → rapid CNS penetration. Produces sedation, anxiolysis, anterograde amnesia, and anticonvulsant effects.
drugs.spectrum: Procedural sedation (endoscopy, cardioversion, intubation), pre-operative anxiolysis, ICU sedation (infusion), status epilepticus (refractory — IM/IN preferred pre-hospital), seizure clusters (buccal/intranasal), palliative terminal sedation.

dose.standard: Procedural sedation: 0.5–2 mg IV titrated q2–3 min (max 5 mg for naïve patients); Elderly: start 0.5 mg IV, max 3.5 mg; ICU sedation: 0.01–0.1 mg/kg/h IV infusion (titrate to RASS target); Status epilepticus: 10 mg IM (adult)
dose.loading: Procedural: initial 0.5–2 mg IV bolus (elderly: 0.5 mg); ICU: 0.01–0.05 mg/kg optional IV load

renalAdj.regimen: No fixed dosage adjustment is established; titrate cautiously because sedation may be prolonged
Use conservative dosing and close monitoring because midazolam and active metabolite effects can be more pronounced and prolonged
No fixed dose adjustment is established; use cautious titration with continuous sedation and respiratory monitoring

sideEffects: Respiratory depression (SIGNIFICANT — airway management equipment mandatory for IV use)
Hypotension (especially in volume-depleted or elderly patients)
Drug accumulation with prolonged ICU infusion → prolonged sedation, tolerance
monitoring: Continuous SpO₂ and capnography (mandatory for procedural sedation)
RASS or Ramsay scale for ICU sedation depth
Flumazenil availability (reversal agent — note: shorter T½ than midazolam; may re-sedate)
Daily spontaneous awakening trial in ICU
publicNotes: Midazolam requires continuous monitoring and airway management readiness when given IV — never for unsupervised administration
Flumazenil reversal: 0.2 mg IV q1 min to max 1 mg — patient may re-sedate after reversal; observe for ≥2 hours
Prolonged ICU infusions lead to drug accumulation, tolerance, and prolonged awakening — daily awakening trials recommended

drugs.name: Minocycline
drugs.pkpd: AUC/MIC-dependent. Bacteriostatic. Best CNS penetration among tetracyclines (lipophilicity). PO bioavailability ~100% — take without food for best absorption. No significant renal elimination.
drugs.mechanism: Binds 30S ribosomal subunit → bacteriostatic. More lipophilic than doxycycline → better intracellular and biofilm penetration. Overcomes some tetracycline-specific efflux mechanisms.
drugs.spectrum: MDR Acinetobacter baumannii (key indication), CA-MRSA SSTI, atypicals (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Rickettsia), MRSA (alternative). NOT reliable GNRs, Streptococcus (resistance), Pseudomonas.

dose.standard: 200 mg PO/IV loading, then 100 mg PO/IV q12h
dose.loading: 200 mg loading dose

renalAdj.regimen: No dose adjustment needed (hepatic/faecal elimination)
Standard dose; not significantly cleared by dialysis

sideEffects: Vestibular toxicity: dizziness, vertigo, ataxia (most important ADR — dose-dependent, usually reversible on stopping)
Photosensitivity (less than doxycycline — but sunscreen still required)
Oesophageal ulceration (take upright with water — same as doxycycline)
monitoring: Vestibular symptoms (dizziness, nausea, tinnitus — reduce dose or switch if persistent)
Avoid driving if vestibular symptoms present
publicNotes: Minocycline can be useful for selected MDR Acinetobacter isolates and as an alternative tetracycline-class agent
Vestibular side effects are common enough that patients should be warned up front

references.text: IDSA Guidance on Resistant Gram-Negatives — Tamma et al., CID 2023

drugs.name: Morphine
drugs.pkpd: Ward-reference summary focused on safety review, renal handling, and monitoring rather than exhaustive prescribing.
drugs.mechanism: See class-specific pharmacology; use this entry as a deterministic bedside safety reminder.
drugs.spectrum: General internal medicine ward reference and medication-lab safety rule support.

dose.standard: Dose depends on opioid tolerance, pain severity, route, and goals of care.

renalAdj.regimen: Avoid or use extreme caution due to active metabolite accumulation

sideEffects: Dose- or exposure-related toxicity in vulnerable patients
publicNotes: Renal impairment can turn routine doses into prolonged sedation.

drugs.name: Moxifloxacin (Avelox)
drugs.pkpd: Concentration-dependent killing; efficacy is linked to AUC/MIC and Cmax/MIC. Oral bioavailability is high enough to support IV-to-PO conversion at the same 400 mg daily dose when enteral therapy is appropriate.
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV, blocking DNA replication, transcription, repair, and recombination; bactericidal against susceptible organisms.
drugs.spectrum: Respiratory-pathogen coverage including susceptible S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis, M. pneumoniae, C. pneumoniae, and Legionella; also covers selected susceptible gram-negative and anaerobic organisms. Not a reliable antipseudomonal agent, and urinary exposure is too low for routine UTI treatment.

dose.standard: 400 mg PO or IV q24h. Labeled adult durations vary by infection (for example, community-acquired pneumonia 7–14 days); select the shortest effective course for the confirmed indication.
dose.loading: No loading dose. Infuse IV over 60 minutes; do not give as a rapid or bolus infusion.

renalAdj.regimen: No dosage adjustment required.

sideEffects: QT prolongation and rare torsades de pointes; avoid with known QT prolongation, uncorrected hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia, significant bradycardia, or class IA/III antiarrhythmics
Potentially disabling or irreversible tendinitis/tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, and CNS or psychiatric effects
Dysglycemia, especially with insulin or glucose-lowering drugs
Nausea, diarrhea, headache, dizziness, hepatotoxicity, and C. difficile-associated diarrhea
monitoring: Baseline QT-risk review; ECG and K+/Mg2+ when risk factors or other QT-prolonging drugs are present
Tendon pain/swelling, new neuropathy, confusion or other CNS/psychiatric symptoms — stop and reassess promptly
Blood glucose in patients with diabetes receiving insulin or other glucose-lowering therapy
Clinical response and culture results; LFTs if symptoms or longer therapy
publicNotes: Reserve fluoroquinolones when safer effective alternatives are available because serious adverse effects may be disabling and potentially irreversible.
Separate oral moxifloxacin from magnesium, aluminum, iron, zinc, sucralfate, and multivitamin products: give moxifloxacin at least 4 hours before or 8 hours after them.
No renal dose adjustment is needed, but renal failure itself increases tendon-risk vulnerability and does not remove the need for safety review.

references.text: DailyMed — Moxifloxacin tablets prescribing information (revised March 2025)
FDA — Avelox tablets and injection prescribing information

drugs.name: Naproxen (Aleve / Naprosyn)
drugs.pkpd: Onset: PO 30–60 min. Peak: 1–2h. Duration: 8–12h (BID dosing sufficient). Half-life ~12–17h (longest common NSAID). Highly protein-bound (~99%). Less CYP2C9 metabolism than ibuprofen.
drugs.mechanism: Non-selective COX-1/COX-2 inhibition. Longer half-life allows BID dosing (better adherence). Among non-aspirin NSAIDs, naproxen has the lowest CV thrombotic risk (likely due to sustained COX-1 inhibition mimicking aspirin).
drugs.spectrum: OA, RA, acute gout, musculoskeletal pain, dysmenorrhoea, headache. Preferred NSAID in patients with elevated CV risk who require an NSAID (best CV safety profile among tNSAIDs).

dose.standard: Standard: 250–500 mg PO BID (with food); Acute gout: 750 mg loading, then 250 mg q8h × 3 days, then 500 mg BID; Max 1500 mg/day (short-term) or 1000 mg/day (long-term)
dose.loading: Gout: 750 mg PO loading dose

renalAdj.regimen: Standard
Reduce dose; shortest effective course; monitor renal function
AVOID — same renal contraindication as other NSAIDs

sideEffects: GI: ulceration/bleeding (take with food; add PPI in high-risk patients)
CV risk: lowest among non-aspirin NSAIDs (FitzGerald evidence, multiple meta-analyses)
publicNotes: Naproxen is often preferred when an NSAID is needed in a patient with higher cardiovascular risk
BID dosing can improve adherence compared with shorter-acting NSAIDs
Acute gout efficacy is comparable to indomethacin with better CNS tolerability in many patients

references.text: PRECISION Trial — Nissen et al., NEJM 2016

drugs.name: Nemonoxacin (Taigexyn)
drugs.pkpd: Quinolone with concentration-dependent antibacterial activity; exposure-response is generally described by AUC/MIC and Cmax/MIC. The Taiwan label does not specify a bedside PK/PD target.
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, suppressing bacterial DNA synthesis and growth.
drugs.spectrum: Taiwan labeling is limited to susceptible pathogens causing adult community-acquired pneumonia: the capsule is for mild disease suitable for outpatient treatment, while the infusion is labeled for adult CAP requiring parenteral therapy. Label-supported activity includes susceptible S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, H. parainfluenzae, K. pneumoniae, M. catarrhalis, and atypical respiratory pathogens; additional in-vitro activity should not be treated as an expanded clinical indication.

dose.standard: Capsule: 500 mg PO q24h (two 250 mg capsules) on an empty stomach, at least 2 hours before or 2 hours after food, for 7–10 days for labeled adult mild outpatient CAP. Infusion: 500 mg/250 mL IV q24h infused over at least 90 minutes; the Taiwan hospital formulary summary recommends 7–14 days according to severity and clinical response.
dose.loading: No loading dose. The IV product is a ready-to-use 250 mL infusion; do not administer as a rapid infusion or bolus.

renalAdj.regimen: 500 mg PO q24h (labeled standard regimen).
No dose adjustment required.
Use is not recommended by the Taiwan capsule label; do not extrapolate an unapproved renal regimen without specialist/pharmacy review.

sideEffects: QTc prolongation; avoid in known QT prolongation, uncorrected hypokalemia, or with class IA/III antiarrhythmics, and use caution with other QT-prolonging drugs
Quinolone-class warning for potentially disabling or irreversible tendinitis/tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, and CNS or psychiatric effects
Nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, dizziness, and headache
Infusion-site erythema, pruritus, or pain with the IV product
Transient ALT/AST elevation, leukopenia, and neutropenia reported in trials
Possible dysglycemia and exacerbation of myasthenia gravis as quinolone-class risks
monitoring: Renal function before treatment; the labeled oral product is not recommended for moderate-to-severe renal impairment or ESRD
Baseline QT-risk and medication review; ECG and K+/Mg2+ when clinically indicated
Tendon symptoms, neuropathy, new CNS/psychiatric symptoms, and weakness suggestive of myasthenia worsening
CBC and LFTs when clinically indicated; glucose in patients receiving antidiabetic therapy
Clinical response and culture/susceptibility results; narrow or change therapy when results support it
publicNotes: Nemonoxacin is not FDA-approved and has no US DailyMed monograph; this entry follows Taiwan labeling and official hospital formulary material for the capsule and IV infusion.
Confirm formulation before acting: the 250 mg capsule is limited to mild outpatient CAP, whereas the 500 mg/250 mL infusion is a separate parenteral product for adult CAP.
Do not generalize in-vitro activity to infections outside the labeled adult CAP indications.

Give aluminum/magnesium antacids, sucralfate, iron, zinc, or multivitamin products at least 2 hours after nemonoxacin; the Taiwan label documents substantial exposure reduction with several polyvalent-cation products.

references.text: Taiwan-approved Taigexyn Capsule 250 mg prescribing information (version 2022-06-20)
NTUH Hsin-Chu Branch Pharmacy — Taigexyn Infusion Solution monograph
Taiwan FDA — Nemonoxacin IV risk-management plan
Taiwan NHI — Nemonoxacin capsule and injection reimbursement criteria
Taiwan FDA — Taigexyn post-marketing safety-monitoring announcement
Phase 3 oral nemonoxacin vs levofloxacin for CAP — J Microbiol Immunol Infect 2019

drugs.name: Nicardipine
drugs.pkpd: Titratable IV infusion with a relatively fast onset and offset, allowing minute-to-minute BP adjustment without the sedation or CNS effects of some alternative agents.
drugs.mechanism: Blocks L-type calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle, producing arterial vasodilation with relatively little direct cardiac depressant effect.
drugs.spectrum: Hypertensive emergency requiring titratable IV BP control across most target-organ-damage patterns, and acute post-thrombolysis/post-thrombectomy stroke BP control.

dose.standard: Start 5 mg/hour IV infusion; increase by 2.5 mg/hour every 5–15 minutes to a maximum of 15 mg/hour, titrated to the target BP

renalAdj.regimen: No routine renal dose adjustment; titrate to hemodynamic response

monitoring: Continuous or very frequent BP monitoring during titration (arterial line preferred when feasible)
Heart-rate response, especially before use in aortic dissection
publicNotes: Reliable large-bore or central access preferred for a titrated infusion
In aortic dissection, control heart rate first with a beta-blocker before or together with nicardipine — vasodilation alone can cause reflex tachycardia and worsen shear stress

references.text: 2024 AHA Scientific Statement — Management of Elevated Blood Pressure in the Acute Care Setting

drugs.name: Nitroglycerin
drugs.pkpd: Rapid venodilation and antianginal effect with sublingual dosing. Tolerance develops with continuous exposure, so intermittent scheduling matters for longer-acting nitrate strategies, but acute SL use is mainly about correct rescue technique and escalation thresholds.
drugs.mechanism: Converted to nitric oxide, increasing cGMP and producing venous and coronary vasodilation with lower preload and myocardial oxygen demand.
drugs.spectrum: Acute angina relief, ischemic chest pain protocols, selected hypertensive pulmonary edema settings, and IV anti-ischemic support in monitored care areas.

dose.standard: Sublingual acute angina: 0.3–0.4 mg under the tongue every 5 minutes as directed for up to 3 doses while following emergency escalation guidance. IV regimens are protocol-based and titrated to symptoms and blood pressure

renalAdj.regimen: No renal dose adjustment needed
Dose is not renal-based, but these clinical situations can make nitroglycerin unsafe regardless of kidney function

monitoring: Whether recent sildenafil, tadalafil, or vardenafil exposure occurred
Ongoing chest-pain cause rather than symptom relief alone
publicNotes: If chest pain is not improving after appropriate emergency-threshold sublingual dosing, the next step is escalation of ACS care, not simply more and more nitroglycerin
Always ask about recent PDE-5 inhibitor use before giving nitrates

drugs.name: Norepinephrine
drugs.pkpd: Ward-reference summary focused on safety review, renal handling, and monitoring rather than exhaustive prescribing.
drugs.mechanism: See class-specific pharmacology; use this entry as a deterministic bedside safety reminder.
drugs.spectrum: General internal medicine ward reference and medication-lab safety rule support.

dose.standard: Continuous infusion is titrated to perfusion/MAP target through central or protocol-approved access.

renalAdj.regimen: No renal dose adjustment; dose is response-guided
Ensure access monitoring and antidote/extravasation protocol availability

sideEffects: Dose- or exposure-related toxicity in vulnerable patients
publicNotes: Norepinephrine dose should always be interpreted with the perfusion target and source-control/resuscitation plan.

drugs.name: Normal Saline 0.9%
drugs.pkpd: Isotonic (308 mOsm/L). Distributes throughout ECF. ~25% remains intravascular at 1h post-infusion. Contains Na⁺ 154 + Cl⁻ 154 mEq/L — supraphysiological chloride.
drugs.mechanism: Expands extracellular fluid volume. High Cl⁻ load → hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis (normal anion gap, NAGMA) with large volumes (>2–3 L). No potassium, calcium, or glucose.
drugs.spectrum: Volume resuscitation (sepsis, haemorrhage), drug diluent (broadest compatibility), hyponatraemia correction (slow), vomiting-induced hypochloraemic alkalosis, pre/post-contrast hydration, blood transfusion line flush.

dose.standard: Resuscitation bolus: 500 mL–1 L IV over 15–30 min (reassess after each); Maintenance: 1–2 mL/kg/h; Hyponatraemia correction: target ≤0.5–1 mEq/L/h, MAX 8–10 mEq/L per 24h (osmotic demyelination risk)

renalAdj.regimen: Standard; reassess fluid balance after each bolus
Use cautiously — reduced Na⁺/water excretion; monitor for volume overload
Restrict volume; 250 mL boluses; discuss fluid strategy with nephrology

sideEffects: Hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis (NAGMA with large volumes — pH ↓, HCO₃⁻ ↓, Cl⁻ ↑, AG normal; prefer LR/balanced crystalloid for >2 L resuscitation)
Volume overload (pulmonary oedema, CHF exacerbation, peripheral oedema)
Dilutional coagulopathy (massive volumes without blood products)
publicNotes: Normal saline remains the preferred fluid for blood product lines
Use caution with large-volume resuscitation because chloride load can worsen hyperchloremic acidosis
Balanced crystalloids are often preferred over NS when repeated large boluses are expected

references.text: SMART Trial — Semler et al., NEJM 2018

drugs.name: NPH Insulin (Humulin N / Insulatard)
drugs.pkpd: Onset: SC 1–4h. Peak: 6–10h (significant peak → nocturnal hypoglycemia risk). Duration: 12–18h. Cloudy suspension — resuspend by rolling gently 10× before use.
drugs.mechanism: Regular insulin complexed with protamine → delayed SC absorption. Pronounced action peak at 6–10h — timing matters for meal and bedtime planning. CAN be mixed with regular insulin.
drugs.spectrum: Basal insulin in T1DM and T2DM (increasingly replaced by long-acting analogues). Premixed formulations (NPH/RI 70/30) for BID dosing. Used in TPN insulin protocols.

dose.standard: 0.2–0.3 u/kg SC BID (morning + bedtime); or 0.1–0.2 u/kg SC at bedtime only (basal-only start); Humulin 70/30 (premix): 0.2–0.3 u/kg BID with meals

renalAdj.regimen: No fixed label-based percentage adjustment. Renal impairment increases hypoglycemia risk and may require more frequent dose adjustment and glucose monitoring
NPH action becomes less predictable; use cautious individualized titration with overnight hypoglycemia surveillance
No standard post-dialysis supplement. Reassess dosing around dialysis days and consider individualized alternatives if nocturnal hypoglycemia is frequent

sideEffects: Nocturnal hypoglycemia (peak 6–10h — highest risk with bedtime dose; set alarm check at 2–3 AM during initiation)
Protamine allergy (rare — may cross-react with fish allergy or prior protamine exposure)
monitoring: 2–3 AM glucose during initiation (nocturnal hypo surveillance)
publicNotes: NPH should be resuspended before use and carries a more pronounced peak than long-acting analogues
Night-time hypoglycemia surveillance matters when starting or escalating bedtime NPH

references.text: ADA Standards of Medical Care in Diabetes (2024)

drugs.name: Octreotide
drugs.pkpd: Reduces splanchnic and portal blood flow; the effect is adjunctive to definitive endoscopic hemostasis, not a substitute for it, and is started empirically before endoscopic confirmation.
drugs.mechanism: Synthetic somatostatin analog that reduces splanchnic arterial blood flow and portal pressure, indirectly lowering variceal wall tension.
drugs.spectrum: Suspected or confirmed acute variceal hemorrhage in cirrhosis/portal hypertension, alongside antibiotic prophylaxis and urgent endoscopy.

dose.standard: 50 microgram IV bolus (may repeat once within the first hour if bleeding continues), then a continuous infusion of 50 micrograms/hour for 2–5 days

renalAdj.regimen: No routine renal dose adjustment for short-term acute variceal-bleeding use

monitoring: Continue only alongside — not instead of — resuscitation and the endoscopy plan
publicNotes: Start at presentation whenever variceal bleeding is suspected — do not wait for endoscopic confirmation
This is adjunctive pharmacologic therapy; definitive hemostasis is endoscopic (band ligation) or, if needed, escalated procedural/surgical management

references.text: AASLD 2016 portal hypertensive bleeding guidance summary

drugs.name: Omeprazole
drugs.pkpd: Acid-activated prodrug with irreversible proton-pump inhibition. Serum half-life is short, but suppression persists until new pumps are synthesized. Full acid-suppression effect builds over several doses.
drugs.mechanism: Covalently inhibits the gastric parietal-cell H+/K+-ATPase, reducing basal and stimulated gastric acid secretion.
drugs.spectrum: GERD, peptic ulcer disease, H. pylori regimens, selected NSAID-related ulcer prevention, and other acid-suppression indications where oral therapy is sufficient.

dose.standard: 20 mg PO daily for many routine acid-suppression indications; some ulcer or H. pylori regimens use 20–40 mg once or twice daily depending on the indication

renalAdj.regimen: No renal dose adjustment needed
Standard dose; no routine post-dialysis supplement

sideEffects: C. difficile or enteric infection risk with unnecessary chronic therapy
monitoring: Mg or vitamin B12 if prolonged therapy or deficiency concerns arise
publicNotes: Omeprazole is a common outpatient PPI, but it is not always the best inpatient default if clopidogrel is also being used
Long-term continuation should be intentional rather than automatic

drugs.name: Ondansetron (Zofran)
drugs.pkpd: Selective serotonin 5-HT3 blockade reduces nausea signaling from the gut and central chemoreceptor trigger pathways. IV onset is fast, while oral and ODT forms remain very practical for ward symptom control.
drugs.mechanism: Blocks 5-HT3 receptors on vagal afferents and in central emetic pathways, reducing nausea and vomiting.
drugs.spectrum: Postoperative nausea and vomiting, chemotherapy-related nausea regimens, and common inpatient nausea control when bowel obstruction or dopamine-blocking toxicity is a concern.

dose.standard: 4 mg PO/IV/ODT q6–8h PRN for many inpatient uses; some protocols use higher scheduled doses depending on the indication

renalAdj.regimen: No renal dose adjustment needed
Daily exposure rises substantially, so lower total daily dosing is generally used

sideEffects: Rare serotonin syndrome when combined with multiple serotonergic drugs
monitoring: QT risk if baseline prolongation, electrolyte disturbance, or multiple QT-prolonging drugs are present
Response versus persistent vomiting that may indicate obstruction or another untreated cause
Bowel pattern if repeated doses are needed
publicNotes: Ondansetron is a strong first-line ward antiemetic, but do not let symptom control delay recognition of ileus, obstruction, intracranial pathology, or severe metabolic illness
IV push convenience can make it feel harmless, but QT and constipation still matter in frail inpatients

drugs.name: Oseltamivir (Tamiflu)
drugs.pkpd: Oral prodrug converted to oseltamivir carboxylate, an active neuraminidase inhibitor eliminated predominantly by the kidneys.
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits influenza neuraminidase, reducing release and spread of influenza A and B virions from infected cells.
drugs.spectrum: Treatment and post-exposure or outbreak prophylaxis of susceptible influenza A and B. It does not replace annual influenza vaccination.

dose.standard: Adults: treatment 75 mg PO BID for 5 days; prophylaxis 75 mg PO daily, with duration determined by exposure or outbreak context. Start treatment as early as possible.

renalAdj.regimen: Treatment 75 mg BID; prophylaxis 75 mg daily
Treatment 30 mg BID; prophylaxis 30 mg daily
Treatment 30 mg daily; prophylaxis 30 mg every other day
Treatment: 30 mg immediately, then 30 mg after each HD cycle for a course not exceeding 5 days; prophylaxis: 30 mg immediately, then after alternate HD cycles
Not recommended because dosing data are insufficient

sideEffects: Neuropsychiatric events reported, especially in pediatric patients; influenza itself can also cause neuropsychiatric symptoms
monitoring: Clinical response and complications of influenza
New confusion, abnormal behavior, or severe skin reaction
publicNotes: Renal adjustment differs between treatment and prophylaxis—verify intent before selecting a row
Starting promptly matters, but hospitalized or severe influenza decisions should not be reduced to a rigid 48-hour cutoff
Use current narrative pregnancy/lactation information rather than historical letter categories

drugs.pkpd: Ward-reference summary focused on safety review, renal handling, and monitoring rather than exhaustive prescribing.

dose.standard: Dose depends on opioid tolerance, pain severity, and route.

renalAdj.regimen: Use lower doses/longer intervals and monitor sedation

sideEffects: Dose- or exposure-related toxicity in vulnerable patients
publicNotes: Less renal-metabolite concern than morphine, but still accumulates clinically in frailty/AKI.

drugs.name: Pantoprazole (Protonix)
drugs.pkpd: Irreversible H+/K+-ATPase inhibition. Serum half-life is short, but acid suppression lasts much longer because new proton pumps must be synthesized. Full effect builds over several doses rather than immediately.
drugs.mechanism: Acid-activated prodrug that covalently binds the gastric parietal-cell proton pump, producing sustained suppression of gastric acid secretion.
drugs.spectrum: GERD, erosive esophagitis, upper-GI-bleed protocols, selected ICU stress-ulcer prophylaxis, and GI protection when high-risk NSAID or antithrombotic therapy cannot be avoided.

dose.standard: 40 mg PO/IV daily for routine acid suppression. Upper GI bleed protocols commonly use higher-dose IV regimens per local pathway

renalAdj.regimen: No renal dose adjustment needed
Standard dose; no routine post-dialysis supplement

sideEffects: C. difficile and enteric infection risk with chronic unnecessary therapy
monitoring: Reassess whether an ongoing indication still exists
Mg and vitamin B12 for prolonged therapy or unexplained deficiency symptoms
GI bleeding or ulcer-recurrence context rather than symptom suppression alone
publicNotes: Not every admitted patient needs stress-ulcer prophylaxis; deprescribe when the indication disappears
Pantoprazole is usually the easiest PPI choice when clopidogrel is also needed because omeprazole and esomeprazole inhibit CYP2C19 more strongly

drugs.name: Piperacillin-Tazobactam (Pip-Tazo)
drugs.pkpd: Time-dependent killing. Extended infusion (3–4h) or continuous infusion optimizes %T>MIC — critical for resistant organisms.
drugs.mechanism: Piperacillin inhibits PBPs (broadest penicillin spectrum); tazobactam inhibits class A/C β-lactamases (NOT ESBL reliably).
drugs.spectrum: Broad: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Enterobacteriaceae, anaerobes, streptococci, MSSA. NOT MRSA, CRE, ESBL (controversial), MDRAB.

dose.standard: 3.375 g IV q6h; nosocomial pneumonia: 4.5 g IV q6h. Extended-infusion protocols may use equivalent q8h schedules

renalAdj.regimen: 3.375 g q6h; nosocomial pneumonia: 4.5 g q6h
2.25 g q6h; nosocomial pneumonia: 3.375 g q6h
2.25 g q8h; nosocomial pneumonia: 2.25 g q6h
HD: 2.25 g q12h; nosocomial pneumonia: 2.25 g q8h; give 0.75 g after each HD session. CAPD: 2.25 g q12h; nosocomial pneumonia: 2.25 g q8h
Not covered by the official label; use institution/pharmacy dosing based on effluent flow and infusion strategy

sideEffects: Neurotoxicity (high doses + renal failure: myoclonus, encephalopathy)
publicNotes: Extended or continuous infusion can improve PK/PD target attainment for higher-MIC organisms
Do not rely on piperacillin-tazobactam for confirmed ESBL bacteremia when a carbapenem is indicated

references.text: MERINO Trial — Harris et al., JAMA 2018

drugs.name: Polyethylene Glycol (PEG) Laxative
drugs.pkpd: Onset: 1–3 days for regular dosing. Not systemically absorbed. PEG 3350 is an inert large polymer — passes through GI tract unchanged, retaining water via osmosis. No fermentation → less gas than lactulose.
drugs.mechanism: High-molecular-weight polymer binds water molecules → osmotic retention in colon → stool softening and increased bulk → stimulates peristalsis. No bacterial fermentation (unlike lactulose) → minimal gas and bloating.
drugs.spectrum: Occasional or chronic constipation, functional constipation, and opioid-associated constipation. Higher-dose disimpaction or bowel-prep regimens are product-specific and clinician-directed.

dose.standard: Generic PEG 3350 powders: 17 g PO once daily dissolved in 4–8 oz liquid. If using an electrolyte-containing PEG sachet product or a fecal-impaction regimen, follow the specific product/protocol rather than assuming the same dose applies

renalAdj.regimen: Not meaningfully systemically absorbed, but OTC labeling advises clinician supervision in kidney disease; monitor electrolytes for high-volume, prolonged, or electrolyte-containing regimens

sideEffects: Abdominal bloating (mild — less than lactulose, no fermentation)
Electrolyte disturbance (rare, associated with disimpaction doses — check electrolytes)
monitoring: Electrolytes before and after disimpaction protocol
publicNotes: PEG causes less gas and bloating than lactulose because it is not fermented by colonic bacteria
Well-tolerated for constipation management and often first-line for non-encephalopathy constipation
Product identity matters: plain PEG 3350 powders, electrolyte-containing sachets, and bowel-prep PEG products do not share one universal dosing scheme

drugs.name: Polymyxin B
drugs.pkpd: Concentration-dependent activity with narrow therapeutic window. Unlike colistin, dosing is less dependent on renal clearance, but toxicity monitoring remains central.
drugs.mechanism: Cationic peptide disrupts Gram-negative outer membrane integrity by binding lipopolysaccharide.
drugs.spectrum: Selected MDR/XDR Gram-negative organisms including Acinetobacter, Pseudomonas, and some CRE when susceptible. NOT Proteus, Serratia, Burkholderia cepacia complex, Gram-positive organisms, or anaerobes.

dose.standard: Weight-based IV dosing is protocol-specific; use ID/pharmacy guidance and avoid casual conversion from colistin units.
dose.loading: Loading dose may be used for severe infection per protocol.

renalAdj.regimen: No simple renal-dose formula; toxicity risk still requires close monitoring
Review concurrent nephrotoxins, hydration/perfusion, and ongoing need daily
Use specialist dosing guidance; do not extrapolate from colistin dosing

sideEffects: Neurotoxicity including paresthesias, weakness, or neuromuscular blockade
monitoring: SCr and urine output at least q48h during active therapy
publicNotes: Polymyxin B is a last-line resistant Gram-negative agent; daily necessity and toxicity review should be explicit
Do not confuse polymyxin B dosing with colistin dosing terminology

renalAdj.regimen: Use conservative replacement and repeat labs because accumulation risk is higher

publicNotes: Always reconcile active KCl when K is elevated or renal function worsens.

drugs.name: Prednisolone (Predonine)
drugs.pkpd: Intermediate-acting glucocorticoid with anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects. Dose, duration, and need for tapering are indication- and exposure-dependent.
drugs.mechanism: Binds cytosolic glucocorticoid receptors and alters gene transcription, reducing inflammatory cytokine signaling, leukocyte trafficking, and capillary permeability.
drugs.spectrum: Systemic treatment of selected inflammatory, allergic, autoimmune, respiratory, hematologic, and other steroid-responsive disorders; it does not treat an infectious cause itself.

dose.standard: Highly indication-dependent: label initial dosing is 5–60 mg PO daily. Use the lowest effective dose, preferably as a morning dose when once daily; document intended duration and whether a taper is required.

renalAdj.regimen: No established renal dose adjustment; individualize to indication and response.
Dose is not CrCl-based. Review fluid retention, blood pressure, glucose, infection, and GI risk rather than automatically reducing the dose.

sideEffects: Mood change, insomnia, agitation, or delirium
GI irritation or ulcer risk, especially with NSAIDs
Adrenal suppression and withdrawal risk after prolonged or high-dose exposure
monitoring: Explicit stop date or taper plan when exposure is prolonged
publicNotes: Prednisolone dosing cannot be safely inferred from the drug name alone; confirm the clinical indication and intended duration.
Do not stop prolonged or high-dose therapy abruptly. Assess cumulative steroid exposure and taper when clinically required.
Live vaccines are generally avoided during immunosuppressive corticosteroid dosing; assess vaccine and infection context before use.

references.text: DailyMed — Prednisolone Sodium Phosphate ODT Prescribing Information

drugs.name: Prednisone
drugs.pkpd: Converted to prednisolone after administration. Broad genomic and non-genomic anti-inflammatory effects, with clinically important hyperglycemia, mood, and infection effects that can appear within days.
drugs.mechanism: Glucocorticoid receptor agonism reduces inflammatory cytokine signaling, leukocyte trafficking, and capillary permeability.
drugs.spectrum: COPD or asthma exacerbations, inflammatory and autoimmune flares, allergic reactions, and many steroid-responsive conditions.

dose.standard: Highly indication-dependent. Common short burst examples include 40 mg PO daily for 5 days in COPD exacerbation or 40–60 mg daily in other inflammatory flares with tapering based on indication

renalAdj.regimen: No renal dose adjustment needed

renalAdj.crcl: Diabetes / acute infection / active GI bleed risk
renalAdj.regimen: Dose is not CrCl-based, but these clinical contexts often matter more than renal function alone when deciding whether to continue or taper

sideEffects: GI irritation or ulcer risk, especially with NSAIDs
monitoring: Sleep, mood, and taper plan if course is prolonged
publicNotes: For short steroid bursts, the operational mistakes are usually forgetting glucose effects, giving them too late in the day, or not clarifying whether a taper is needed
Prednisone is not a benign default add-on when infection source control or GI bleeding risk is already unstable

drugs.name: Procainamide
drugs.pkpd: Sodium-channel blocker with an active metabolite (NAPA) that itself has class III activity and is renally cleared, so the infusion is stopped at defined clinical endpoints rather than continued to a fixed total dose.
drugs.mechanism: Blocks fast sodium channels, slowing conduction velocity and prolonging the action potential, which widens the QRS and prolongs the QT.
drugs.spectrum: Stable, regular, monomorphic wide-complex tachycardia and select atrial arrhythmias when other agents are unsuitable, per the ACLS tachycardia algorithm.

dose.standard: 20–50 mg/min IV infusion until the arrhythmia is suppressed, hypotension develops, the QRS widens by more than 50% of baseline, or a maximum of 17 mg/kg total is given; maintenance infusion 1–4 mg/min

renalAdj.regimen: Standard dosing with routine ECG/BP monitoring
The active metabolite NAPA accumulates in renal impairment; reduce the maintenance rate and monitor QTc more closely

sideEffects: Drug-induced lupus-like syndrome with prolonged use
monitoring: Continuous ECG and BP throughout the infusion
QRS width and QTc trend against baseline
Renal function for NAPA accumulation with any ongoing use
publicNotes: Stop at any defined endpoint (arrhythmia suppressed, hypotension, QRS widening >50%, or max dose) rather than continuing to a fixed total
Avoid combining with other QT-prolonging antiarrhythmics without expert guidance

sideEffects: Dose- or exposure-related toxicity in vulnerable patients
publicNotes: Can compound QT risk when electrolytes are low or other QT drugs are active.

drugs.name: Rapid-Acting Insulin (NovoRapid / Humalog)
drugs.pkpd: SC onset: 10–20 min. Peak: 1–3h. Duration: 3–5h. Inject immediately before meals (within 15 min of eating). Faster and shorter vs. regular insulin → less interprandial hypoglycemia.
drugs.mechanism: Amino acid modifications reduce self-association → faster SC absorption. Same receptor and mechanism as regular insulin. Primarily used SC for mealtime coverage; some rapid-acting products have IV labeling, but routine inpatient IV insulin protocols usually use regular insulin.
drugs.spectrum: Mealtime insulin in basal-bolus regimen (T1DM, intensive T2DM), corrective (supplemental) doses, insulin pumps (CSII). Superior to regular insulin for post-prandial glucose control.

dose.standard: Mealtime: 0.05–0.1 u/kg SC with meals; correction: per ISF (insulin sensitivity factor = 1800/TDD); titrate doses based on carbohydrate intake and glucose trends

renalAdj.regimen: No fixed label-based percentage adjustment. Renal impairment increases hypoglycemia risk; individualize prandial dosing with more frequent glucose monitoring
Dose reduction is often needed, but the amount is patient-specific; monitor closely for delayed hypoglycemia, especially when appetite is variable
No standard supplemental dose. Reassess mealtime needs around dialysis and use individualized dosing with frequent glucose checks

sideEffects: Hypoglycemia (must eat immediately after injection — have fast-acting carbohydrate available)
publicNotes: Rapid-acting analogues are primarily mealtime insulins; routine inpatient IV insulin protocols usually use regular insulin instead
Hold prandial dosing when a patient is not eating, while continuing appropriate correction or basal strategy

references.text: ADA Standards of Medical Care in Diabetes (2024)

drugs.name: Regular Insulin (RI / Actrapid)
drugs.pkpd: IV: immediate onset, controlled by infusion rate. SC: onset 30–60 min, peak 2–4h, duration 6–8h. 100 u/mL — confirm correct vial before IV use.
drugs.mechanism: Binds insulin receptor → GLUT4 translocation → cellular glucose uptake. Inhibits hepatic gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis. Drives K⁺ intracellularly via Na/K-ATPase (useful in hyperkalemia).
drugs.spectrum: DKA/HHS (IV infusion), perioperative glucose control (IV), hyperkalemia with glucose (Dextrose 50% + 10 u RI IV), prandial corrective bolus (SC), NPO patients on TPN.

dose.standard: DKA/HHS IV drip: 0.1 u/kg/h; corrective SC bolus: 0.1 u/kg per protocol; hyperkalemia: 10 u RI IV + D50 50 mL IV push
dose.loading: DKA loading: 0.1 u/kg IV bolus optional (omit if initiating infusion directly)

renalAdj.regimen: No fixed label-based percentage adjustment. Renal impairment increases hypoglycemia risk; use more frequent glucose monitoring and individualized dose titration
Follow institution-specific protocol with hourly glucose and close potassium monitoring; renal impairment often lowers insulin requirements
No routine post-dialysis supplement rule. Use individualized dose reduction and frequent glucose monitoring around dialysis sessions

sideEffects: Hypoglycemia (have D50W at bedside; Q1h glucose on drip)
Hypokalemia (insulin drives K⁺ into cells — CHECK K⁺ before starting DKA drip; do NOT start if K⁺ <3.5 mEq/L)
monitoring: Bedside glucose: Q1h on IV infusion, Q4–6h on SC regimen
K⁺ before and during DKA insulin drip (target K⁺ 3.5–5.0 mEq/L)
publicNotes: Regular insulin is the standard IV insulin for DKA, HHS, and hyperkalemia protocols
Do not start a DKA insulin infusion until potassium is safe enough to tolerate intracellular shift

references.text: ADA Standards of Medical Care in Diabetes (2024)

drugs.name: Rifampicin (Rifampin)
drugs.pkpd: Concentration-dependent (AUC/MIC). Bactericidal — uniquely kills slow-growing/stationary-phase organisms and biofilm-embedded bacteria. Rapid resistance develops with monotherapy → ALWAYS use in combination.
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (β-subunit) → blocks mRNA synthesis. Resistance via rpoB mutations — emerges rapidly (1/10⁷–10⁸ organisms) if used alone.
drugs.spectrum: Staphylococcus (MSSA and MRSA — biofilm activity), Mycobacterium tuberculosis (cornerstone of TB therapy), Neisseria meningitidis (prophylaxis), Legionella (combination). NOT used alone for non-TB indications.

dose.standard: Biofilm/foreign body: 300–450 mg PO BID in combination; TB: 10 mg/kg (max 600 mg) PO q24h; Meningococcal prophylaxis: 600 mg PO BID × 2d

renalAdj.regimen: No dose adjustment needed (hepatic metabolism, biliary excretion)
Standard dose; not significantly cleared by dialysis

sideEffects: Orange-red discolouration of body fluids (urine, tears, sweat, saliva — harmless but MUST counsel patient; stains contact lenses permanently)
Hepatotoxicity (significant — monitor LFTs; avoid with other hepatotoxic drugs)
Flu-like syndrome (intermittent dosing — switch to daily dosing)
Drug interactions: MAJOR CYP3A4/2C9 inducer — dramatically reduces levels of many drugs: warfarin, calcineurin inhibitors, antiretrovirals, antifungals, oral contraceptives, many others
monitoring: Drug interactions — CRITICAL: check every co-medication (warfarin INR↓↓; tacrolimus levels → may need 3–5× dose increase)
publicNotes: Rifampicin should not be used as monotherapy outside specific TB regimens because resistance emerges rapidly
Its interaction burden is so large that medication reconciliation is mandatory

drugs.name: Senna (Sennoside / Glax)
drugs.pkpd: Onset PO: 6–12h. Metabolized by colonic bacteria to active anthrone metabolites. Minimal systemic absorption.
drugs.mechanism: Colonic bacteria convert sennosides to rheinanthrone → stimulates enteric nerve plexus and colonic smooth muscle → peristalsis → shortened transit time. Also inhibits water/electrolyte absorption from colon.
drugs.spectrum: Short-term constipation, opioid-induced constipation (preferred agent), post-operative constipation, constipation in palliative/cancer patients.

dose.standard: Adults: 1 tablet PO QD–BID (standard tablets); titrate up to 4 tablets BID for opioid-induced constipation (higher doses tolerated in palliative care)

renalAdj.regimen: No adjustment needed

sideEffects: Melanosis coli (dark discolouration of colonic mucosa with chronic use — benign, reversible)
monitoring: Duration of use (avoid chronic daily use >1 week without evaluation)
publicNotes: Senna is a preferred agent for opioid-induced constipation and widely used in palliative care
Prescribe prophylactically when starting opioids — do not wait for constipation to develop
Melanosis coli is a benign colonoscopy finding — not a sign of harm if use is appropriate

drugs.name: Spironolactone
drugs.pkpd: Slow onset compared with loop diuretics because downstream sodium handling and aldosterone signaling must shift. Hyperkalemia risk rises substantially when kidney function falls or other potassium-raising drugs are added.
drugs.mechanism: Competitive mineralocorticoid receptor antagonism in the distal nephron reduces sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion; also has antiandrogen effects.
drugs.spectrum: HFrEF mortality reduction, resistant hypertension, cirrhotic ascites, edema states with hyperaldosteronism, and primary hyperaldosteronism workup or treatment.

dose.standard: HF or hypertension: 12.5–25 mg PO daily, titrated as tolerated. Ascites regimens often start around 100 mg/day and are frequently paired with furosemide

renalAdj.regimen: 12.5–25 mg daily is a common start if serum potassium is acceptable
Consider 12.5–25 mg every other day or very cautious daily dosing with early potassium/creatinine recheck
Usually avoid routine use because hyperkalemia risk is high unless there is a specific expert-guided indication

monitoring: K⁺ and creatinine within about 1 week of start or dose change, then periodically
Breast or endocrine adverse effects on longer courses
publicNotes: Spironolactone is often low-dose high-value therapy, but only if potassium and kidney follow-up actually happen
Combining spironolactone with ACEi/ARB, potassium supplements, or NSAIDs is where many preventable hyperkalemia problems begin

drugs.name: Taita No. 1 Injection
drugs.pkpd: Low-sodium maintenance fluid with dextrose plus mixed electrolytes. Official listed ingredients are sodium chloride, potassium acetate, sodium acetate, magnesium chloride, potassium phosphate monobasic, and dextrose.
drugs.mechanism: Provides maintenance water, calories, and modest sodium with built-in potassium, magnesium, acetate, and phosphate. It is a Taiwanese maintenance formulation, not a crystalloid resuscitation fluid.
drugs.spectrum: Manufacturer-listed water, electrolyte and nutrient supplementation, including neonatal maintenance. The label listing does not establish a neonatal dosing protocol in this reference.

dose.standard: Manufacturer label statement: usually 500 mL per IV administration, adjusted for age and clinical condition. This is not a universal patient volume or infusion rate; the reviewed insert does not provide a neonatal/paediatric calculation or a CrCl/haemodialysis algorithm.

renalAdj.regimen: The reviewed manufacturer insert does not provide a CrCl or haemodialysis dosing table. Individualize the fluid/electrolyte prescription; for adults with renal, hepatic or cardiac impairment, NICE CG174 recommends expert assessment. This is not a default renal-adjusted dose or an assertion that no adjustment is needed.

sideEffects: General adult IV-fluid safety considerations include fluid overload and fluid/electrolyte imbalance; assess these risks in the patient's clinical context (NICE CG174).
This is a glucose/electrolyte-containing product. Review the actual formulation, the patient's current laboratory results and all other fluid/electrolyte inputs before prescribing.
monitoring: Use an individualized IV-fluid assessment and monitoring plan; assess clinical fluid status, fluid balance and relevant laboratory results (NICE CG174, adult guidance).
Review renal function and the total prescribed electrolyte/glucose intake. The cited product inserts do not establish product-specific laboratory intervals.
NICE CG174 monitoring guidance is for adults; neonatal/paediatric monitoring requires an age-specific clinical plan. No fixed Q-hourly schedule is supplied here.
publicNotes: Taita No. 1 is a distinct electrolyte/glucose formulation; confirm the bag composition rather than substituting another fluid by name alone.

Source review is limited to the product facts and administration wording identified below. Product-specific weight-based rates, CrCl/haemodialysis regimens, fixed monitoring intervals and neonatal/paediatric protocols are not established by this review.
NICE CG174 is cited for general adult IV-fluid assessment/reassessment only; it is not a Taita-specific dosing source. Clinician review of this monograph remains pending.
