drugs.name: Teicoplanin
drugs.pkpd: AUC/MIC-driven glycopeptide exposure with a long half-life. Loading doses are needed to reach target concentrations promptly.
drugs.mechanism: Binds D-Ala-D-Ala termini of peptidoglycan precursors, inhibiting Gram-positive cell wall synthesis.
drugs.spectrum: Gram-positive organisms including MRSA and many Enterococcus faecalis/faecium isolates when susceptible. NOT Gram-negative organisms.

dose.standard: Loading and maintenance are indication- and weight-specific; use local protocol or pharmacy guidance for serious infection.
dose.loading: Repeated loading doses are commonly required before maintenance because of long half-life.

renalAdj.regimen: Use protocol maintenance after loading
Maintenance interval or dose reduction often required
Use level-guided dosing where available

sideEffects: Nephrotoxicity is less common than vancomycin but still possible
publicNotes: Do not skip loading when treating serious infection; otherwise therapeutic exposure may be delayed
Confirm susceptibility and source control just as with vancomycin-class therapy

drugs.name: Tenecteplase
drugs.pkpd: Longer half-life than alteplase, allowing single-bolus administration; current evidence treats it as a noninferior alternative to alteplase for acute ischemic stroke.
drugs.mechanism: Genetically engineered variant of tissue plasminogen activator with greater fibrin specificity and a longer half-life than alteplase.
drugs.spectrum: Acute ischemic stroke within the eligible time window, as a single-bolus alternative to alteplase. Other indications (e.g., STEMI) use different, much higher protocol-specific doses not covered by this entry.

dose.standard: Acute ischemic stroke: 0.25 mg/kg IV, maximum 25 mg, given as a single bolus

renalAdj.regimen: Dose is weight-based, not renal-based

sideEffects: Intracranial or systemic hemorrhage — the major, defining risk
Angioedema (orolingual), especially with concurrent ACE inhibitor use
monitoring: Same post-thrombolysis neuro/BP monitoring as alteplase
Urgent repeat imaging for any unexplained neurologic decline
publicNotes: Single-bolus dosing simplifies administration compared with alteplase's bolus-plus-infusion regimen, but the eligibility and exclusion assessment is identical
Confirm the exact preparation and dose used locally — tenecteplase is also used at different, much higher doses for other indications, and mixing up the regimen is a real risk

references.text: AHA/ASA 2026 Guideline for Early Management of Acute Ischemic Stroke

drugs.name: Thiamine (Vitamin B1)
drugs.pkpd: A required cofactor for glucose metabolism; giving glucose to a thiamine-deficient patient without first (or simultaneously) replacing thiamine can precipitate or worsen Wernicke encephalopathy by consuming the last available thiamine stores.
drugs.mechanism: Cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase — enzymes required for carbohydrate metabolism and neuronal energy production.
drugs.spectrum: Given before or alongside dextrose whenever alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, or another thiamine-deficiency risk is possible, including during acute seizure/hypoglycemia management.

dose.standard: 100 mg IV or IM once for empiric prophylaxis/treatment in a patient with possible deficiency; higher doses (typically 200–500 mg IV) are used when Wernicke encephalopathy is clinically suspected, per local protocol

renalAdj.regimen: No renal dose adjustment needed

sideEffects: Rare hypersensitivity/anaphylactoid reaction with IV administration
monitoring: Clinical response (mentation, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia) if given for suspected Wernicke encephalopathy
No routine lab monitoring required for a single empiric dose
publicNotes: Give thiamine before or together with dextrose, not after, in a patient with a plausible deficiency risk — reversing the order is the classic avoidable error
A single empiric dose in a low-risk patient is low-harm; do not let uncertainty about deficiency risk delay dextrose in a genuine hypoglycemic emergency

drugs.name: Tigecycline
drugs.pkpd: AUC/MIC-dependent. Bacteriostatic. Extensive tissue distribution (Vd ~500–700 L) → low serum levels — NOT reliable for bacteremia or UTI. Biliary excretion.
drugs.mechanism: Binds 30S ribosomal subunit with ~5× higher affinity than tetracyclines → overcomes tetracycline-specific efflux pumps (TetM/O).
drugs.spectrum: Very broad: MRSA, VRE, ESBL/KPC-producing Enterobacteriaceae, Acinetobacter baumannii (MDR/XDR), anaerobes. NOT Pseudomonas (intrinsic efflux resistance), Proteus, Morganella.

dose.standard: 100 mg IV loading, then 50 mg IV q12h (or 100 mg q12h for XDR infections — off-label high-dose)
dose.loading: 100 mg IV loading dose

renalAdj.regimen: No dose adjustment needed (biliary excretion)
Standard dose; not significantly dialysed

sideEffects: Nausea/vomiting (very common — ~30%; most dose-limiting; prophylactic antiemetics recommended)
Hypofibrinogenaemia / coagulopathy (prolonged courses — monitor PT/APTT and fibrinogen)
Black box: increased all-cause mortality in clinical trials vs. comparators — use only when other options inadequate
monitoring: Clinical response — bacteriostatic agent; failure in bacteremia common
publicNotes: Tigecycline is generally a tissue-focused salvage agent, not a good bacteremia or urinary drug
Expect nausea and vomiting unless you pre-empt them

references.text: FDA Safety Communication — Increased Mortality Risk (2013)

drugs.name: Tiotropium (Spiriva)
drugs.pkpd: Once-daily long-acting antimuscarinic bronchodilator with sustained airway smooth-muscle relaxation. It is a maintenance inhaler, not a rescue medication.
drugs.mechanism: Blocks muscarinic receptors in airway smooth muscle, reducing cholinergic bronchoconstriction.
drugs.spectrum: Maintenance therapy for COPD and selected maintenance asthma regimens depending on formulation and inhaler device.

dose.standard: Device-specific once-daily inhaled maintenance dosing. Follow the exact product device instructions because HandiHaler capsules and Respimat inhalers are not interchangeable

renalAdj.regimen: Standard inhaled maintenance dosing
No automatic inhaler dose change, but monitor more closely for anticholinergic adverse effects because systemic exposure can rise

sideEffects: Blurred vision if powder or spray reaches eyes
monitoring: COPD symptom burden and rescue-inhaler frequency
publicNotes: Tiotropium is for maintenance control, not acute symptom rescue
Capsule-based inhalation products are inhaled through the device and should never be swallowed whole

drugs.name: TMP-SMX (Co-trimoxazole / Bactrim)
drugs.pkpd: AUC/MIC-dependent. Synergistic sequential folate pathway blockade. Excellent oral bioavailability (~90%).
drugs.mechanism: Sulfamethoxazole inhibits DHPS; trimethoprim inhibits DHFR → sequential double-blockade of folate synthesis → bactericidal synergy.
drugs.spectrum: CA-MRSA SSTI, PJP (high-dose), Stenotrophomonas maltophilia (drug of choice), Nocardia, Toxoplasma (prophylaxis/treatment), Listeria. Susceptible Enterobacteriaceae for UTI (if MIC confirms).

dose.standard: DS tablet (160/800 mg TMP/SMX) PO BID for UTI/SSTI; PJP treatment: 15–20 mg/kg TMP/day IV/PO in 3–4 divided doses × 21d

renalAdj.regimen: Standard dose
50% of standard dose
Use not recommended by the official label; if essential (for example severe PJP), use individualized specialist/pharmacy dosing with close monitoring
Label does not support routine standard dosing; use individualized post-HD dosing with close monitoring if therapy is essential

sideEffects: Hyperkalemia (TMP inhibits distal tubular K⁺ secretion — significant with ACEi/ARB/K⁺-sparing diuretics, CKD, elderly)
Pseudo-nephrotoxicity: SCr rises without true GFR change (TMP blocks creatinine secretion — check cystatin C if uncertain)
Bone marrow suppression (folate-depleted patients — leucovorin supplement for high-dose PJP)
SJS/TEN (sulfonamide component — rare but life-threatening; discontinue immediately if rash)
monitoring: K⁺ especially with ACEi/ARB, CKD, or elderly patients
SCr (may rise without true renal damage)
publicNotes: TMP-SMX is an important option for PJP and Stenotrophomonas and can also cover susceptible CA-MRSA SSTI
Watch for hyperkalemia and creatinine rise, especially in CKD or with RAAS blockers

references.text: IDSA UTI Guidelines — Gupta et al., CID 2011

drugs.name: Trazodone
drugs.class: Sedating Antidepressant / Serotonin Antagonist and Reuptake Inhibitor
drugs.pkpd: Sedation occurs at relatively low doses through histamine and alpha-1 effects, while antidepressant dosing is typically higher. Hepatic metabolism and additive sedation with other CNS depressants matter more clinically than renal clearance alone.
drugs.mechanism: Serotonin antagonist and reuptake inhibitor with prominent antihistamine and alpha-1 blocking effects at common sleep doses.
drugs.spectrum: Insomnia adjunct when dependence-prone hypnotics are undesirable, depression, and selected agitation or sleep-maintenance problems where sedation is acceptable.

dose.standard: Sleep-focused dosing often starts at 25–50 mg PO at bedtime; antidepressant dosing is higher and indication-specific

renalAdj.regimen: No standard renal dose adjustment, but start low in frailty or organ dysfunction because sedation and orthostasis still accumulate clinically
Use conservative bedtime dosing and monitor for oversedation, falls, and hypotension

monitoring: Need for ongoing bedtime use rather than reflex continuation
publicNotes: Trazodone is often chosen because it is not a benzodiazepine, but that does not make it benign in frail or fall-prone patients
Low-dose bedtime use is common on wards, yet the biggest practical risks are morning grogginess, orthostasis, and interaction stacking

drugs.name: Triazolam (Halcion)
drugs.pkpd: Onset: 15–30 min. Peak: 1–2h. Duration: 6–7h. T½: 1.5–5h (ultra-short — minimal daytime carry-over). Hepatic CYP3A4 metabolism → inactive metabolites (no active metabolite). Highly sensitive to CYP3A4 inhibitors (azoles, macrolides).
drugs.mechanism: Positive allosteric modulator of GABA-A receptor → sedation, anxiolysis, anterograde amnesia. Shortest-acting benzodiazepine hypnotic — selected to minimise next-day impairment versus longer-acting agents.
drugs.spectrum: Short-term insomnia (sleep onset and early maintenance), situational insomnia (travel, pre-procedure).

dose.standard: Adults: 0.125–0.25 mg PO at bedtime; Elderly/frail: 0.125 mg PO at bedtime strictly; Maximum: 0.25 mg/night; Limit to ≤2 weeks; avoid concurrent CYP3A4 inhibitors

renalAdj.regimen: Official labeling does not provide a renal-specific dose adjustment; observe usual precautions in renal impairment and use the lowest effective dose

sideEffects: Anterograde amnesia (travellers amnesia with high doses)
Rebound insomnia on discontinuation (more pronounced than with longer-acting agents)
Paradoxical agitation or aggression (rare, especially in elderly)
monitoring: CYP3A4 drug interactions (azoles dramatically increase triazolam levels → toxicity)
publicNotes: Triazolam is contraindicated with potent CYP3A inhibitors such as ketoconazole, itraconazole, nefazodone, and several HIV protease inhibitors; other azoles and macrolides can still raise levels substantially
Rebound insomnia on stopping is more pronounced than with longer-acting agents — taper if used >2 weeks
Shortest-acting benzodiazepine hypnotic — preferred when minimal daytime carry-over is a priority

drugs.name: Valproate (Valproic Acid)
drugs.pkpd: Broad-spectrum antiseizure medication available as a rapid IV load for acute status epilepticus; hepatic metabolism means significant drug-interaction and hepatotoxicity considerations with ongoing use.
drugs.mechanism: Multiple proposed mechanisms including enhanced GABAergic transmission and blockade of voltage-gated sodium and T-type calcium channels, broadly raising the seizure threshold.
drugs.spectrum: Second-line agent for benzodiazepine-refractory convulsive status epilepticus, alongside levetiracetam and fosphenytoin.

dose.standard: 40 mg/kg IV, maximum 3000 mg, infused over about 10 minutes

renalAdj.regimen: Dose is not renal-based; hepatic impairment is the primary dosing/safety concern

monitoring: Seizure activity and level of consciousness about 20 minutes after the infusion completes
Ammonia and LFTs if clinically indicated or with ongoing use
publicNotes: Avoid when a reasonable alternative exists in known hepatic disease, mitochondrial disease (e.g., suspected POLG mutation), or pregnancy
Hyperammonemic encephalopathy can mimic ongoing seizure/postictal state — consider it if consciousness does not improve as expected

references.text: ESETT trial — Randomized Trial of Three Anticonvulsant Medications for Status Epilepticus (NEJM 2019)

drugs.name: Valsartan
drugs.pkpd: Ward-reference summary focused on safety review, renal handling, and monitoring rather than exhaustive prescribing.
drugs.mechanism: See class-specific pharmacology; use this entry as a deterministic bedside safety reminder.
drugs.spectrum: General internal medicine ward reference and medication-lab safety rule support.

dose.standard: Indication-specific oral dosing; titrate to BP, renal function, and potassium.

renalAdj.regimen: No routine renal adjustment, but reassess during AKI, hypotension, or hyperkalemia

sideEffects: Dose- or exposure-related toxicity in vulnerable patients
publicNotes: ARB effects on potassium and renal perfusion are the key ward safety checks.

drugs.name: Vancomycin
drugs.pkpd: Time-dependent (AUC/MIC). Target AUC₂₄/MIC 400–600 mg·h/L (ASHP/IDSA/SIDP 2020). Replaced trough-only monitoring. Renal elimination → strict dose-adjust.
drugs.mechanism: Binds D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of peptidoglycan precursors → inhibits transglycosylation + transpeptidation. Bactericidal for staphylococci.
drugs.spectrum: MRSA, MRSE, Enterococcus (not VRE), penicillin-resistant S. pneumoniae, C. difficile (PO only). NOT Gram-negative organisms.

dose.standard: 15–20 mg/kg IV q8–12h (AUC-guided dosing)
dose.loading: 25–30 mg/kg IV loading dose for severe/life-threatening infections (meningitis, endocarditis, septic shock)

renalAdj.regimen: 15–20 mg/kg q8–12h (AUC-guided)
15–20 mg/kg q24–48h (level-guided)
Load 25 mg/kg; redose when AUC/level indicates (q48–72h)
Load 25 mg/kg; redose when pre-HD level <15–20 mg/L
15 mg/kg q24–48h (monitor levels closely)

sideEffects: Nephrotoxicity (dose-dependent; synergistic with aminoglycosides, NSAIDs, diuretics, contrast)
Red man syndrome (rate-related histamine release — infuse over ≥60 min; NOT a true IgE allergy)
Linear IgA bullous dermatosis (rare — drug reaction)
monitoring: Infusion rate: max 10 mg/min (15 mg/min for loading)
publicNotes: Prefer AUC-guided monitoring over trough-only monitoring where operationally possible
Use a loading dose for severe MRSA infection to reach target exposure sooner
Infuse slowly to prevent rate-related red man syndrome

references.text: IDSA MRSA Guidelines — Liu et al., CID 2011

drugs.name: Vasopressin
drugs.pkpd: Ward-reference summary focused on safety review, renal handling, and monitoring rather than exhaustive prescribing.
drugs.mechanism: See class-specific pharmacology; use this entry as a deterministic bedside safety reminder.
drugs.spectrum: General internal medicine ward reference and medication-lab safety rule support.

dose.standard: Shock dosing is protocol-based and usually adjunctive rather than titrated like catecholamines.

renalAdj.regimen: No renal dose adjustment; monitor ischemia and sodium/water effects
Review if digital, mesenteric, or cardiac ischemia emerges

sideEffects: Dose- or exposure-related toxicity in vulnerable patients
publicNotes: Vasopressin is a shock adjunct; persistent need should prompt reassessment of shock source and resuscitation rather than silent continuation.

drugs.name: Voriconazole
drugs.pkpd: AUC/MIC-dependent. Nonlinear (saturable) PK — small dose changes → large level changes. TDM mandatory for serious infections. Target trough 1–5.5 mg/L.
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits CYP51 (ergosterol synthesis) — broader spectrum vs. fluconazole via higher affinity for fungal CYP51.
drugs.spectrum: Drug of choice for invasive aspergillosis. Most Candida species (incl. C. krusei, C. glabrata). NOT Mucorales (critical — voriconazole failure risk in mucormycosis).

dose.standard: IV: 6 mg/kg q12h ×2 (loading), then 4 mg/kg q12h; PO: 400 mg BID loading, then 200–300 mg BID
dose.loading: 6 mg/kg IV q12h ×2 doses (loading)

renalAdj.regimen: IV or PO — standard dose
PO preferred; avoid IV unless benefit outweighs risk because SBECD accumulates in renal impairment
PO preferred. Voriconazole and SBECD are hemodialyzed, but a routine dose adjustment is not required; administer using specialist/pharmacy guidance

sideEffects: Visual disturbances (~30%): photopsia (flashing lights), altered colour perception, blurred vision — usually reversible, warn patient
Photosensitivity → squamous cell carcinoma risk (prolonged use)
Encephalopathy / hallucinations (check trough — toxicity if >5.5 mg/L)
Major drug interactions: CYP2C19/2C9/3A4 inhibitor (tacrolimus — reduce dose 66%; sirolimus — CONTRAINDICATED; warfarin; statins; many others)
monitoring: Visual acuity and colour vision (patient to report any changes immediately)
Drug interactions: reduce tacrolimus dose 66%; sirolimus CONTRAINDICATED (hold before starting)
CYP2C19 genotype ideally (poor metabolizers common in Asians ~15–25% — 4× higher levels)
publicNotes: Voriconazole is first-line for invasive aspergillosis but should not be relied on for mucormycosis
Therapeutic drug monitoring and interaction review are central to safe use

references.text: IDSA Aspergillosis Guidelines — Patterson et al., CID 2016

drugs.name: Warfarin
drugs.pkpd: Delayed onset and offset because active clotting factors must turn over. Narrow therapeutic index with large effects from diet, liver function, genetics, interacting drugs, and acute illness. INR is the operational exposure marker.
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1), reducing activation of factors II, VII, IX, and X plus proteins C and S.
drugs.spectrum: Mechanical valves, selected atrial fibrillation or VTE patients, APS or other situations where a DOAC is unsuitable or not preferred.

dose.standard: Individualized. Common adult starts are 2–5 mg PO daily with INR-guided adjustment. Acute VTE generally needs overlap with parenteral anticoagulation until the INR is therapeutic as indicated

renalAdj.regimen: No formal renal dose adjustment; dose to INR and start conservatively in frailty, malnutrition, liver disease, or high bleeding risk
Still INR-guided rather than CrCl-guided, but bleeding and calciphylaxis risk are higher so closer follow-up is important

publicNotes: Warfarin remains first-line for mechanical valves and some APS patients
Antibiotics, amiodarone, azoles, rifampin, herbal products, and vitamin K diet changes can all shift INR substantially
Never assume a stable outpatient dose will stay stable through an acute admission

drugs.name: Zolpidem (Stilnox)
drugs.pkpd: Onset: 15–30 min. Peak: 1–2h. Duration: 6–8h. T½: 2–3h. Hepatic metabolism (CYP3A4, CYP2C19). Preferential α1 subunit binding → sedation with less anxiolytic/muscle relaxant effect than benzodiazepines.
drugs.mechanism: Positive allosteric modulator of GABA-A receptor at the benzodiazepine site → preferentially binds α1 subunit (BZ1 receptor) → sedation. Less anticonvulsant and muscle relaxant effect compared to traditional benzodiazepines.
drugs.spectrum: Short-term insomnia (sleep onset), acute insomnia in hospitalised patients.

dose.standard: Women: 5 mg PO at bedtime; Men: 5–10 mg PO at bedtime; Elderly/debilitated: 5 mg PO at bedtime; use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration

renalAdj.regimen: No dosage adjustment recommended in the official label; use the lowest effective dose and monitor closely for oversedation, falls, and next-day impairment
Pharmacokinetics are not markedly changed in renal impairment, but clinical caution is still appropriate; start low and reassess frequently

sideEffects: Daytime sedation and next-day impairment (especially at 10 mg or in elderly)
Complex sleep behaviours: sleepwalking, sleep-driving, sleep-eating (FDA black box warning)
Dependence (schedule IV controlled — use only short-term)
CNS depression potentiated by alcohol and other CNS depressants
monitoring: Complex sleep behaviour enquiry at follow-up
Duration of use (limit to 2–4 weeks; reassess regularly)
publicNotes: Zolpidem is not appropriate for long-term insomnia — it addresses symptoms without treating the underlying cause
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the evidence-based long-term treatment
FDA lowered recommended doses for women (5 mg) due to higher blood levels — an effect also observed in many Asian populations

references.text: FDA Black Box Warning — Complex Sleep Behaviours (2019)

pocus.reviewLabel: Focused source check · clinician review pending
pocus.scope: Adult bedside reference. Scan prompts and selected measurements; interpret with image quality and the clinical picture.

topics.title: Lung / BLUE profiles
topics.summary: Pleural signs, anterior profiles and posterior findings.

steps.title: Compare both anterior lungs
steps.text: Identify pleura, sliding and A/B-line patterns on each side.

steps.title: Extend laterally and posteriorly
steps.text: Look for consolidation or pleural fluid (PLAPS: posterolateral alveolar and/or pleural syndrome).

steps.title: Combine the findings
steps.text: Use the profile as a differential prompt; include venous assessment when pulmonary embolism is suspected.

findings.meaning: Anterior A-lines with sliding. Obstructive airways disease is one possibility.
findings.caution: PE and posterior pneumonia remain possible.

findings.meaning: Bilateral anterior B-lines with sliding support an interstitial pattern.
findings.caution: B-lines are not specific to cardiogenic edema; consider ARDS, infection and fibrosis, plus distribution and pleural appearance.

findings.meaning: Consolidation, A/B asymmetry or B-lines without sliding can support pneumonia in the BLUE framework.
findings.caution: These findings also have noninfectious causes.

pitfalls: BLUE is a 2008 study framework, not a complete dyspnea rule-out pathway. Its original cohort excluded uncertain and rare diagnoses.
The 2026 consensus update was checked at abstract level only; this demo does not claim full guideline alignment.

checklist.label: Image quality and alternatives considered
checklist.detail: A completed checklist is not a diagnosis.

atlas.title: Pleural, interstitial & posterior signs
atlas.intro: Record the sampled site, pleural appearance and whether motion was actually seen; the published stills are morphology examples.
atlas.caution: A still B-mode frame cannot establish lung sliding, B-line synchrony, lung pulse or a dynamic air bronchogram.

items.title: A-lines · aerated pattern
criteria: Horizontal reverberations repeat at regular depth intervals below the pleural line.
Document sliding separately; A-lines with sliding and A-lines without sliding have different implications.
items.caution: A-lines alone neither exclude pneumothorax nor establish obstructive airways disease.

items.title: B-lines · interstitial pattern
criteria: Discrete bright vertical artefacts arise at the pleura, reach the far field without fading and erase A-lines.
In the original BLUE framework, at least three B-lines in one view form B+ lines; compare their distribution and pleural appearance.
items.caution: The still illustrates shape only. Confirm movement with sliding live; B-lines occur with several causes of reduced aeration.

items.title: Tissue-like consolidation
criteria: Loss of subpleural air permits direct visualization of tissue-like lung, sometimes similar to liver (hepatization).
Record location and extent; seek additional signs and clinical context for cause.
items.caution: Pneumonia, atelectasis, infarction and other processes can consolidate lung. Lesions that do not reach the pleura can be missed.

items.title: Irregular deep border · shred sign
criteria: A subpleural tissue-like area has an irregular interface with aerated lung; the source image also contains adjacent pleural fluid.
items.caution: Morphology supports consolidation but does not identify an infectious cause.

items.title: Pleural fluid at a dependent site
criteria: Identify a fluid space between chest wall/parietal pleura and lung/visceral pleura; dependent posterior or lateral fluid contributes to PLAPS.
Compare an anechoic simple example with a complex nonseptated example containing adjacent atelectatic lung.
items.caution: Appearance alone does not establish transudate, exudate, infection or a drainage indication. Figure 2B shows adjacent atelectatic lung, not proof of pneumonia.

atlas.title: Original BLUE anterior profiles
atlas.intro: BLUE combines bilateral upper/lower anterior observations with a posterolateral search and, for the A branch, venous assessment when indicated.
atlas.caution: These are pattern names from the 2008 ICU acute respiratory failure cohort, not stand-alone diagnoses or a general dyspnea rule-out test.

items.title: A profile
criteria: Predominant bilateral anterior A-lines with lung sliding.
The original study then considered PLAPS and venous thrombosis to distinguish conditional pathways.
items.caution: Pulmonary embolism and posterior pneumonia remain possible.

items.title: A′ profile
criteria: Predominant anterior A-lines with abolished sliding and no lung point identified in the original BLUE nomenclature.
Search for a lung point when first finding a nonsliding A-line pattern.
items.caution: Absent sliding alone is nonspecific; a lung point may be absent even with pneumothorax.

items.title: B profile
criteria: Predominant bilateral anterior B+ lines with sliding.
In the original cohort, a diffuse B profile strongly supported cardiogenic pulmonary edema.
items.caution: B-lines are not specific to cardiogenic edema in broader practice; assess distribution, pleura and context.

items.title: B′ profile
criteria: Anterior B+ pattern with abolished sliding; this supported pneumonia in the original framework.
items.caution: Neither the B-lines nor absent sliding identify infection on their own.

items.title: A/B profile
criteria: Predominant anterior B+ lines on one side and A-lines on the other; this asymmetric pattern supported pneumonia in the original cohort.
items.caution: Check focal noninfectious causes and the full clinical picture.

items.title: C profile
criteria: One or more anterior alveolar consolidations.
items.caution: Consolidation is a morphology finding, not a specific pneumonia diagnosis.

atlas.title: A-profile conditional pathways
atlas.intro: The A profile requires further assessment; preserve unexamined regions and unperformed venous scanning as unknown.
atlas.caution: Do not infer a negative venous or PLAPS examination from a limited anterior scan.

items.title: A profile + venous thrombosis
criteria: A profile with demonstrated lower-extremity venous thrombosis supported pulmonary embolism in the original BLUE study.
items.caution: A negative or unperformed venous scan does not exclude pulmonary embolism.

items.title: A profile + PLAPS
criteria: PLAPS means posterolateral alveolar and/or pleural syndrome: a dependent consolidation and/or pleural effusion.
After a negative venous assessment, an A profile with PLAPS supported pneumonia in the original pathway.
items.caution: PLAPS has other causes, including atelectasis or noninfectious fluid. A source still cannot establish dynamic air bronchograms.

items.title: A profile without PLAPS or DVT
criteria: After a negative venous assessment, an A profile without PLAPS favored COPD/asthma in the original cohort.
items.caution: This does not exclude all other causes of acute dyspnea; limited posterior access must remain unassessed.

topics.title: Pneumothorax signs
topics.summary: Sliding, B-lines, lung pulse and lung point—with an inconclusive path.

steps.title: Find the true pleural line
steps.text: Examine both anterior hemithoraces in a supine patient. Confirm the ribs and pleura before interpreting motion.

steps.title: Look for pleural contact
steps.text: Sliding, a true B-line or lung pulse excludes pneumothorax at that examined site.

steps.title: If all are absent, seek a lung point
steps.text: Extend the scan. Absence of all three signs is suspicious, but does not establish pneumothorax.

findings.meaning: A transition between sliding and non-sliding pleura strongly supports pneumothorax.
findings.caution: Mimics occur; confirm the anatomy and clinical context.

findings.meaning: Inconclusive: pneumothorax remains possible, including a large pneumothorax.
findings.caution: Reassess or obtain further imaging as clinically appropriate. Do not delay emergency care for a scan.

pitfalls: Absent sliding or an M-mode barcode alone is nonspecific: apnea, mainstem intubation, adhesions, bullae and severe lung disease can mimic it.
Poor windows are unassessed, not negative. A normal sign excludes pneumothorax only where it was seen.

checklist.label: Pleural line identified
checklist.detail: Avoid chest-wall motion and subcutaneous artifacts.

checklist.label: Uncertainty considered
checklist.detail: No lung point does not exclude pneumothorax.

atlas.title: Signs of pleural contact at the sampled site
atlas.intro: First identify the true pleural line between rib shadows. In a supine patient, scan anterior nondependent sites and compare sides.
atlas.caution: A reassuring sign excludes pneumothorax only where it was actually observed; a poor window is unassessed.

items.title: Sliding / seashore
criteria: Live pleural sliding shows respiratory motion at the pleural line.
M-mode seashore has parallel chest-wall lines above the pleura and a granular motion trace below it.
items.caution: The M-mode still records motion over time; an ordinary B-mode still cannot establish sliding. Exclusion applies only at this site.

items.title: True B-line
criteria: A true B-line originates at the pleura, reaches the far field and moves with the pleural interface when sliding is present.
items.caution: Confirm pleural origin; superficial E-lines from subcutaneous air are not B-lines. The still does not show movement.

items.title: Lung pulse
criteria: Cardiac-synchronous pleural movement with little or no ventilation indicates apposed pleural layers at that site.
items.caution: Requires live observation. The neonatal clip shows consolidated lung pulsing above the aorta, not the subtle adult pleural-line pulse described here.

atlas.title: When pleural contact signs are absent
atlas.intro: Absent sliding with anterior A-lines (A′), no true B-lines and no lung pulse raises suspicion; extend the scan to look for a transition.
atlas.caution: Absent sliding and a barcode pattern are nonspecific in apnea, mainstem intubation, adhesions, severe lung disease and other settings.

items.title: Barcode / stratosphere M-mode
criteria: Parallel horizontal lines persist above and below the pleural line, reflecting absent motion along the M-mode cursor.
items.caution: This records absent motion, not pneumothorax itself. Interpret with B-lines, lung pulse, location and clinical context.

items.title: No lung point found
criteria: If a transition is not found, record the examined area and result as inconclusive when suspicion persists.
items.caution: A large or complete pneumothorax may have no reachable lung point. Do not delay emergency care to complete scanning.

atlas.title: Lung point and mimics
atlas.intro: At the boundary of a partial pneumothorax, the respiratory cycle can bring the lung back into contact at one location.
atlas.caution: Confirm a respiratory-synchronous transition on live B-mode or M-mode, in the correct pleural anatomy; apparent lung points have published mimics.

items.title: M-mode transition
criteria: At the same pleural cursor position, seashore and barcode patterns alternate over time with respiration.
The published figure marks the transition with an arrow.
items.caution: Confirm respiratory timing and pleural anatomy; pleural thickening, bullae and other mimics can resemble a lung point.

items.title: B-mode transition example
criteria: The published two-panel example marks the point where sliding lung meets a nonsliding A-line pattern.
items.caution: Still frames cannot show the required respiratory alternation; confirm during a live scan.

items.title: Respiratory lung point · motion
criteria: Compare the non-sliding side at the dashed arrow with the adjacent lung entering and leaving the field during respiration.
This adult severe-ARDS case has a fragmented pleural line and subpleural consolidation beside the lung point.
items.caution: Absent sliding alone is nonspecific; confirm the respiratory transition and consider mimics.

topics.title: Shock / RUSH survey
topics.summary: Pump → tank → pipes. A scan sequence for undifferentiated shock.

steps.title: Pump · heart
steps.text: Assess pericardial fluid, gross LV function and RV size in available cardiac windows.

steps.title: Tank · filling and leakage
steps.text: Combine IVC context with lungs, pleural spaces and abdominal free-fluid views.

steps.title: Pipes · vessels
steps.text: Assess the abdominal aorta and proximal deep veins when relevant and within scan competence.

findings.meaning: Use the combined survey to focus the shock differential and subsequent assessment.
findings.caution: Mixed shock occurs. RV enlargement alone does not diagnose acute PE; pericardial fluid alone does not establish tamponade.
A negative focused scan cannot exclude all dangerous causes of shock.

pitfalls: RUSH is a structured adjunct to resuscitation. Do not delay urgent treatment or definitive imaging to complete every window.

checklist.label: Tank assessed
checklist.detail: IVC context, lungs and free fluid.

checklist.label: Pipes considered
checklist.detail: Aorta and venous assessment as indicated.

checklist.label: Unassessed windows identified
checklist.detail: Completion does not confirm a shock category.

atlas.title: Pump · heart
atlas.intro: Seek pericardial fluid, gross LV function and RV size in available windows.

items.title: Pericardial fluid
criteria: In parasternal long axis, locate fluid within the pericardial space, anterior to the descending aorta; distinguish pleural fluid posterior to it.
If fluid is seen, assess chamber behavior dynamically and integrate hemodynamics.
items.caution: Fluid alone does not establish tamponade; a still cannot demonstrate diastolic chamber collapse.

items.title: Gross LV function
criteria: Compare LV cavity size and wall thickening through systole and diastole in more than one view when possible.
The paired source frames illustrate a hypocontractile example; they do not provide a quantified EF.
items.caution: A still pair cannot replace a live cine assessment; visual EF is not biplane EF.

items.title: RV size
criteria: Compare RV with LV in an appropriate cardiac view; enlargement can raise concern for right-heart pressure or volume load.
items.caution: RV enlargement alone does not diagnose acute PE; chronic pulmonary hypertension and other causes are possible.

atlas.title: Tank · filling and leakage
atlas.intro: Combine venous context, lung/pleural findings and abdominal free-fluid windows.

items.title: IVC through respiration
criteria: Observe IVC caliber and respiratory change as one clue to right-sided pressure; integrate with heart and lung findings.
items.caution: IVC size/collapse is not a stand-alone test of fluid responsiveness.

items.title: Lung interstitial pattern
criteria: Compare bilateral lung zones for B-lines and pleural findings; distribution matters.
items.caution: B-lines are nonspecific; a still cannot demonstrate pleural sliding.

items.title: Abdominal free-fluid survey
criteria: Scan dependent right upper, left upper and suprapubic windows for free intraperitoneal fluid when clinically relevant.
items.caution: A negative or incomplete FAST survey does not exclude bleeding, retroperitoneal injury or other causes of shock. Free fluid alone does not identify its composition or source.

items.title: FAST · RUQ free fluid
criteria: Sweep the perihepatic and hepatorenal spaces. This published case shows fluid above the liver; it is not a Morison-recess example.
items.caution: One view from a postprocedural splenic-rupture case; complete the other windows.

items.title: FAST · LUQ free fluid
criteria: Survey the perisplenic and splenorenal spaces. The right-hand arrow marks fluid between spleen and left kidney in this published example.

items.title: FAST · pelvic free fluid
criteria: Scan above and around the bladder in longitudinal and transverse planes. The source labels this collection above the bladder.
items.caution: From the same case as the RUQ example; do not relabel the collection as a posterior cul-de-sac pocket.

atlas.title: Pipes · vessels
atlas.intro: Assess abdominal aorta and proximal leg veins when indicated and within scan competence.
atlas.caution: Select views to answer the immediate question; an unrevealing RUSH survey does not rule out all causes of shock.

items.title: Abdominal aorta
criteria: Sweep the aorta in long and short axes through the bifurcation; measure maximal diameter outer wall to outer wall, including mural thrombus.
An abdominal aorta >3.0 cm is aneurysmal.
items.caution: A visible aneurysm does not prove rupture; ultrasound can miss retroperitoneal bleeding or dissection.

items.title: Proximal leg veins
criteria: Use compression at the common femoral, proximal femoral and popliteal veins when indicated; failure of the vein to compress supports thrombosis.
items.caution: The still illustrates clot morphology. Assess compression dynamically; a limited negative scan does not exclude all DVT or PE.

items.title: Venous compression · probe positions
criteria: Use a linear probe in transverse orientation at the common femoral, femoral and popliteal levels, including junctions and intervening segments as the chosen protocol requires.
Center the vein and apply perpendicular pressure to bring its walls together.
items.caution: The diagrams show acquisition sites, not a scan result.

items.title: Venous compression · normal and abnormal
criteria: Normal: right common femoral vein collapses and reopens.
DVT case: left femoral vein remains open during compression.
items.caution: Separate cases/sites. Weak or off-axis pressure can mimic noncompressibility; one normal site does not exclude DVT elsewhere or PE.

topics.title: Fluid assessment / IVC
topics.summary: Separate perfusion, fluid responsiveness and congestion.

steps.title: Start with perfusion
steps.text: Frame the clinical question and reassess perfusion alongside the scan.

steps.title: Assess response dynamically
steps.text: For sepsis/septic shock, SSC 2026 suggests dynamic measures over static examination alone: for example passive leg raising with measured stroke-volume response.

steps.title: Reassess tolerance
steps.text: Integrate cardiac findings, lung patterns and the clinical course before further fluid decisions.

findings.meaning: May inform right atrial pressure assessment in a suitable spontaneous-breathing examination.
findings.caution: IVC alone does not establish fluid responsiveness or mandate a bolus.

findings.meaning: Reassess cause, distribution and the wider clinical picture.
findings.caution: B-lines are not a direct volume meter; ARDS, infection and fibrosis are alternatives.

findings.meaning: The original protocol used lung patterns during sequential shock assessment.
findings.caution: This demo does not turn 'give fluid until B-lines appear' into a treatment instruction.

pitfalls: SSC's dynamic-measure recommendation is conditional with low-certainty evidence.
Positive-pressure ventilation and altered respiratory effort limit simple IVC collapse interpretation.

checklist.label: Dynamic response considered
checklist.detail: Only interpret measures under appropriate conditions.

checklist.label: Fluid tolerance reassessed
checklist.detail: Include lung, cardiac and clinical findings.

atlas.title: IVC & right atrial pressure
atlas.intro: In spontaneous breathing, combine end-expiratory diameter with inspiratory collapse.
atlas.caution: IVC estimates pressure, not fluid responsiveness. Positive-pressure ventilation, effort and right-heart disease alter interpretation.

items.title: Acquisition examples
criteria: Identify the IVC entering the right atrium. Measure perpendicular to its long axis, 0.5–3.0 cm from the atrium.
Keep the M-mode cursor centered on the IVC during respiration.

items.title: ASE adult RAP bands
criteria: ≤2.1 cm + ≥50% collapse → 3 mmHg (0–5).
>2.1 cm + <50% collapse → 15 mmHg (10–20).
Discordant size/collapse → 8 mmHg initially; use secondary signs.
items.caution: These are reference bands; the teaching images are acquisition examples, not assigned RAP categories.

atlas.title: Lung A- / B-lines
atlas.intro: Compare multiple zones, pleural appearance and serial change.
atlas.caution: B-lines may occur in edema, ARDS, pneumonia or fibrosis; distribution and context matter.

items.title: A-line pattern
criteria: Horizontal reverberations repeat below the pleura.
items.caution: A-lines also occur in pneumothorax: assess sliding and other signs at that site.

items.title: B-line pattern
criteria: Vertical artefacts originate at pleura, reach the far field and erase A-lines; assess motion with sliding.
Multiple bilateral B-lines support an interstitial pattern, not a specific cause.

atlas.title: VExUS · venous congestion
atlas.intro: Original VExUS C: maximal respiratory IVC diameter plus three venous Doppler patterns.
atlas.caution: Derived in 145 cardiac-surgery patients. Grades inform congestion assessment, not a fluid or diuretic prescription.

items.title: Grade 0–3 criteria
criteria: IVC <2.0 cm → grade 0.
IVC ≥2.0 cm: no severe patterns → grade 1; one → grade 2; two or three → grade 3.
items.caution: The 2.0 cm gate differs from ASE RAP’s 2.1 cm threshold. Missing Doppler is not normal; grade 0 does not exclude all congestion.

items.title: Hepatic vein
criteria: Normal: S > D. Mild: S < D without reversal. Severe: systolic reversal.
items.caution: Use ECG timing; tricuspid regurgitation affects this waveform.

items.title: Portal vein
criteria: Pulsatility fraction = (Vmax − Vmin) / Vmax × 100%.
Normal: <30%. Mild: 30–<50%. Severe: ≥50% (Fig. 1 definition).
items.caution: Portal disease and cirrhosis affect interpretation.

items.title: Intrarenal vein
criteria: Normal: continuous. Mild: interrupted S + D. Severe: interrupted D-only flow.
items.caution: In these examples, inspect venous flow below baseline; the arterial signal is above.

atlas.title: Fluid responsiveness
atlas.intro: Assess perfusion, responsiveness and congestion separately.
atlas.caution: A positive response does not by itself establish a need for more fluid.

items.title: Measure a reversible response
criteria: For sepsis/septic shock, SSC 2026 suggests dynamic assessment: e.g. passive leg raise with a measured stroke-volume response.
Compare before/during the maneuver using a suitable validated method; a static IVC image is insufficient.
items.caution: The SSC recommendation is conditional with low-certainty evidence.

topics.title: Renal / bladder assessment
topics.summary: Hydronephrosis grades, parenchymal patterns and bladder assessment.

steps.title: Assess the bladder
steps.text: Scan in two planes for distension. Interpret with voiding and catheter status.

steps.title: Examine both kidneys
steps.text: Sweep long and short axes for collecting-system dilation; compare sides.

steps.title: Resolve equivocal findings
steps.text: Consider a post-void reassessment and further imaging when suspicion persists.

findings.caution: A full bladder, pregnancy or high urine flow can also cause dilation; correlate clinically.

findings.meaning: No dilation seen in the assessed views.
findings.caution: Early obstruction or dehydration can have little or no dilation. This does not exclude obstruction or determine the cause of AKI.

pitfalls: Extrarenal pelvis, cysts and vessels can mimic hydronephrosis. Color Doppler may help distinguish vessels.
POCUS may not show the obstructing stone or an alternative cause of abdominal pain.

checklist.label: Both kidneys assessed
checklist.detail: Use two planes and note limited views.

checklist.label: Mimics and residual uncertainty considered
checklist.detail: No dilation is not a complete obstruction rule-out.

atlas.title: Hydronephrosis · SFU 0–4
atlas.intro: Grades 0–4, with published ultrasound examples and SFU diagrams.
atlas.caution: SFU is a pediatric morphology scale. In adults, describe dilation and thinning; grade does not establish obstruction or renal function.

items.title: Grade 0 · no dilation
criteria: No visible collecting-system dilation; parenchyma preserved.

items.title: Grade 1 · pelvis only
criteria: Renal pelvis visible/dilated; calyces remain undilated.

items.title: Grade 2 · some calyces
criteria: Pelvis and some, but not all, calyces are dilated; parenchyma preserved.

items.title: Grade 3 · all calyces
criteria: Pelvis and virtually all calyces are dilated; parenchymal thickness preserved.

items.title: Grade 4 · parenchymal thinning
criteria: Pelvicalyceal dilation plus parenchymal thinning.
items.caution: Grade 4 spans a wide severity range; document the thinning separately.

atlas.title: Parenchymal disease
atlas.intro: Compare cortical brightness, thickness, size and corticomedullary distinction.
atlas.caution: Echogenicity is nonspecific. Ultrasound alone cannot assign an AKI cause or establish chronicity.

items.title: Pattern suggesting chronic disease
criteria: Small kidney, thin cortex and increased echogenicity together support chronic parenchymal disease.

items.title: Acute injury can also look bright
criteria: Normal or enlarged size with increased cortical echogenicity can occur in acute injury.
items.caution: The source diagnosis required biopsy; this appearance does not diagnose ATN.

items.title: Brightness without a specific diagnosis
criteria: Reduced corticomedullary distinction may accompany several parenchymal processes.

atlas.title: Dilation & mimics
atlas.intro: Sweep in two planes; look for communicating fluid spaces and use color Doppler when needed.
atlas.caution: A full bladder, pregnancy or brisk urine flow can dilate the collecting system; early obstruction may show little dilation.

items.title: Branching, communicating spaces
criteria: Hydronephrosis follows the pelvis and calyces. Compare both kidneys and reassess the bladder.

items.title: Cyst versus collecting system
criteria: Simple cortical cyst: round, thin-walled, anechoic, with posterior enhancement.

items.title: Extrarenal pelvis / vessels
criteria: Extrarenal pelvis lacks dilated calyces. Parapelvic cysts are noncommunicating fluid spaces. Color flow helps identify vessels; equivocal views need further assessment.

topics.title: Cardiac measurements
topics.summary: Selected adult EF, TAPSE and IVC/RAP references with acquisition context.

measurements.name: LV ejection fraction · 2D biplane
measurements.technique: Biplane volume-derived EF from apical 4- and 2-chamber views; avoid foreshortening.
measurements.context: ASE/EACVI 2015 adult reference ranges. A visual bedside estimate is not equivalent to a measured biplane EF.

measurements.name: TAPSE
measurements.technique: RV-focused apical 4-chamber view; M-mode aligned with lateral tricuspid annular motion.
measurements.context: ASE 2025 normal threshold. Angle/load dependent; interpret with other RV findings.

measurements.name: IVC → estimated RAP
measurements.technique: Subcostal view; end-expiratory diameter 0.5–3 cm from the RA junction; assess inspiratory collapse with sniff/quiet breathing.
measurements.context: Spontaneous breathing. Estimate range 0–5 mmHg; not a fluid-responsiveness test.

measurements.name: IVC → estimated RAP
measurements.technique: Use the same acquisition method; avoid oblique diameter measurement.
measurements.context: Estimate range 10–20 mmHg. Discordant size/collapse gives an intermediate estimate of 8 mmHg (5–10); integrate other findings.

pitfalls: IVC estimates have special limitations with positive-pressure ventilation, pregnancy, athletes and inadequate respiratory maneuvers.
Selected adult references only; pediatric, valve and comprehensive diastolic assessment are outside this demo.

atlas.title: LV ejection fraction
atlas.intro: 2D biplane EF is a volume-derived measurement from apical four- and two-chamber views.

items.title: Biplane acquisition
criteria: Avoid apical foreshortening; trace the LV endocardial border in both views at end-diastole and end-systole.
EF = (EDV − ESV) / EDV × 100%; the four frames illustrate acquisition, not a bedside visual EF estimate.
items.caution: Poor borders or foreshortening weaken the volume estimate. A static example cannot demonstrate contraction over a full cardiac cycle.

items.title: ASE/EACVI adult reference
criteria: Biplane EF reference: male 52–72%; female 54–74%.
A qualitative bedside impression of LV function is not a measured biplane EF.
items.caution: Sex-specific 2015 adult reference ranges; interpret a measured result with image quality and clinical context.

atlas.title: TAPSE
atlas.intro: M-mode distance traveled by the lateral tricuspid annulus during systole.

items.title: Apical four-chamber M-mode
criteria: Use an RV-focused apical four-chamber view; align the M-mode cursor with lateral tricuspid annular motion.
Measure excursion from end-diastolic position to peak systolic displacement; ASE 2025 normal reference is >1.7 cm.
items.caution: TAPSE reflects basal longitudinal motion and is angle/load dependent; do not treat it alone as global RV function.

atlas.title: IVC and estimated RAP
atlas.intro: In spontaneous breathing, pair end-expiratory IVC diameter with inspiratory collapse.

items.title: IVC acquisition
criteria: Identify IVC entry into the right atrium; measure 0.5–3 cm from the junction, perpendicular to its long axis.
Observe inspiratory change with a sniff or quiet breathing.
items.caution: These stills demonstrate acquisition; respiratory behavior requires a dynamic scan.

items.title: ASE adult RAP bands
criteria: ≤2.1 cm with ≥50% collapse: estimate 3 mmHg (0–5).
>2.1 cm with <50% collapse: estimate 15 mmHg (10–20).
Discordant size/collapse: intermediate estimate 8 mmHg (5–10), integrated with secondary signs.
items.caution: IVC-derived RAP is not fluid responsiveness. Positive-pressure ventilation, respiratory effort and right-heart disease limit interpretation.

topics.title: Abdominal measurements
topics.summary: Aorta, gallbladder wall and bile duct: use the correct plane and wall convention.

measurements.name: Abdominal aorta
measurements.technique: Measure maximum diameter outer wall to outer wall, perpendicular to the vessel; sweep in two planes to the bifurcation.
measurements.context: Include mural thrombus within the wall-to-wall measurement. POCUS does not reliably exclude rupture or dissection; urgent assessment follows clinical concern.

measurements.name: Gallbladder wall
measurements.technique: Measure thickness perpendicular to the anterior wall, with the beam directed normally to it and the gallbladder sufficiently distended.
measurements.context: A contracted/nonfasting gallbladder can look thick. Thickening alone does not diagnose cholecystitis.

measurements.name: Common bile duct
measurements.technique: Trace the extrahepatic duct from hilum to pancreatic head. Measure inner wall to inner wall at multiple visible points; distinguish common hepatic duct from common bile duct.
measurements.context: Gallbladder in situ. Diameter varies with age and after cholecystectomy; do not apply a single cutoff to every patient. Correlate with symptoms and biochemistry.

pitfalls: Poorly visualized structures remain unassessed. A normal diameter alone does not exclude clinically important pathology.

atlas.title: Abdominal aorta
atlas.intro: Follow the full aorta through the bifurcation and record the maximum outer-wall diameter.
atlas.caution: A limited view is indeterminate. Diameter assessment alone does not establish or exclude rupture or dissection.

items.title: Aneurysmal diameter and mural thrombus
criteria: Sweep proximal, mid and distal aorta in longitudinal and transverse planes. Measure maximum diameter outer wall to outer wall, perpendicular to its long axis; include mural thrombus within the wall-to-wall diameter.

ACEP Sonoguide and 2022 ACC/AHA use >3.0 cm for an adult AAA threshold. A screening review uses ≥3.0 cm for infrarenal AAA; at exactly 3.0 cm, record the measured value and follow the local reporting convention.
items.caution: The image is a large AAA case illustrating lumen versus thrombus, not a diagnostic example of rupture.

atlas.title: Gallbladder wall and stones
atlas.intro: Interpret wall thickness in a fasting, adequately distended gallbladder and scan for stones and inflammatory context.
atlas.caution: Wall thickening alone is nonspecific; acute cholecystitis requires clinical and imaging synthesis.

items.title: Thin wall in a distended gallbladder
criteria: A well-distended fasting gallbladder normally has a thin single-layer wall, commonly ≤3 mm; measure thickness perpendicular to the anterior wall with the beam directed normally to it.
items.caution: Source Fig. 2 calipers measure gallbladder size, not wall thickness. Postprandial contraction can make the wall appear thick.

items.title: Shadowing stone with secondary findings
criteria: An echogenic focus with posterior acoustic shadowing supports a gallstone. Assess wall layering/thickening, gallbladder distension, pericholecystic fluid and focal sonographic Murphy tenderness.
Tokyo Guidelines 2018 combine local inflammation, systemic inflammation and characteristic imaging; this image shows one published acute cholecystitis case.
items.caution: A stone or thick wall alone does not diagnose acute cholecystitis; missing or poor-quality views remain unassessed.

items.title: Thick wall from congestion
criteria: A thick stratified wall may also occur with right heart failure, cirrhosis, ascites, hypoalbuminemia or hepatitis; review symptoms, stones, Murphy tenderness and systemic findings.
items.caution: Published Fig. 7a is a right-heart-failure case without gallbladder inflammation; it is a contextual example, not a rule-out image.

atlas.title: Extrahepatic bile duct
atlas.intro: Trace the duct and identify the cystic duct junction before assigning a diameter.
atlas.caution: A single duct diameter neither proves nor excludes obstruction; correlate with symptoms, laboratory findings and visible anatomy.

items.title: CBD measurement near the cystic duct junction
criteria: Measure inner wall to inner wall, perpendicular to the duct in a longitudinal view. Check multiple visible portions, report the largest valid diameter, and avoid including the cystic duct confluence.

The usual 6–7 mm upper reference applies chiefly with gallbladder in situ; published reference ranges vary, and age and prior cholecystectomy may enlarge the duct. Source Fig. 3a shows 5.1 and 6.1 mm readings at nearby sites.
items.caution: The source figure illustrates location-dependent measurement, not a universal normal cutoff or proof of an unobstructed duct.

sources.label: BLUE original study · Lichtenstein & Mezière, Chest 2008
Lung B-line artefacts and their use · Dietrich et al., 2016
International PoCLUS consensus · 2026 publication (abstract checked)

guides.title: Delirium / acute confusional state
guides.reviewNotice: NICE delirium recognition and support; MHRA haloperidol safeguards. A screen is not the final diagnosis.
guides.resourceNotice: Internal hospital resource tables are omitted from this shared edition.
guides.scope: Adult ward/long-term-care delirium recognition, screening, cause review, support, short-term behavioural-safety consideration and reassessment. It is not a diagnosis, emergency-neurology protocol, medication order, dosing protocol or discharge decision.
reviewLimitations: NICE supplies the current ward-screening and short-term-haloperidol principles, not a universal numeric delirium regimen.
The linked 106 local source rows are retained as product/order identity references. Their headings, raw doses and embedded advice were not treated as current prescribing guidance.

sources.label: NICE CG103 delirium guidance (updated 2023)
MHRA haloperidol safety reminder for acute delirium (2021)

entry.title: Confirm presentation and current danger
entry.scope: Entry, actual treatment exposure and current response are separate. Unknown remains unconfirmed.

fields.label: Medical / neurologic emergency now?
fields.threshold: New focal deficit, unresponsiveness, seizure/status, airway or circulatory compromise overrides a delirium screen.

fields.label: Acute or fluctuating change?
fields.threshold: Ask the person, family or staff about a change over hours to days in attention, awareness, cognition, mobility, sleep, perception or behaviour.

fields.label: Care setting for the screen?
fields.threshold: NICE specifies 4AT for ward/long-term care and CAM-ICU or ICDSC for critical care/recovery.

fields.label: Delirium screen result?
fields.threshold: A positive 4AT, CAM-ICU or ICDSC prompts a competent clinical assessment; it does not itself establish a final diagnosis.

fields.label: Possible cause review?
fields.threshold: Consider more than one cause. Use symptoms, observations, examination, medicines and directed testing rather than a routine panel.

fields.label: Distress or risk to self / others?
fields.threshold: Hypoactive delirium can still be distressing. This is separate from an immediate medical emergency.

fields.label: Verbal / non-verbal de-escalation?
fields.threshold: Use communication, reorientation, reassurance and a suitable environment first when it is safe to do so.

fields.label: Haloperidol safety review?
options: ECG / electrolytes reviewed; no PD / Lewy-body dementia
fields.threshold: In frail or older people, MHRA advises baseline ECG, correction of electrolyte disturbance and monitoring. Parkinson disease and dementia with Lewy bodies are contraindications.

fields.label: Short-term calming medicine already given?
options: Given · agent, dose and time recorded
fields.threshold: Reconcile the exact product, dose, route, time, response and adverse effects before any further medicine.

fields.label: Current course?
fields.threshold: Persistent symptoms need renewed cause review. A new deterioration overrides earlier reassurance or apparent control.

quickReference.summary: Confirm acute change and current danger; a positive screen starts clinical assessment and cause treatment.
recognition: Hours-to-days, fluctuating disturbance in attention, awareness or cognition; hypoactive presentations are easily missed.
redFlags: New focal deficit, unresponsiveness, seizure/status, airway, breathing or circulatory compromise.
Worsening after initial care or medication.

steps.text: 4AT on the ward; CAM-ICU or ICDSC in critical care/recovery.
Identify and manage one or more causes; reorient and reassure.

monitoring: Reassess consciousness, attention, current safety, trigger treatment and any medicine effect.

guides.title: Acute Transfusion Reaction
guides.reviewNotice: Stop and assess suspected reactions; no automatic transfusion restart.
guides.resourceNotice: Internal hospital resource tables are omitted from this shared edition.
guides.scope: Adult suspected acute transfusion-reaction recognition, initial safety response, pattern-directed investigation, and reassessment. It is not a blood-bank SOP, component-selection interface, medication-administration record, transfusion order, or authorization to restart.
reviewLimitations: The BSH guideline is the branch source for recognition, initial response, mild/severe distinctions and symptom-directed investigation. It explicitly does not provide detailed cardiac/respiratory-failure or bacterial-sepsis treatment protocols.

No local blood-bank SOP, component identity, compatibility/crossmatch order, product availability, administration preparation, or restart authority was verified here. Those remain local transfusion-service decisions.
TACO/TRALI categories require clinical and laboratory/radiographic review; this guide deliberately does not classify either from timing alone or select a diuretic regimen.

sources.label: BSH guideline on acute transfusion reactions (2023)
CDC bacterial-contamination clinical guidance (2024)
AABB/NHSN adverse-reaction definitions

entry.title: Confirm presentation and immediate danger
entry.scope: Unknown findings remain unconfirmed; initial treatment and response are separate.

fields.label: Review point
fields.essential: Initial safety and later response are separate; an unknown phase never hides a suspected reaction.

fields.label: New symptom or sign plausibly related to a recent component?
fields.essential: A suspected reaction triggers the stop-and-assess response before a subtype is assigned.

fields.label: Implicated component status
fields.essential: Stop a suspected component and keep compatible-saline access; completed units are not restarted here.

fields.label: Immediate identity, component and observation check
fields.essential: Check identity/label and component, assess ABC/observations, and notify the transfusion service.

fields.label: Current airway, breathing or circulation compromise?
fields.essential: Current ABC compromise overrides every earlier label: call emergency support and do not restart.

fields.label: Current symptom pattern after immediate safety review
options: Suspected anaphylaxis · airway, breathing or circulation involvement
Sustained fever/rigors, shock, pain, dark urine, or bleeding
Acute dyspnoea / hypoxaemia; allergy not the explanation
Alternative explanation more likely after assessment
fields.essential: This is a working pattern; severe reactions can overlap and treatment does not wait for tests.

fields.label: Strictly isolated mild pattern?
options: Yes — fever 38–<39 C / rise 1–<2 C, or rash only
fields.essential: Mild means isolated fever/rash with no concerning feature or observation change.

fields.label: Hemolysis or bacterial-contamination concern?
options: Not supported after clinical and laboratory review
fields.essential: Sustained fever/rigors, shock, pain, dark urine or bleeding need haemolysis/bacterial review.

fields.label: Pulmonary assessment beyond timing
options: Pulmonary transfusion reaction not supported after assessment
fields.essential: Time alone never establishes TRALI or TACO; reconcile oxygenation, imaging and overload evidence.

fields.label: Current course after the first response
fields.essential: Repeat ABC and observations; improvement does not replace work-up or authorize a restart.

fields.label: If resumption is contemplated, is explicit local clearance documented?
options: Yes — accountable clearance and direct observation
No — clearance absent / serious cause open
fields.essential: Only explicit local clearance plus direct observation can support a contemplated resumption.

stages.title: Recognize and stop the implicated component
stages.empty: Establish whether there is a suspected acute reaction before assigning a benign explanation.

stages.title: Immediate safety and severity
stages.empty: Current ABC findings and the first-response checks remain separate from later classification.

stages.title: Pattern-directed work-up and treatment
stages.empty: Use the symptom pattern and investigations; timing alone does not diagnose a pulmonary reaction.

stages.title: Reassess before any future component decision
stages.empty: Improvement does not itself authorize resumption of an implicated transfusion.

quickReference.summary: Stop the component, assess ABC and identity, then use the evolving symptom pattern rather than a premature subtype label.
recognition: New fever, rigors, rash, pain, dark urine, dyspnoea, hypoxaemia, hypotension, bleeding, or anxiety during or after a component can be an acute reaction.
redFlags: Any airway, breathing or circulation compromise; severe dyspnoea/hypoxaemia; shock; new bleeding; dark urine/loin pain; sustained fever or rigors.
Suspected anaphylaxis, haemolysis, bacterial contamination, TRALI, TACO, or mixed pulmonary reaction: do not restart the implicated component.

steps.text: Stop the implicated component, maintain IV access with saline, check identity/label and inspect the component.
Treat current ABC compromise immediately; investigations must not delay severe-reaction care.
Use explicit local transfusion-service/clinical clearance and direct observation for any contemplated resumption.

monitoring: Repeat ABC and observations while symptoms evolve; reassess new fever, respiratory findings, pain, urine change, bleeding and haemodynamics.
Communicate urgency and clinical pattern to the transfusion service; retain implicated material through the local process.

guides.scope: Adult inpatient HF review: emergency routing, congestion/perfusion, source-labelled loop references, cautious nitrate consideration, and a handoff to existing GDMT/discharge workspaces. It uses AHA/ACC 2022 and ACC 2024 sources; ESC 2026 review is pending. It is not a diagnosis engine, medication order interface, dose calculator, or discharge authority.
reviewLimitations: The current 2026 ESC material defines HFrEF as LVEF <50%, while the legacy 2022 US workspace uses ≤40%. A dedicated ESC 2026 source mode remains review pending; this engine does not claim ESC 2026 implementation.
The engine intentionally retains the existing local HF dose, four-pillar readiness and cardiovascular discharge workspaces rather than duplicating their numeric catalogues or changing their behavior.

entry.title: Confirm HF presentation and current stability
entry.guidance: Emergency physiology overrides phase. Acute decongestion and chronic optimization use separate current findings; unknown never means safe or absent.
entry.scope: Entry, current danger and treatment response are separate findings. Unknown remains unconfirmed.

fields.label: Review lane
fields.essential: Emergency findings override the lane.

fields.label: Emergency finding now?
options: Present — shock, severe respiratory failure, ischemia, unstable rhythm, or mechanical concern
No immediate emergency finding after assessment
fields.threshold: Assess ABCs, perfusion, escalating support, ischemia, rhythm and mechanical concern.

fields.label: HF working route?
fields.threshold: This is a working route, not a diagnosis; reconcile current evidence and alternatives.

fields.label: Congestion now?
fields.threshold: Use symptoms, examination, weight/fluids and objective data in context.

fields.label: Perfusion now?
fields.threshold: Use BP with mentation, extremities, urine output, lactate and organ trajectory.

fields.label: Trigger review?
options: Identified and being managed in parallel
fields.threshold: Review ischemia, rhythm, BP, infection, medicines, renal change, PE and mechanical causes.

fields.label: Loop exposure?
options: Home drug, daily dose, route and last dose/time reconciled
Recent IV total dose, time and response window reconciled
fields.threshold: Never infer loop-naive status; reconcile agent, total dose, route, time, delivery and response.

fields.label: Loop safety?
fields.threshold: Review perfusion/BP, renal/electrolytes, dialysis, allergy, exposure/delivery and local protocol.

fields.label: Response to recent IV loop?
fields.threshold: Before another action, record symptoms, support, output, balance, weight, perfusion and renal/electrolytes.

fields.label: Hypertensive pulmonary-edema pattern?
options: Yes — reviewed hypertensive pulmonary-edema / afterload pattern
No — this pattern is not established
fields.threshold: Nitrates are not routine; review pattern, BP, perfusion and cause first.

fields.label: Nitrate safety?
options: No systemic hypotension or other entered contraindication after review
Hypotension / contraindication concern or review incomplete
fields.threshold: Confirm pressure/perfusion, contraindications, interactions and monitored local setup.

fields.label: Phenotype for legacy GDMT?
options: HFrEF explicitly confirmed by the treating team
Other phenotype or phenotype remains uncertain
fields.threshold: Use the documented phenotype and LVEF source/date; no cut-off is computed here.

fields.label: Stable GDMT window?
options: Active decompensation, hypotension/hypoperfusion, or other blocker remains
fields.threshold: The legacy workspace checks four pillars, exact drug/formulation, safety, tolerance and ownership.

fields.label: Transition plan?
options: Plan reconciled; remaining items have a named owner and review date
Residual congestion or unresolved transition gap
fields.threshold: Review congestion, oral plan, medicines, labs, education/access and named early follow-up.

stages.title: Emergency, syndrome & profile
stages.empty: Complete the current assessment.

stages.title: Emergency / low-perfusion escalation
stages.empty: Escalate urgent physiology before routine therapy.

stages.title: Congestion, exposure & response
stages.empty: Reconcile actual loop exposure and response.

stages.title: Stable HFrEF readiness
stages.empty: Complete the stable-window and phenotype review.

stages.title: Transition gaps & ownership
stages.empty: Complete the transition review.

quickReference.summary: Treat emergency physiology first. Review congestion and perfusion together, then reconcile actual loop exposure and response before a repeat or chronic-GDMT decision.
recognition: State the current review lane; acute treatment response and chronic optimization are separate states.
Confirm current congestion and perfusion; a prior HF label or stale medication list is not enough.
redFlags: Shock/hypoperfusion, altered mentation, severe respiratory failure or escalating support.
Ongoing ischemia, unstable arrhythmia, syncope, or acute valvular/mechanical concern.
Worsening after a recent loop, resistant congestion, or new renal/electrolyte concern.

steps.text: Escalate immediately; routine loop, nitrate, GDMT and discharge branches are withheld.
Require confirmed congestion, adequate perfusion, reconciled exposure and a safety review before a local loop plan.
Record symptoms, oxygen/support, urine output, balance, weight, BP/perfusion and renal/electrolytes before any repeat or intensification.
Use the existing four-pillar readiness workspace only after a compensated window is explicit.

monitoring: Trend current congestion, oxygen/support, BP/perfusion, urine output, balance, weight and kidney/electrolyte trajectory at a frequency matched to severity.
At transition, keep the oral plan, medication reconciliation, laboratory plan, education/access barriers and named early follow-up visible.

guides.title: Syncope
guides.reviewNotice: Focused adult event, risk and reassessment review.
guides.resourceNotice: Internal hospital resource tables are omitted from this shared edition.
guides.scope: Adult event recognition, initial risk assessment, directed testing and reassessment. Not a complete specialist syncope or automatic discharge protocol.
reviewLimitations: ESC 2018 official recommendation slides reviewed; ACC/AHA/HRS 2017 official summary used for routine-test cautions. No newer replacement found on the inspected society hubs.
No automatic risk-score calculation, device therapy or empirical syncope medication regimen.

sources.label: ESC 2018 Syncope — official guideline teaching slides
ACC/AHA/HRS 2017 Syncope — recommendations summary

entry.title: Was this syncope, and is there current danger?
entry.scope: Entry, current danger and treatment response are separate findings. Unknown remains unconfirmed.

fields.label: Was the event consistent with syncope?
options: Brief loss of consciousness; rapid, complete recovery
fields.threshold: Confirm rapid onset, short duration and spontaneous complete recovery. Ask witnesses; a fall or dizziness alone is not syncope.

fields.label: Current emergency features?
fields.threshold: Persistent altered consciousness, shock, ongoing chest pain/dyspnea, focal deficit, major bleeding or serious injury requires urgent assessment.

fields.label: History and examination complete?
fields.threshold: Review trigger, posture, prodrome, witness account, medications, cardiac/family history, injury and examination.

fields.label: Reviewed 12-lead ECG?
fields.threshold: Review ischemia, conduction block, bradycardia, ventricular arrhythmia, QT, Brugada pattern, pre-excitation and device function.

fields.label: Other high-risk features?
fields.threshold: Exertional/supine event, preceding palpitations, severe heart disease, unexplained SBP <90, bleeding or unexplained murmur. Review short/no prodrome and family sudden death in context.

fields.label: Supine and standing BP/HR review?
fields.threshold: When safe, measure supine and during 3 minutes standing. A fall ≥20 systolic or ≥10 diastolic, or SBP <90, with reproduced symptoms supports orthostatic syncope.

fields.label: Mechanism supported by the assessment?
fields.threshold: A typical trigger and prodrome support reflex syncope. Do not infer a benign cause from a negative test alone.

fields.label: Additional testing indication?
fields.threshold: Choose tests for the suspected cause. The linked source folders are not a routine syncope panel.

fields.label: Current course after evaluation / treatment?
options: Recovered; no recurrence or ongoing symptoms
fields.threshold: An earlier recovery or benign label cannot override the current course.

fields.label: Follow-up and safety plan established?
fields.threshold: Document reassessment, return precautions, injury risk and locally applicable driving/work advice. This is not an automatic discharge decision.

quickReference.summary: Confirm the event, assess danger and choose cause-directed evaluation.
recognition: Brief loss of consciousness with rapid onset and spontaneous complete recovery.
redFlags: Current instability, persistent altered consciousness, focal deficit, major bleeding or serious injury.
Exertional/supine events, concerning ECG or structural cardiac disease warrant prompt risk review.

steps.text: History, examination, ECG and safe orthostatic BP/HR; targeted tests only.
High risk needs prompt monitored evaluation. Unknown findings or recurrent symptoms do not establish low risk.

monitoring: Repeat current safety, symptoms and ECG as indicated; document rationale for disposition.

guides.scope: Adult pulse-tachycardia recognition, emergency electrical routing, selected stable-rhythm strategies and post-treatment response. Not automated ECG interpretation or device configuration.

entry.title: Confirm presentation and urgency
entry.scope: Unknown findings remain unconfirmed; assess immediate danger before selecting a treatment phase.

fields.label: Tachyarrhythmia established for this episode?
fields.threshold: Assess whether the rate fits the clinical condition. AHA notes tachyarrhythmia is typically ≥150/min; the number alone does not determine treatment.

fields.label: Current cardiopulmonary compromise?
fields.threshold: Assess hypotension, altered mental status, shock, ischemic chest discomfort or acute heart failure. Current compromise overrides a prior improvement.

fields.label: Current wide-complex morphology?
fields.threshold: Sustained polymorphic VT needs immediate unsynchronized shock, regardless of a reassuring stability selection.

fields.label: Pre-excited AF / accessory-pathway concern?
fields.threshold: Pre-excited AF: avoid adenosine, beta-blockers, diltiazem/verapamil, digoxin and IV amiodarone. Obtain urgent specialist rhythm review.

fields.label: Reversible causes reviewed?
fields.threshold: Review oxygenation, ischemia, electrolytes, medications/toxins and other acute illness in parallel.

fields.label: Recent rhythm-drug exposure?
options: Already given / timing or dose uncertain
fields.threshold: Reconcile actual doses and responses. Do not restart a loading sequence; use response review after treatment.

fields.label: Standard adenosine regimen suitable?
options: Peripheral IV; no asthma/bronchospasm or transplant concern
fields.threshold: Asthma/bronchospasm excludes routine adenosine. Central access or heart transplant can require a much lower dose; obtain expert review.

fields.label: Selected stable wide-complex strategy?
fields.threshold: Choose one expert-monitored strategy. Adenosine is only an option for a stable, regular, monomorphic rhythm; these are not combined loading instructions.

fields.label: Selected infusion safety reviewed?
fields.threshold: Procainamide: exclude prolonged QT and heart failure. Review QT, interactions, BP and delivery for amiodarone; no routine route for pre-excited AF.

fields.label: Observed response?
fields.threshold: Use current rhythm and perfusion above. An earlier conversion does not cancel a recurrence or current instability.

quickReference.summary: Identify the rhythm and its effect on perfusion before selecting a treatment.
recognition: Confirm pulse and ECG mechanism; assess clinical rate appropriateness.
redFlags: Sustained polymorphic VT: immediate unsynchronized shock.
Compromise caused by organized tachyarrhythmia: synchronized cardioversion; do not delay for drugs.
Pre-excited AF excludes routine AV-nodal drugs and IV amiodarone.

steps.text: Stable regular narrow rhythm: vagal maneuvers, then eligible adenosine. Stable regular monomorphic wide rhythm: expert-guided selection of one strategy.
Review current rhythm, perfusion and actual treatment; do not restart loading automatically.

monitoring: ECG, BP, oximetry, rhythm/perfusion response and reversible causes.
