entry.title: Select Initial assessment or After treatment
entry.scope: The phase is a review context, not a clinical normal finding. Initial severity/ECG/dialysis assessment and post-treatment insulin/response surveillance remain separate.

fields.label: Review phase
fields.essential: Select Initial assessment or After treatment. No phase is a clinical finding, and it does not expose either treatment branch.

fields.label: Airway, breathing, circulation or consciousness compromised?
fields.essential: Airway, breathing, circulation or consciousness compromise takes priority; do not wait to finish the assessment.

fields.label: Current credible potassium result (mmol/L)
fields.essential: K 5.5–5.9, 6.0–6.4 and ≥6.5 mmol/L are distinct reviewed bands. Unknown is not a non-hyperkalemic result.

fields.label: ECG changes attributed to hyperkalemia?
fields.essential: Attribute ECG changes clinically. A normal reviewed ECG does not reduce the urgency of severe hyperkalemia.

fields.label: Clinically unwell or a rapid potassium rise anticipated?
Does the patient receive maintenance hemodialysis?

stages.title: Assess & monitor
stages.empty: Review ECG, sample, trend and causes.

stages.title: Protect the heart
stages.empty: Review ECG to assess the need for IV calcium.

stages.title: Shift potassium
stages.empty: Select a credible K value to assess lowering therapy.

stages.title: Remove potassium
stages.empty: Review causes and kidney function; removal depends on severity.

stages.title: Reassess
stages.empty: Set the next K check from severity and treatment.

quickReference.summary: Prioritize clinical stability, potassium severity, ECG findings and dialysis context; treatment and reassessment run in parallel.
recognition: Review the potassium value, sample quality/hemolysis, renal function, acid-base state, glucose, medications, intake, and recent potassium trend.
Obtain or review an ECG promptly for clinically significant hyperkalemia; a reassuring ECG does not exclude risk.
Treat a dangerous presentation without waiting for a repeat result when the clinical picture and initial value are credible.
redFlags: Compromised airway, breathing, circulation or consciousness; K ≥6.5 mmol/L; hyperkalemic ECG changes; or rapidly rising potassium/clinical illness.
Maintenance hemodialysis with K ≥6.5 mmol/L, treatment-resistant hyperkalemia, or persistent/recurrent potassium elevation after treatment.
Unknown stability, potassium, ECG or hemodialysis status does not establish a lower-risk route.

steps.text: UKKA 16.2a suggests IV calcium for hyperkalemia with ECG changes (grade 2C, updated July 2026). Use calcium chloride in arrest/peri-arrest and calcium gluconate otherwise. Calcium protects the heart temporarily but does not lower potassium.

UKKA recommends insulin/glucose for K ≥6.5 mmol/L and suggests it for K 6.0–6.4 mmol/L. Salbutamol is an adjunct, not monotherapy for severe hyperkalemia. Baseline glucose and post-treatment glucose surveillance are essential.

UKKA recommends sodium zirconium cyclosilicate in severe hyperkalemia and suggests considering it in moderate hyperkalemia; patiromer is an option at K ≥6.0. Severe hyperkalemia in maintenance-hemodialysis patients requires urgent dialysis. Binders do not replace immediate stabilization. IV bicarbonate and calcium resonium are not routine acute treatments.

monitoring: UK Kidney Association suggests potassium checks at least 1, 2, 4, 6, and 24 hours after identifying and treating moderate or severe hyperkalemia.
After insulin/glucose, use timed glucose surveillance through 6 hours because delayed hypoglycemia can occur.
Document whether each intervention stabilizes, shifts, or removes potassium so temporary improvement is not mistaken for definitive control.

guides.scope: Adult inpatient diabetes hypoglycaemia; JBDS 01 <4.0 mmol/L pathway.
reviewLimitations: Uses JBDS 01’s below-4.0 mmol/L threshold, 10–15-minute oral/enteral recheck and 10-minute parenteral recheck; it does not mix ADA 70/54 mg/dL thresholds or a 15-minute-only rule.
Covers non-pregnant adults aged 16 years or older with diabetes in hospital, not pregnancy, paediatric-team care, or hypoglycaemia without diabetes.

Local products, concentrations, pump settings, nutrition plans, prescription authority and order-set reconciliation remain local-policy work. The general-admission glucometer resource is not a hypoglycaemia set and does not replace the JBDS timing.
The TPN option means oral intake is not permitted. Select “Oral permitted” if oral rescue is actually available; the engine otherwise asks for a parenteral route.
The 4.0–6.0 mmol/L band is individualised prevention guidance, not an automatic rescue regimen.

The rescue phase is an assessment state, not a medication-administration record, dose counter, timestamp, or authorization. Unknown phase, nutrition or safety keeps urgent clinician review explicit rather than assuming an initial or repeat dose.

entry.text: JBDS inpatient rescue threshold · glucose below 4.0 mmol/L (about 72 mg/dL).
entry.scope: Adults aged 16+ with diabetes; pregnancy and non-diabetic hypoglycaemia need a separate pathway.

fields.label: Rescue phase / current response?
fields.help: Glucose remains the current measured result. JBDS recovery wording requires glucose above 4.0 mmol/L and clinical recovery; do not select recovery while the current result is below 4.0 mmol/L or repeat an initial rescue while a recheck is still due.

fields.label: Nutrition route
options: Enteral feed route in use and usable

quickReference.summary: JBDS adult inpatient pathway: below 4.0 mmol/L is the treatment threshold. Choose a safe route, recheck to recovery, then prevent recurrence.
recognition: Treat any glucose below 4.0 mmol/L in this source population, with or without symptoms.
4.0–6.0 mmol/L is “looming” hypoglycaemia: review risk and individualise; it is not the same rescue threshold.
Check ABCDE and capillary glucose promptly; do not delay urgent treatment when a seizure or unsafe state prevents immediate measurement.
redFlags: Unconsciousness, seizure, very aggressive behaviour, unsafe swallow, or persistent altered consciousness.
Glucose still below 4.0 mmol/L after 30–45 minutes or 3 rescue cycles.
Severe or recurrent event, long-acting insulin or sulfonylurea exposure, renal impairment, interrupted nutrition, or prolonged fasting.

steps.text: ABCDE; stop an active insulin infusion during confirmed hypoglycaemia.
15–20 g rapid carbohydrate; recheck in 10–15 min; no more than 3 cycles.
IV: 20% glucose 100 mL or 10% glucose 200 mL over 15 min. No IV: glucagon 1 mg IM while obtaining access.
steps.dosingNote: Confirm local product, concentration and pump setting.

steps.text: When above 4.0 mmol/L and recovered: 20 g longer-acting carbohydrate; 40 g after glucagon. NPO requires a separate IV-glucose bridge plan.
Review active treatment, meals/feeds and illness. Do not automatically omit the next insulin dose; continue regular glucose monitoring 24–48 h.

monitoring: Oral, buccal or enteral rescue: recheck capillary glucose after 10–15 minutes; maximum 3 treatment cycles before escalation.
IV glucose or IM glucagon: recheck capillary glucose after 10 minutes.
After sulfonylurea or long-acting insulin, recurrence may persist 24–36 hours; this adds prolonged risk to the general 24–48-hour monitoring plan.

AAFP is a published clinical review rather than a local hospital protocol; DailyMed labels are U.S. product-specific prescribing information. Local formulation, availability, concentration, access, monitoring and authorization still govern care.
The engine never assigns an IV dose, total replacement deficit, infusion rate, line or automatic repeat dose. It deliberately excludes a routine high-rate ward regimen and never supports IV push.

entry.title: Measured K below 3.5 mmol/L
entry.scope: K at or below 2.5 mmol/L, ECG/rhythm abnormality, paralysis, respiratory failure, or severe weakness are urgent features. Unknown findings are not normal.

fields.label: Potassium · mmol/L
fields.help: Use the current measured potassium. ≤2.5 mmol/L is a severe feature. >2.5 to <3.5 covers every value between those boundaries; ≥3.5 does not trigger hypokalaemia replacement. Unknown is never treated as normal.
fields.essential: Hypokalaemia is measured potassium below 3.5 mmol/L. Potassium at or below 2.5 mmol/L is a severe biochemical feature; unknown is not normal.

fields.label: Urgent ECG / neuromuscular feature?
fields.help: Present/suspected means any ECG abnormality or arrhythmia, paralysis, respiratory failure, or severe weakness. Absent means these urgent features were actively assessed.
fields.essential: Danger: ECG/rhythm abnormality, paralysis, respiratory failure or severe weakness.

fields.label: Oral / GI route safe?
fields.help: Safe/functioning means a safe swallow, a functioning GI tract, and an appropriate available formulation. No includes unsafe swallowing, an unavailable route, or a nonfunctioning GI tract.
fields.essential: A safe oral route requires a safe swallow, functioning GI tract, and an appropriate available formulation.

fields.label: Reduced K clearance / risk?
fields.help: Risk present includes renal impairment, oliguria/anuria, or potassium-retaining treatment such as RAAS inhibition, potassium-sparing diuretics, or NSAIDs. No risk requires active review.

fields.label: Magnesium status?
fields.help: Unknown means magnesium has not been checked. Low captures a documented deficit; not low requires a reviewed result. This finding does not prescribe a magnesium dose or route.

fields.label: Most likely mechanism?
fields.help: Select only a reviewed mechanism: GI loss/poor intake, renal loss/diuretic exposure, or intracellular shift. Unclear means initial review has not established the cause and prompts clinician-owned work-up.

stages.title: Verify & triage
stages.empty: Confirm the potassium result and urgent features.

stages.title: Choose route
stages.empty: A safe route follows verified severity and findings.

stages.title: Safeguard replacement
stages.empty: Review renal clearance and IV controls.

stages.title: Correct contributors
stages.empty: Review magnesium and the mechanism.

stages.title: Recheck response
stages.empty: Set the next potassium and clinical review.

quickReference.summary: Confirm a true low potassium, identify urgent features, choose oral versus supervised IV replacement, correct contributors, and measure the response.
recognition: AAFP defines hypokalaemia as potassium below 3.5 mmol/L; confirm an unexpected result and review its trend.
Urgent features include potassium ≤2.5 mmol/L, ECG/rhythm abnormality, paralysis, respiratory failure, or severe weakness.
Obtain an ECG when hypokalaemia is identified, but an absent ECG change does not exclude clinically important depletion.
redFlags: Arrhythmia, ECG change, syncope/cardiac instability, paralysis, respiratory failure, or severe weakness.
Potassium ≤2.5 mmol/L, rapidly falling potassium, digoxin/cardiac disease context, or inability to take oral treatment.
Oliguria/severe renal impairment, potassium-retaining medicines, uncontrolled loss, hypomagnesaemia, DKA, refeeding, or uncertain route/monitoring context.

steps.text: Confirm the potassium result when appropriate, review trend and obtain ECG. Do not delay urgent clinical response for an arrhythmia, paralysis, respiratory failure or severe weakness.

With K >2.5 mmol/L, no severe features and a functioning safe GI route, oral potassium is preferred. The reviewed ER KCl label lists 40–100 mEq/day divided for treatment, with no more than 40 mEq in one dose.
steps.dosingNote: Product-specific detail: take ER tablets with meals and liquid; swallow whole. Verify the stocked product and renal plan.

steps.role: Use supervised IV only when indicated
steps.text: For severe features, K ≤2.5 mmol/L, or no safe oral route, use a clinician-directed IV pathway. AAFP describes 5–10 mEq IV KCl over 15–30 min with cardiac monitoring for severe symptoms; stable IV replacement is generally up to 10 mEq/hour peripherally.
steps.dosingNote: 20 mEq/hour is a monitored central-access exception in the AAFP review, not a routine ward regimen. Never IV push; verify local product, pump, concentration and line.

steps.text: Check magnesium, renal clearance, medications, ongoing GI/renal loss and transcellular-shift context. Correct documented deficits and causes through the appropriate local protocol.
Set the next potassium, ECG and clinical review with the selected route. AAFP describes 2–4-hour potassium checks during urgent severe-symptom IV treatment; use local timing for other situations.

monitoring: Use cardiac monitoring for severe symptoms and for IV potassium rates at or above 10 mEq/hour in the AAFP review; verify the local high-risk infusion policy.
Monitor potassium and adjust dosing with renal impairment, oliguria, RAAS inhibitors, NSAIDs, or other potassium-retention risk.
Record the actual product, concentration, line, infusion device, response result, ECG/rhythm and continuing losses. A product catalog does not establish a safe prescription.

reviewLimitations: The final KDIGO AKI guideline currently available is the 2012 guideline. The KDIGO 2027 AKI/AKD document released for public review in March 2026 is a public-review draft whose own cover says it may change and should not be used beyond its review purpose; it is recorded for currency status, not used for clinical branches.
NICE NG148 was last updated October 2024, with 2024 changes focused on iodinated-contrast risk assessment. It supplies current UK timing and referral recommendations used here.
This is not a numeric AKI-stage calculator, a complete differential diagnosis, a fluid-order protocol, a diuretic order, an RRT modality/order interface, or a safe acute drug-dose calculator.

A changing creatinine does not establish stable renal drug clearance. Medication choice, dose and monitoring require drug-specific acute guidance, pharmacist input and therapeutic levels where relevant.
Local product availability, ultrasound access, medical/surgical/urology pathways, goals-of-care discussions and clinician validation remain outside this prototype.

entry.title: Does this meet AKI criteria?
entry.guidance: Any one criterion establishes AKI. Missing baseline or timing stays unconfirmed.

fields.label: Creatinine rise in 48 hours
fields.threshold: At least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours
fields.definition: Serum creatinine rose by at least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours.

fields.label: Creatinine relative to baseline
fields.threshold: At least 1.5 times baseline within 7 days
fields.definition: Serum creatinine reached at least 1.5 times a known or presumed baseline within the prior 7 days.

fields.label: Urine output observation
fields.threshold: Below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours
fields.definition: Urine volume was below 0.5 mL/kg/h for a defined 6-hour observation window.

entry.text: Any one criterion establishes AKI. Missing baseline or timing stays unconfirmed.

fields.label: Creatinine rise in 48 hours
fields.threshold: At least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours
fields.definition: Serum creatinine rose by at least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours.
fields.help: Any one fully assessed criterion establishes AKI. Missing baseline, comparator timing, body weight, or a defined urine-output observation interval remains unconfirmed.

fields.label: Creatinine relative to baseline
fields.threshold: At least 1.5 times baseline within 7 days
fields.definition: Serum creatinine reached at least 1.5 times a known or presumed baseline within the prior 7 days.
fields.help: Any one fully assessed criterion establishes AKI. Missing baseline, comparator timing, body weight, or a defined urine-output observation interval remains unconfirmed.

fields.label: Urine output observation
fields.threshold: Below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours
fields.definition: Urine volume was below 0.5 mL/kg/h for a defined 6-hour observation window.
fields.help: Any one fully assessed criterion establishes AKI. Missing baseline, comparator timing, body weight, or a defined urine-output observation interval remains unconfirmed.

fields.label: Refractory life threat?
fields.help: For this field, a refractory life threat means hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, uraemic complications, fluid overload or pulmonary oedema that is not responding to medical management. It requires immediate escalation.
fields.essential: Refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis, uraemic complications, fluid overload, or pulmonary oedema despite medical management.

fields.label: Volume / perfusion picture?
fields.help: Choose this from the current physiology, not from AKI alone. The depletion option excludes haemorrhagic shock, which needs its own emergency haemorrhage pathway. Congestion does not make diuretics a treatment for AKI itself.

fields.label: Obstruction or cause concern?
fields.help: Suspected pyonephrosis means possible infected upper-tract obstruction and needs immediate action. In AKI, an unknown cause or obstruction risk calls for urinary-tract ultrasound within 24 hours; suspected pyonephrosis needs ultrasound within 6 hours.

fields.label: Nephrology referral feature?
fields.help: NICE advises nephrology discussion within 24 hours for possible specialist kidney disease (such as vasculitis, glomerulonephritis, tubulointerstitial nephritis or myeloma), no clear cause, inadequate response, AKI complications, stage 3 AKI, transplant, or CKD stage 4–5. A clear cause that responds promptly usually does not need routine referral, except in transplant recipients.
fields.essential: Stage 3, unclear or nonresponsive AKI, complications, suspected specialist kidney disease, transplant, or CKD stage 4–5.

fields.label: Medicine / contrast risk?
fields.help: Review potentially kidney-harmful or renally cleared medicines, interactions, therapeutic-drug monitoring needs and recent contrast. A changing creatinine does not prove stable drug clearance.

stages.title: Recognize
stages.empty: Verify the AKI data before assigning a stage.

stages.title: Treat life threats
stages.empty: No medical-refractory RRT trigger entered.

stages.title: Assess perfusion
stages.empty: AKI alone does not select a fluid maneuver.

stages.title: Look for cause
stages.empty: Continue cause-directed assessment.

stages.title: Monitor & refer
stages.empty: Set follow-up to the clinical trajectory.

quickReference.summary: Confirm actual creatinine/urine timing, treat complications first, choose fluid strategy from physiology, then find the cause and set monitoring/referral.
recognition: KDIGO AKI: creatinine rise ≥0.3 mg/dL in 48 h, ≥1.5× baseline within 7 days, or urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 h.
Use the worse creatinine or urine-output stage; do not invent a baseline or a urine-output window.
A changing creatinine is not a stable eGFR/CrCl drug-clearance estimate.
redFlags: Hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, pulmonary oedema/fluid overload or uraemic complication not responding to medical management.
Suspected infected obstruction/pyonephrosis, anuria, shock, rapidly worsening trajectory or impaired oxygenation.
Stage 3, transplant, CKD stage 4–5, unclear/nonresponsive AKI, complication or suspected specialist kidney disease.

steps.text: Confirm time-stamped creatinine and observed urine output; stage by the worse criterion.
Escalate refractory potassium, acid-base, uraemic or pulmonary-oedema/fluid-overload complications without waiting for a creatinine threshold.
Use isotonic crystalloid only for credible depletion and reassess response; avoid reflex fluid loading in congestion. Vasomotor shock requires a local fluids-plus-vasopressor plan.
Urinalysis promptly; ultrasound within 6 h for suspected pyonephrosis and within 24 h for unknown cause/obstruction risk. Review medicines and contrast urgency.
Set creatinine, electrolyte and urine-output timing; discuss qualifying AKI with nephrology within 24 h, or immediately for RRT indications.

monitoring: Monitor serum creatinine and a defined urine-output interval; daily creatinine is typical in hospital but frequency follows clinical need.
Trend potassium, acid-base status, volume balance, weight/congestion and response to each intervention.
After AKI, monitor creatinine based on stability and degree of recovery; NICE considers nephrology referral after recovery when eGFR is 30 mL/min/1.73 m² or less.

reviewLimitations: This is compact adult decision support, not a local electrolyte prescription, infusion-pump protocol, order set, diagnosis engine or patient-specific plan.

The Society acute guidance (2016) and its 2019 addendum govern the emergency wording; the 2025 ESE guideline is used only for established chronic hypoparathyroidism and explicitly excludes studies primarily selecting end-stage renal disease.

The 2019 addendum makes calcium salts non-volume-equivalent. This module exposes only calcium-gluconate source actions and never treats local calcium chloride as a gluconate equivalent or selects a chloride product.

The IV route is source detail, not an order. This aid never selects an infusion pump, line, dilution, volume, repeat dose, calcium-chloride conversion, local concentration or automatic replacement schedule.

End-stage renal failure/dialysis blocks the general large-volume infusion and chronic oral/active-vitamin-D resource links. Severe symptoms remain urgent and require renal/monitored-care decisions outside this engine.
A catalog product or local resource link establishes only product identity, not availability, suitability, dose, route safety, prescribing authorization or an approved local regimen.

entry.title: Calcium below the local reference range; adjusted Ca <1.9 mmol/L is severe.
entry.scope: Ionised calcium can establish a low result; do not assign an unadjusted total value to an adjusted-calcium treatment band.

fields.label: Verified calcium status?
fields.help: The Society acute threshold uses albumin-adjusted calcium. Ionised calcium can confirm hypocalcaemia, but an unadjusted total-calcium value is not assigned a treatment band here.
fields.essential: Calcium below the local reference range; adjusted Ca <1.9 mmol/L is severe.

fields.label: Symptoms / ECG feature?
fields.help: Emergency features include seizure, laryngospasm, prolonged QT or arrhythmia. Other symptoms include tetany, carpopedal spasm and paraesthesia. “None” requires active assessment.
fields.essential: Emergency features: seizure, laryngospasm, prolonged QT or arrhythmia. “None” requires active assessment.

fields.label: IV calcium treatment phase?
fields.help: Choose a documented phase. “Resolved” means symptoms improved after IV calcium; it does not establish normocalcaemia or a completed cause-treatment plan.

fields.label: Oral route safe?
fields.help: Safe requires an appropriate swallow, GI absorption and an available formulation. An unsafe or unknown route is not converted into an automatic IV-calcium indication for otherwise mild asymptomatic hypocalcaemia.

fields.label: Renal / dialysis status?
fields.help: Dialysis includes end-stage kidney failure on dialysis. It blocks this guide’s large-volume infusion and chronic oral/active-vitamin-D resource links; it does not make severe symptoms benign.

fields.label: Magnesium status?
fields.help: Low magnesium can impair PTH secretion and action. Correcting a documented deficit is part of cause treatment, but must not delay urgent calcium rescue for a severe symptomatic presentation.

fields.label: Likely cause context?
fields.help: Use a reviewed context, not a diagnosis made by this aid. The source work-up includes phosphate, PTH, vitamin D, magnesium and kidney function alongside calcium and albumin/ionised calcium.

stages.title: Verify & triage
stages.empty: Confirm calcium physiology and urgent features.

stages.title: Choose calcium route
stages.empty: Select a route only from established severity and phase.

stages.title: Protect IV / renal care
stages.empty: Verify the line, monitoring and renal context.

stages.title: Correct cause & cofactors
stages.empty: Review magnesium, PTH, vitamin D and cause.

stages.title: Reassess response
stages.empty: Record symptoms, calcium and the follow-up plan.

quickReference.summary: Verify calcium physiology, triage symptoms and ECG, distinguish monitored IV rescue from mild oral review, then correct the cause and measure the response.
recognition: Society guidance defines severe hypocalcaemia as adjusted calcium <1.9 mmol/L and/or symptoms at any low calcium value. Symptoms may be rate-dependent, so a number alone does not prove safety.
Urgent features include seizure, laryngospasm, tetany/carpopedal spasm, prolonged QT and arrhythmia. Assess airway, neurologic state and ECG while confirming calcium physiology.
Initial cause work-up includes adjusted or ionised calcium context, phosphate, PTH, kidney function, vitamin D and magnesium.
redFlags: Adjusted calcium <1.9 mmol/L, seizure, laryngospasm, tetany, prolonged QT, arrhythmia, or a rapidly deteriorating clinical state.
Current or recent IV calcium with missing calcium trend, treatment phase, elemental-calcium amount, ECG result, line details or response.

Dialysis/end-stage kidney failure, renal impairment, hypomagnesaemia, hyperphosphataemia, post-neck surgery, low/inappropriately normal PTH, vitamin-D deficiency, pancreatitis, rhabdomyolysis or large-volume transfusion.

steps.text: Use albumin-adjusted or ionised calcium and assess seizure, airway, tetany and QT/rhythm features. Do not let cause work-up delay emergency assessment.
Society guidance uses 10–20 mL 10% calcium gluconate in 50–100 mL 5% dextrose IV over 10 minutes with ECG monitoring, repeated only under reassessment until asymptomatic.
steps.dosingNote: Source reminder only: confirm the actual gluconate product, elemental calcium, dilution, line, pump, renal status and local authority.

steps.text: The Society mild branch uses oral calcium when adjusted calcium is above 1.9 mmol/L and symptoms are absent. For established chronic HypoPT, ESE advises adequate elemental calcium intake and splitting supplemental elemental calcium above 500 mg/day.
steps.dosingNote: Do not convert source elemental-calcium guidance into a local tablet count without product and renal review.

steps.text: Use secure-line, dilution and ECG safeguards for IV calcium. Do not mix calcium gluconate with bicarbonate- or phosphate-containing fluids. Dialysis blocks the generic large-volume infusion branch.
Check and correct magnesium, clarify PTH/vitamin-D/acute-process causes, and document serial calcium, symptoms, ECG and renal context. Symptom improvement does not prove normocalcaemia.

monitoring: During intermittent calcium-gluconate infusion, the May 2026 label measures serum calcium every 4–6 hours; during continuous infusion, every 1–4 hours. These are source points, not auto-scheduled observations.
Use ECG monitoring during emergency IV calcium; continuous ECG monitoring is specifically called for with arrhythmia or digoxin context in the Society guidance.

For established chronic HypoPT after a treatment change, the 2025 ESE guideline recommends biochemical reassessment every 1–2 weeks, then regular calcium/phosphate/magnesium/creatinine review when stable. Dialysis needs its own renal plan.

guides.title: Acute Hypotension
guides.reviewLabel: Upgraded · shock entry and reassessment review
guides.guideVersion: ESICM circulatory shock and haemodynamic monitoring guideline (2025), NICE CG174/NG253, SSC 2026, ESC ACS 2023, and RCUK special-circumstances guidance (2025), as recorded in the prototype review
guides.resourceNotice: Internal hospital resource tables are omitted from this shared edition.
guides.scope: Adult acute hypotension and suspected circulatory shock: entry, escalation, mechanism routing and response reassessment.
reviewLimitations: This is not a shock diagnosis, a blood-pressure calculator, a complete trauma/haemorrhage/cardiogenic-shock protocol, a fluid or vasopressor order, or a substitute for critical-care, procedural or specialty escalation.
Shock may occur without hypotension. Conversely, low BP alone does not establish hypoperfusion, fluid responsiveness or a safe fluid/pressor treatment path.

NICE NG253 (2025) uses reassessed 250 mL sepsis boluses, while SSC 2026 suggests at least 30 mL/kg in 3 hours for sepsis-induced hypoperfusion or septic shock. The engine deliberately delegates this choice to the dedicated sepsis pathway and never combines the standards.

The NICE CG174 500 mL crystalloid criterion is limited here to credible non-haemorrhagic hypovolaemia with current hypoperfusion and no high/unknown fluid-harm concern; it never authorizes automatic repeats.

Norepinephrine is referenced only as a septic-shock critical-care handoff. Concentration, access, duration, monitoring, titration, add-on agents and patient-specific MAP target require the local protocol and clinician assessment.

Local shock rows, catalog identity, product availability, major-haemorrhage process, pressor safety, antimicrobial selection, anaphylaxis dosing and ACS treatment remain separately reviewed local work.

NICE CG174 intravenous fluid therapy in adults
NICE NG253 suspected sepsis in adults (2025)
Surviving Sepsis Campaign adult guideline (2026)
ESC acute coronary syndromes guideline (2023)
Resuscitation Council UK special circumstances guidance (2025)

entry.title: Assess low BP and tissue perfusion separately.
entry.scope: Shock can occur without hypotension. Emergency assessment and cause-directed care proceed in parallel.

fields.label: Current circulation finding?
fields.help: Low BP: MAP <65 mmHg, SBP <90 mmHg or a major fall from baseline. Perfusion: mentation, capillary refill/skin, urine output and lactate in context. Shock is acute circulatory failure with hypoperfusion and can occur without low BP. Record the current assessed state, not a presumed diagnosis.
fields.essential: Low BP: MAP <65 mmHg, SBP <90 mmHg or a major baseline fall. Perfusion: mentation, capillary refill/skin, urine output and lactate in context.

fields.label: Immediate emergency priority?
fields.help: This priority is independent of the BP/perfusion answer. An emergency feature requires immediate ABCDE support and escalation even when the circulation entry is incomplete or appears improved.
fields.essential: Emergency: ABC compromise, altered consciousness, rapid deterioration or peri-arrest.

fields.label: Likely primary mechanism?
fields.help: Use haemorrhagic for active significant bleeding; hypovolaemic means non-haemorrhagic fluid loss. These choices name the physiology being acted on. Mixed or unclear shock stays unclassified and needs bedside echo/POCUS, ECG and cause review before a mechanism-specific fluid or pressor action.

fields.label: Fluid harm / overload concern?
fields.help: This is not a fluid-responsiveness test. Look for current congestion and fluid-harm risk; use dynamic response assessment and serial lung/perfusion review before any additional fluid.

fields.label: Current resuscitation phase?
fields.help: This is an assessment state, not a medication record. “Reassessment” and “refractory” do not authorize another bolus or a pressor dose; establish what was given, the response, and the cause.

fields.label: Time-critical cause cue?
fields.help: A cause cue routes urgent work in parallel. It does not prove the mechanism or import a routine fluid, pressor, antimicrobial, antithrombotic or anaphylaxis regimen into this guide.

stages.title: Reassess perfusion and route the cause

quickReference.summary: Separate low BP from hypoperfusion, escalate emergency features independently, classify physiology, and reassess response before any further fluid or pressor change.
recognition: Shock is acute circulatory failure with hypoperfusion; hypotension is common but is not required.
Low BP alone needs a credible repeat, baseline and tissue-perfusion assessment before it triggers a shock regimen.
Track mentation, capillary refill/skin perfusion, urine output, lactate/acid-base context and trajectory alongside BP/MAP.
redFlags: Airway/breathing compromise, altered consciousness, rapidly worsening trajectory or peri-arrest features.
Low BP plus hypoperfusion, or hypoperfusion despite apparently preserved BP.
Active major bleeding, suspected tamponade/tension pneumothorax/high-risk PE, cardiogenic congestion, or refractory hypoperfusion after initial response-guided treatment.

steps.text: Enter the current BP/perfusion state visibly. Unknown is not normal, and hypoperfusion can establish acute circulatory failure without hypotension.
Treat emergency ABCDE features independently of the circulation finding; call for urgent senior/critical-care help when perfusion persists or deteriorates.
Differentiate hypovolaemic, distributive, cardiogenic, obstructive and haemorrhagic physiology with bedside echo/POCUS, ECG, examination and targeted work-up.
For credible non-haemorrhagic hypovolaemia with low fluid-harm risk, NICE CG174 uses one 500 mL crystalloid bolus over less than 15 minutes. Reassess before any further fluid.
steps.dosingNote: Sepsis fluid standards are delegated to the dedicated sepsis pathway; do not combine them.

steps.text: Send suspected sepsis, ACS, anaphylaxis, bleeding or obstruction to its emergency pathway. Persistent shock needs critical-care review rather than an improvised pressor regimen.

monitoring: After every material intervention, trend BP/MAP, mentation, capillary refill/skin, urine output, lungs/oxygenation and lactate/acid-base context.
Use dynamic fluid-responsiveness assessment and serial echo where available; do not infer response from a single BP value.
For refractory shock or vasopressor use, escalate haemodynamic monitoring and cause control with critical care.

guides.title: New Inpatient Fever
guides.guideVersion: SCCM/IDSA new fever guideline (2023; adult ICU), NICE CG151, CDC/NIOSH heat guidance, CMAJ serotonin-toxicity review, and DailyMed acetaminophen label, as recorded in the prototype review
guides.resourceNotice: Internal hospital resource tables are omitted from this shared edition.
guides.scope: Adult ICU fever evaluation; special-risk routes are separately source-scoped.
reviewLimitations: SCCM/IDSA directly covers new fever after ICU admission in adult ICU patients without severe immunocompromise. It does not create a general-ward fever bundle, and its recommendations are largely weak or best-practice statements.

The engine deliberately separates SCCM/IDSA’s single 38.3°C ICU definition from the 38.0°C sustained-for-one-hour chemotherapy-neutropenia definition cited in its text. Neither a lower temperature nor an unverified temperature rules out infection or deterioration.

NICE CG151 is an official but older 2012 anticancer-treatment guideline; its 2019 surveillance decision found no evidence requiring an update. It supplies the emergency neutropenic-sepsis route, not a local antimicrobial regimen, dose, or Taiwan formulary recommendation.

The heat branch uses CDC/NIOSH heat-exposure guidance for emergency recognition/cooling only. A separate focused CMAJ serotonin-toxicity review supports recognition-only escalation for drug/toxin concern; neither branch diagnoses a toxic syndrome or provides syndrome-specific treatment.

The conditional IV acetaminophen amounts come from a 2025 DailyMed injection label. They are not a reconciled local regimen or automatic local-vial selection; verify product compatibility, weight, route, all-source exposure, organ/volume risk, allergy, local policy and prescribing authority.

Resource groups are inspectable source references, not proposed orders. The complete local folders remain visible separately; source-row presence, catalog identity, regimen alignment and live orderability are distinct statuses.

The existing fever-episode tracker is a durable local documentation loop. This data engine neither opens an episode nor writes a culture, medication, source-control, precaution, chart, or order state.

entry.title: Adult inpatient fever review · ICU reference threshold ≥38.3°C.
entry.scope: ICU-specific testing is labelled and gated to that setting. Lower or unverified temperature does not exclude infection or deterioration.

fields.label: Temperature evidence
fields.help: SCCM/IDSA uses one measured temperature of 38.3°C or higher for its adult ICU fever definition. It prefers central measurement when accuracy is critical; otherwise oral or rectal over axillary, tympanic, or temporal measurement. The 38.0 to <38.3°C sustained-for-one-hour option is the chemotherapy-neutropenia definition cited in that guideline, not its general ICU threshold.

fields.label: Care setting
fields.help: The SCCM/IDSA fever recommendations directly cover adults with new fever after ICU admission, without severe immunocompromise. “Other inpatient area” keeps ICU-specific tests from becoming a ward default.

fields.label: Acute deterioration?
options: Yes — instability, organ or mental change
fields.essential: New instability, respiratory compromise, altered consciousness or organ dysfunction takes priority over the temperature.

fields.label: Anticancer / severe immune risk?
options: Current/recent anticancer therapy or known neutropenia
fields.help: This is a special-population screen, not a diagnosis. NICE says to suspect neutropenic sepsis when a person having anticancer treatment becomes unwell; WBC alone is not a measured ANC. SCCM/IDSA does not directly address transplant or other severe immunocompromise.

fields.label: Heat-hyperthermia emergency?
options: No heat/exertion or drug/toxin emergency — reviewed
Heat/exertion + marked heat or CNS change
Drug/toxin + rigidity, clonus, autonomic or mental change
fields.help: This is an emergency-recognition screen. It does not diagnose serotonin syndrome, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, malignant hyperthermia, or another toxic syndrome, and it does not choose a syndrome-specific regimen.

fields.label: Context after bedside assessment
options: No focus after history and exam
Line, device, wound, or recent surgery
fields.help: Choose the clinical context, not a test bundle. SCCM/IDSA says history and examination should focus subsequent diagnostics; an immediately postoperative, clearly noninfectious temperature may not need an infection investigation.

fields.label: Episode phase
fields.help: This describes the documented clinical trajectory. It is not a culture result, medication-administration record, or authorization to change therapy.

fields.label: Comfort medication status
options: Comfort requested; weight, route, exposure and risk checked
Comfort requested; exposure or risk unresolved
fields.help: “Ready” requires a documented indication, the route and current weight, all oral/IV/rectal and combination-product acetaminophen exposure in the last 24 hours, and liver, renal, volume, and allergy review. It does not select a local product or order.

quickReference.summary: Confirm measured temperature, exclude deterioration/special immune risk/hyperthermia emergency, then target the evaluation and record reassessment.
recognition: SCCM/IDSA defines adult ICU fever as one measured temperature of 38.3°C or higher; central measurement is preferred when accuracy is critical, otherwise oral or rectal is preferred over peripheral routes.
A 38.0 to <38.3°C temperature sustained for at least 1 hour is the chemotherapy-neutropenia definition cited by SCCM/IDSA, not its general ICU threshold.
A lower or unverified temperature does not exclude infection, acute deterioration, or an anticancer-treatment emergency.
redFlags: Any acute instability, new organ dysfunction, hypoxemia, altered mental status, or other deterioration.
A person having anticancer treatment who becomes unwell: suspect neutropenic sepsis and use the emergency oncology/antimicrobial pathway.
Heat/exertion with very high temperature and CNS change, or drug/toxin exposure with rigidity, clonus, autonomic, or mental-status change: urgent emergency assessment.

steps.text: Document temperature value, route, time and peak. Use a more reliable route when the measurement changes management.
Deterioration, hyperthermia concern, severe immune risk, and possible neutropenic sepsis override a stable fever workup.
Use history, examination and focus to choose imaging/specimens. Do not reflexively order urine, sputum, line, stool, viral, or broad imaging panels.
For ICU comfort treatment only after safety review: conditional IV acetaminophen reference is ≥50 kg 1,000 mg q6h or 650 mg q4h; <50 kg 15 mg/kg q6h or 12.5 mg/kg q4h.
steps.dosingNote: All routes/products: max 4,000 mg/24 h at ≥50 kg; otherwise 75 mg/kg/24 h (max 3,750 mg). Check hepatic, renal, volume and allergy risks; local product/policy still govern.

steps.text: Record trajectory, working source, pending results, response, escalation triggers and an explicit next review; a lower temperature alone does not close an episode.

monitoring: Trend temperature with the same documented route/method when feasible; record antipyretic time and every route/product in the daily exposure total.
Set a patient- and setting-specific reassessment interval. The reviewed ICU source does not provide one universal schedule.
For persistent/recurrent fever, re-evaluate focused findings, results, noninfectious causes and escalation need before repeating broad tests or changing treatment.
